column4:
3 hrs  \(\cdot\) asked in 19 of 24 papers  \(\cdot\) 3 syllabus sub-topics  \(\cdot\) core foundational chapter \(\rightarrow\) qualitative comparisons, equivalent circuits, frequency tables, and system protocols.
READ THIS FIRST
This chapter provides guaranteed theory marks in almost every paper (typically 8–14 marks). The examiner repeatedly asks three core questions:
  1. Conventional low frequency vs RF/microwave circuit behavior (asked in 18 papers) \(\rightarrow\) contrast lumped vs distributed analysis (\(d \ll \lambda\) vs \(d \gtrsim 0.01\lambda\)), breakdown of Kirchhoff's laws, skin effect, and equivalent circuit parasitics of \(R\), \(L\), \(C\).
  2. Detailed real-world protocols and specifications of microwave communication systems (asked in 11 papers) \(\rightarrow\) prepare full parametric tables for GSM 900/1800, Satellite C/Ku-band, Terrestrial Microwave link, and WiFi 802.11.
  3. IEEE microwave frequency band classification (asked in 7 papers) \(\rightarrow\) memorise the letter-code frequency boundaries (L, S, C, X, Ku, K, Ka, mmWave) and their primary application.

column1: How is microwave frequency band classified by IEEE? Enumerate features, advantages and disadvantages of microwaves
column4:
Microwave definition and spectrum
  • Frequency range: \(300\text{ MHz}\) to \(300\text{ GHz}\).
  • Wavelength range: \(\lambda = c/f = 1\text{ m}\) down to \(1\text{ mm}\) (free space).
  • Millimeter waves (mmWave): \(30\text{ GHz}\) to \(300\text{ GHz}\) (\(\lambda = 10\text{ mm}\) to \(1\text{ mm}\)).
  • Sub-millimeter / Terahertz: \(300\text{ GHz}\) to \(3\text{ THz}\) (\(\lambda < 1\text{ mm}\)).
Wavelength in metres: microwaves span \(1\) m to \(1\) mm, between VHF/FM and far infrared. Pozar Fig 1.1, bar only: its band list uses older letter-band edges, so quote the IEEE table below.

Advantages of microwaves
  • High bandwidth:
    • Bandwidth is \(1\text{--}10\%\) of carrier frequency.
    • Carrier at \(10\text{ GHz}\) offers \(1\text{ GHz}\) bandwidth \(\rightarrow\) accommodates thousands of high-speed data channels.
  • High directivity and gain:
    • Antenna gain \(G \propto (D/\lambda)^2\).
    • Small physical antenna diameter \(D\) produces sharp, pencil-beam radiation \(\rightarrow\) high EIRP, low interference.
  • Compact physical size:
    • Component dimensions scale with \(\lambda\) (\(\lambda/2, \lambda/4\)).
    • RF circuits fit on compact MMICs and microstrip boards.
  • Ionospheric transparency:
    • Waves above \(100\text{ MHz}\) penetrate ionosphere without total reflection \(\rightarrow\) enables satellite and space communication.
  • Dielectric (dipolar) heating:
    • Polar water molecules follow the alternating field, and the friction of that rotation heats the material \(\rightarrow\) cooking, industrial drying, vulcanisation.
    • verified/added Not a “resonance of water”: that is a Debye relaxation peaking near \(20\text{ GHz}\). \(2.45\text{ GHz}\) is an ISM band whose absorption is weak enough to penetrate centimetres — a true resonance would cook only the surface.
Disadvantages of microwaves
  • Atmospheric attenuation:
    • Rain fade and gaseous absorption (\(\text{H}_2\text{O}\) at \(22.2\text{ GHz}\), \(\text{O}_2\) at \(60\text{ GHz}\)) degrade signals over long paths.
  • Line of sight (LOS) required:
    • Cannot bend around obstacles (diffraction is minimal); shadows and terrain block transmission.
  • High manufacturing cost:
    • Tight mechanical tolerances (\(<\mu\text{m}\)); requires GaAs, InP, or GaN instead of cheap silicon.
  • Complex circuit analysis:
    • Lumped analysis fails; distributed transmission lines, scattering parameters, and electromagnetic field equations required.

column1: Compare the behavior of microwave circuits against conventional low frequency circuits. Differentiate lumped vs distributed analysis
column4:
The fundamental governing criterion: \(\boldsymbol{d/\lambda}\)
  • Let \(d =\) maximum physical dimension of the circuit.
  • Let \(\lambda = c/f =\) operating wavelength.
  • Low frequency (\(d \ll \lambda\), typically \(d < 0.01\lambda\)):
    • Propagation time of EM wave across the circuit is negligible compared to wave period \(T = 1/f\).
    • Phase change across any conductor: \(\Delta\theta = \beta d = \frac{2\pi d}{\lambda} \approx 0\).
    • Voltage is instantaneous and uniform along an ideal node.
    • Kirchhoff's Laws (KVL, KCL) hold strictly.
  • RF / Microwave (\(d \gtrsim 0.01\lambda\) to \(d \approx \lambda\)):
    • Propagation delay cannot be ignored; wave travel causes finite phase shift along conductors.
    • Voltage and current become functions of both position \(z\) and time \(t\): \(v(z,t), i(z,t)\).
    • Reflections arise at every impedance discontinuity.
    • Wires exhibit distributed inductance and capacitance; open lines radiate energy like antennas.
    • Distributed transmission line theory and Maxwell's equations replace KVL/KCL.

column1: Why are S-parameters used in microwave network analysis instead of Z, Y, or h-parameters?
column4:
Limitations of H, Z, Y parameters at microwave bands
  • Requires open and short circuits:
    • \(Z\)-parameters require open circuits (\(I = 0\)): \(Z_{11} = V_1/I_1 |_{I_2=0}\).
    • \(Y\)-parameters require short circuits (\(V = 0\)): \(Y_{11} = I_1/V_1 |_{V_2=0}\).
    • \(h\)-parameters require both short and open circuits.
  • Ideal opens and shorts are physically impossible:
    • An open-circuited line at microwave frequencies radiates energy like an open-ended antenna \(\rightarrow\) radiation loss causes \(I \neq 0\).
    • Stray fringe capacitance exists at open ends.
    • A short circuit has finite lead inductance (\(L_{\text{lead}} > 0\)) \(\rightarrow \omega L \gg 0\), not a true short (\(V \neq 0\)).
  • Active device instability:
    • Transistors (MESFETs, BJTs) frequently become conditionally unstable and oscillate violently under pure open/short terminations.
  • Direct voltage/current measurement impossible:
    • Probes perturb fields; standing waves make \(V\) and \(I\) position-dependent.
Why S-parameters succeed
  • Terminated in matched characteristic impedance \(Z_0\):
    • S-parameter measurement terminates ports in matched loads (\(Z_L = Z_0 = 50\,\Omega\)).
    • Matched load absorbs all incident energy \(\rightarrow\) zero reflection (\(a_2 = 0\)).
    • Precision \(50\,\Omega\) broadband loads are easy to manufacture.
  • No parasitic radiation or lead reactance:
    • Complete absorption eliminates open-circuit radiation and short-circuit inductive ringing.
  • Active devices remain stable:
    • Resistive \(50\,\Omega\) loading prevents self-oscillation of active transistors during testing.
  • Based on traveling power waves:
    • Relies on incident wave \(a\) and reflected wave \(b\): \[ a = \frac{V + Z_0 I}{2\sqrt{Z_0}}, \quad b = \frac{V - Z_0 I}{2\sqrt{Z_0}} \]
    • Directly measurable using directional couplers and Vector Network Analyzers (VNA).

column1: Explain the characteristic behavior of passive components (resistor, inductor, capacitor) at RF/microwave frequencies
column4:
1. Resistors at RF/Microwave
  • Parasitic effects:
    • Lead inductance \(L\): metal leads introduce serial inductance (\(L \approx 1\text{--}5\text{ nH}\)).
    • Stray capacitance \(C_a\): capacitive coupling between resistor terminals.
    • Skin effect: current concentrates in outer conductor layer (\(\delta = 1/\sqrt{\pi f \mu \sigma}\)) \(\rightarrow\) cross-sectional area decreases \(\rightarrow\) AC resistance increases: \(R_{ac} \propto \sqrt{f}\).
  • Equivalent circuit:
    • Resistor \(R\) in series with lead inductance \(L\), shunted by terminal capacitance \(C_a\).
    • At low freq: \(Z \approx R\).
    • At medium freq: \(L\) causes inductive impedance rise.
    • At high freq: shunt \(C_a\) bypasses \(R\), causing impedance to drop.
Resistor equivalent model
Equivalent circuit: ideal \(R\) with series lead \(L\) and parallel parasitic \(C_a\).
2. Inductors at RF/Microwave
  • Parasitic effects:
    • Winding resistance \(R_s\): coil wire resistance, increased by skin and proximity effects (\(R_{ac} \propto \sqrt{f}\)).
    • Inter-turn capacitance \(C_d\): electric field lines between adjacent coil turns create distributed parallel capacitance.
  • Self-Resonant Frequency (SRF), \(f_{SR}\): \[ f_{SR} = \frac{1}{2\pi \sqrt{L C_d}} \]
  • Behavioral regions:
    • \(f < f_{SR}\): inductive reactance dominates (\(\omega L > 1/\omega C_d\)); \(X_L\) increases with \(f\).
    • \(f = f_{SR}\): parallel resonance \(\rightarrow\) impedance peaks to a very large purely resistive value; quality factor \(Q \rightarrow 0\).
    • \(\boldsymbol{f > f_{SR}}\): Inductor acts as a capacitor! Inter-turn capacitance bypasses the coil (\(\omega C_d > 1/\omega L\)).
Inductor equivalent model
Inductor equivalent circuit: inductance \(L\) with series loss \(R_s\) shunted by distributed winding capacitance \(C_d\).
3. Capacitors at RF/Microwave
  • Parasitic effects:
    • Lead inductance \(L_s\) (ESL): connecting leads and plates introduce series inductance (\(L_s \approx 1\text{--}2\text{ nH}\)).
    • Dielectric loss \(R_p\): leakage resistance across dielectric (\(\tan\delta = \epsilon''/\epsilon'\)).
    • Equivalent series resistance \(R_s\) (ESR): resistance of plates and leads.
  • Series Self-Resonant Frequency, \(f_{SR}\): \[ f_{SR} = \frac{1}{2\pi \sqrt{L_s C}} \]
  • Behavioral regions:
    • \(f < f_{SR}\): capacitive reactance dominates (\(1/\omega C > \omega L_s\)); impedance drops with \(f\).
    • \(f = f_{SR}\): series resonance \(\rightarrow\) impedance reaches a minimum equal to ESR (\(R_s\)); optimal for bypass/decoupling.
    • \(\boldsymbol{f > f_{SR}}\): Capacitor acts as an inductor! ESL dominates (\(\omega L_s > 1/\omega C\)); impedance rises with \(f\).
Capacitor equivalent model
Capacitor equivalent circuit: ideal \(C\) with series lead inductance \(L_s\), series resistance \(R_s\), and dielectric leakage \(R_p\).

column1: Compare and contrast microwave signals with acoustic and seismic waves
column4:
Physical wave nature
  • Microwave signals:
    • Electromagnetic transverse waves (\(\vec{E} \perp \vec{H} \perp \vec{k}\)).
    • Propagates in vacuum (no medium required).
    • Propagation speed: \(c \approx 3 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}\).
    • Frequencies: \(300\text{ MHz}\) to \(300\text{ GHz}\); wavelengths: \(1\text{ m}\) to \(1\text{ mm}\).
  • Acoustic (sound) waves:
    • Mechanical longitudinal pressure waves (compression / rarefaction).
    • Requires material medium (gas, liquid, solid); zero propagation in vacuum.
    • Speed: \(\sim 343\text{ m/s}\) in air, \(\sim 1500\text{ m/s}\) in water.
    • Frequencies: \(20\text{ Hz}\) to \(20\text{ kHz}\) (ultrasound \(> 20\text{ kHz}\)).
  • Seismic waves:
    • Mechanical waves traveling through Earth's geological strata.
    • Body waves (\(P\)-waves longitudinal, \(S\)-waves transverse shear) + Surface waves (Rayleigh, Love).
    • Speed: \(2\text{--}8\text{ km/s}\) depending on rock density.
    • Infrasonic frequencies: \(0.01\text{ Hz}\) to \(50\text{ Hz}\).

column1: Prepare the detail real-world protocols and specifications of any 3 (or 5) major microwave communication systems
column4:
General microwave communication system architecture
  • Transmitter (Tx): Baseband source \(\rightarrow\) Modulator (QPSK/QAM) \(\rightarrow\) Up-converter (Mixer \(+\) Local Oscillator) \(\rightarrow\) Bandpass Filter \(\rightarrow\) High Power Amplifier (HPA: TWT or GaN SSPA) \(\rightarrow\) Duplexer/Circulator \(\rightarrow\) Directional Antenna.
  • Channel: Free space line-of-sight (LOS) path with atmospheric attenuation and multipath fading.
  • Receiver (Rx): Directive Antenna \(\rightarrow\) Duplexer \(\rightarrow\) Low Noise Amplifier (LNA) \(\rightarrow\) Down-converter (Mixer \(+\) LO) \(\rightarrow\) IF Filter / Amplifier \(\rightarrow\) Demodulator \(\rightarrow\) Baseband output.
Major application areas
  • Telecommunications: Cellular BTS, satellite, microwave LOS trunk radio.
  • Radar & Navigation: Air traffic control (ASR), weather radar, GPS/GLONASS.
  • Industrial & Domestic: Microwave ovens (\(2.45\text{ GHz}\)), rubber vulcanization, food drying.
  • Medical: Hyperthermia cancer treatment, microwave diathermy, tomography.
  • Scientific: Radio astronomy, remote sensing, atmospheric sounding.

column1: Differentiate between microstrip lines and strip-lines. Discuss their transmission properties
column4:
Microstrip Line
(a) geometry, (b) field lines: part in the substrate, part in air, hence quasi-TEM. Pozar Fig 3.25.
  • Geometry:
    • Conducting strip of width \(W\) on top of dielectric substrate (\(h, \epsilon_r\)).
    • Ground plane on the bottom; upper surface exposed to air (\(\epsilon_0\)).
  • Wave mode:
    • Quasi-TEM mode: fields exist partly in dielectric (\(\epsilon_r\)) and partly in air (\(\epsilon_0 = 1\)).
    • Phase velocities in the two media differ \(\rightarrow\) pure TEM cannot be supported.
    • Characterized by effective dielectric constant \(\epsilon_{\text{eff}}\): \[ 1 < \epsilon_{\text{eff}} < \epsilon_r, \quad v_p = \frac{c}{\sqrt{\epsilon_{\text{eff}}}} \]
Strip-line
(a) geometry, (b) field lines: all inside one dielectric between two ground planes, hence pure TEM. Pozar Fig 3.22.
  • Geometry:
    • Conducting strip embedded symmetrically inside dielectric medium between two parallel ground planes.
  • Wave mode:
    • Pure TEM mode: dielectric is completely homogeneous around the conductor.
    • Phase velocity is frequency-independent: \[ v_p = \frac{c}{\sqrt{\epsilon_r}} \]
  • Dispersion: Moderate dispersion at higher frequencies as fields pull into substrate.
  • Fabrication: Very easy; standard photolithography; surface accessible for discrete component mounting (SMD, diodes, FETs).
  • Radiation: Unshielded; radiates at bends and discontinuities.
  • Dispersion: Non-dispersive; wide broadband operation.
  • Shielding: Completely enclosed between two ground planes \(\rightarrow\) zero radiation loss, no crosstalk with adjacent circuits.
  • Fabrication: Difficult; multi-layer sandwich lamination; impossible to mount surface components after manufacturing.
  • Applications: High-performance broadband passive circuits (couplers, filters, power dividers).

READ THIS FIRST
This is the second-heaviest chapter in the subject and the most predictable one. Of its 297 marks, roughly 230 are stub-matching constructions, and double-stub tuning alone appears in 17 of the 24 papers — the single most reliably asked item in RF and Microwave Engineering. Learn the construction, not the answers.
  1. Double-stub matching (17 papers, usually 8–12 marks) \(\rightarrow\) master one procedure: spacing circle, constant-\(g\) arc, rotate, cancel. It works for every variant the examiner prints (stub spacing \(\lambda/8\) or \(3\lambda/8\), short or open, first stub at the load or offset).
  2. The S-matrix rider (10 papers) \(\rightarrow\) “prepare the S-matrix of the matched network” is tacked onto most stub questions and is worth 2–6 marks for two lines of work. See §2.8; do not leave it.
  3. Single-stub matching (6 papers) and the immittance chart (5 papers) \(\rightarrow\) both are short, self-contained and frequently the easy half of a long question.
Numerical work is in the companion, Ch2 — RF and MW Transmission Lines — Numerical Problems & Solutions, where all 24 PYQ constructions are solved step by step.

column1: Differentiate the behaviour of a transmission line at conventional low frequency and at microwave bands. Compare microwave transmission lines with conventional low-frequency lines
column4:
A transmission line is a guiding structure
  • At low frequency, power is thought of as travelling in the wire; the pair of conductors merely completes a circuit.
  • At microwave frequency, power travels in the \(\vec{E}\) and \(\vec{H}\) fields between and around the conductors. Any structure that guides that field from place to place is a transmission line.
  • The governing criterion is again \(d/\lambda\) (§1.2): once the line length is a noticeable fraction of \(\lambda\), voltage and current are functions of position.
Classification
  • Two-conductor (TEM) lines — support a pure TEM mode, no low-frequency cut-off:
    • Two-wire open line, twisted pair (UTP / STP), coaxial cable, stripline.
  • Quasi-TEM lines — inhomogeneous dielectric, so no exact TEM:
    • Microstrip, coplanar waveguide (CPW), slot line, fin line.
  • Single-conductor (waveguide) lines — TE/TM modes only, and a cut-off frequency below which nothing propagates:
    • Rectangular and circular waveguide, dielectric waveguide, optical fibre.
  • Balanced vs unbalanced: two-wire and twisted pair are balanced (equal and opposite currents, common-mode noise cancels); coaxial is unbalanced (signal referred to the grounded outer). A balun converts between them.
Choosing a line — the four practical trade-offs
  • Loss: waveguide \(<\) coax \(<\) microstrip at a given frequency.
  • Power handling: waveguide (kW–MW) \(\gg\) coax \(\gg\) microstrip (W).
  • Bandwidth: TEM lines are broadband; waveguide is limited by cut-off and the next higher mode.
  • Cost and integration: microstrip is photolithographic and near-free; waveguide is machined and expensive.

column1: Derive the transmission line (telegrapher's) equations and obtain the characteristic impedance, reflection coefficient, VSWR and input impedance
column4:
Distributed model and the telegrapher's equations
(a) \(v\), \(i\) on a length \(\Delta z\); (b) its equivalent cell. Draw (b) before writing KVL and KCL. Pozar Fig 2.1.
  • A length \(\Delta z\) of line is modelled by series \(R'\Delta z\), \(L'\Delta z\) and shunt \(G'\Delta z\), \(C'\Delta z\), all per unit length.
  • Applying KVL and KCL to that cell and letting \(\Delta z \rightarrow 0\): \[ \frac{\partial v}{\partial z} = -R'i - L'\frac{\partial i}{\partial t}, \qquad \frac{\partial i}{\partial z} = -G'v - C'\frac{\partial v}{\partial t} \]
  • In phasor form these decouple into the wave equations \[ \frac{d^2V}{dz^2} = \gamma^2 V, \qquad \frac{d^2I}{dz^2} = \gamma^2 I \]
  • Propagation constant and characteristic impedance: \[ \gamma = \alpha + j\beta = \sqrt{(R'+j\omega L')(G'+j\omega C')} \] \[ Z_0 = \sqrt{\frac{R'+j\omega L'}{G'+j\omega C'}} \]
  • Solution: \(V(z) = V_0^{+}e^{-\gamma z} + V_0^{-}e^{+\gamma z}\) — a forward and a reflected travelling wave.
Lossless line (\(R'=G'=0\)) — used for every PYQ in this chapter
  • \(\alpha = 0\),  \(\beta = \omega\sqrt{L'C'}\),   \(Z_0 = \sqrt{L'/C'}\) (purely real).
  • \(\lambda = 2\pi/\beta = v_p/f\),  \(v_p = 1/\sqrt{L'C'} = c/\sqrt{\epsilon_r}\).
Distortionless line
  • Condition: \(R'C' = L'G'\). Then \(\alpha = \sqrt{R'G'}\) is frequency-independent and \(\beta = \omega\sqrt{L'C'}\) is linear in \(\omega\), so all frequencies travel at the same \(v_p\) and the pulse shape survives.
Terminated line: the four quantities every problem needs
  • Load reflection coefficient \[ \Gamma_L = \frac{Z_L - Z_0}{Z_L + Z_0} = \frac{z_L - 1}{z_L + 1}, \qquad z_L = \frac{Z_L}{Z_0} \]
  • At a distance \(d\) toward the generator, only the phase changes on a lossless line: \[ \Gamma(d) = \Gamma_L\,e^{-j2\beta d}, \qquad |\Gamma(d)| = |\Gamma_L| \] This is why the Smith chart works: moving along the line is a rotation at constant radius.
  • VSWR \[ S = \frac{V_{\max}}{V_{\min}} = \frac{1+|\Gamma_L|}{1-|\Gamma_L|}, \qquad 1 \le S \le \infty \]
  • Input impedance \[ Z_{in}(d) = Z_0\,\frac{Z_L + jZ_0\tan\beta d}{Z_0 + jZ_L\tan\beta d} \]
  • Return loss \(= -20\log_{10}|\Gamma|\) dB; mismatch loss \(= -10\log_{10}(1-|\Gamma|^2)\) dB.
Special line lengths — memorise these
CaseInput impedance
Matched \(Z_L=Z_0\)\(Z_{in}=Z_0\) for any length; \(\Gamma=0\), \(S=1\).
Short \(Z_L=0\)\(Z_{in} = jZ_0\tan\beta d\) — purely reactive, inductive for \(d<\lambda/4\).
Open \(Z_L=\infty\)\(Z_{in} = -jZ_0\cot\beta d\) — purely reactive, capacitive for \(d<\lambda/4\).
\(d=\lambda/2\)\(Z_{in} = Z_L\) — the line repeats every half wavelength.
\(d=\lambda/4\)\(Z_{in} = Z_0^2/Z_L\) — the quarter-wave transformer; it inverts, so a short looks open.
\(d=\lambda/8\)\(Z_{in} = Z_0\,\dfrac{Z_L+jZ_0}{Z_0+jZ_L}\)  (\(\tan\beta d = 1\)).
A shorted or open stub is therefore a pure reactance whose value you choose by cutting it to length — that single fact is the whole basis of stub matching.

column1: Explain the construction of the Smith chart. What does each family of curves represent, and how is it read?
column4:
What the chart is
  • A plot of normalised impedance \(z = r + jx\) mapped onto the complex \(\Gamma\) plane by the bilinear transform \[ \Gamma = \frac{z-1}{z+1}, \qquad z = \frac{1+\Gamma}{1-\Gamma} \]
  • Because \(|\Gamma| \le 1\) for a passive load, the entire right half of the \(z\) plane folds into the unit circle — an infinite plane on one sheet of paper.
The two families of curves
  • Constant resistance \(r\): circles centred on \(\left(\dfrac{r}{1+r},\,0\right)\) with radius \(\dfrac{1}{1+r}\). All pass through the open-circuit point \(\Gamma = +1\).
  • Constant reactance \(x\): arcs centred on \(\left(1,\,\dfrac{1}{x}\right)\) with radius \(\left|\dfrac{1}{x}\right|\). Upper half \(= +x\) (inductive), lower half \(= -x\) (capacitive).
  • The two families are orthogonal everywhere they cross.
Landmarks
  • Centre \(z=1\): matched, \(\Gamma=0\), \(S=1\).
  • Left \(z=0\): short circuit, \(\Gamma=-1\).
  • Right \(z=\infty\): open circuit, \(\Gamma=+1\).
  • Rim \(|\Gamma|=1\): pure reactance, total reflection, \(S=\infty\).
  • Horizontal axis: \(x=0\), i.e. purely resistive. To the right of centre lies \(V_{\max}\) (and \(r = S\)); to the left lies \(V_{\min}\) (and \(r = 1/S\)).
Reading it — the five rules
  1. Normalise: \(z_L = Z_L/Z_0\). Plot it.
  2. \(|\Gamma_L|\) = distance from centre \(\div\) chart radius; its angle is read on the angle of reflection coefficient scale.
  3. Draw the constant-\(|\Gamma|\) (SWR) circle through the point. Read \(S\) where it cuts the right-hand real axis.
  4. Move toward the generator = clockwise; toward the load \(=\) anticlockwise. One full lap is \(\lambda/2\), so a quarter turn is \(\lambda/8\).
  5. Read distances on the WTG (wavelengths toward generator) rim scale, which runs \(0 \rightarrow 0.5\) clockwise starting at the short-circuit point.
The impedance chart. Constant-\(r\) circles (all through the open point) and constant-\(x\) arcs; the rim carries the WTG scale, on which one complete lap is half a wavelength of line.
Why the chart is worth using at all
  • It turns the awkward \(Z_{in}\) formula into a rotation, and \(z \rightarrow y\) into a half-turn — both done with a compass instead of complex arithmetic.
  • \(\Gamma\), \(S\), \(Z_{in}\), \(Y_{in}\), return loss and the positions of \(V_{\max}\) and \(V_{\min}\) are all read off one diagram.
  • It shows graphically which matching solutions exist, and lets you pick the one with the shortest stub or the widest bandwidth — something a formula does not show you.

column1: Sketch an immittance chart. List the duality parameters and compare the two scales
column4:
The admittance chart
  • Since \(y = 1/z\), and \[ \Gamma_y = \frac{y-1}{y+1} = -\frac{z-1}{z+1} = -\Gamma_z \] the admittance chart is the impedance chart rotated through \(180^\circ\) (a \(\lambda/4\) line length).
  • So on a plain Smith chart you convert \(z \rightarrow y\) by drawing a diameter through the point and reading the diametrically opposite intersection.
The immittance chart
  • Both grids printed on one chart, usually in two colours: the impedance grid and the admittance grid superimposed.
  • A single location then carries two readings at once — \(z\) on one grid, \(y\) on the other. The \(\lambda/4\) half-turn is built into the printing.
  • Why it matters: stub matching is done in admittance (shunt stubs add susceptance) but loads are quoted as impedance. Without an immittance chart every problem costs an extra half-turn, and each half-turn is a chance to misread.
Duality parameters
Impedance gridAdmittance grid
\(z = r + jx\)\(y = g + jb\)
Resistance \(r\)Conductance \(g\)
Reactance \(x\)Susceptance \(b\)
\(+x\) inductive (upper)\(+b\) capacitive (upper)
\(-x\) capacitive (lower)\(-b\) inductive (lower)
Short \(z=0\) at \(\Gamma=-1\)Open \(y=0\) at \(\Gamma=-1\)
Open \(z=\infty\) at \(\Gamma=+1\)Short \(y=\infty\) at \(\Gamma=+1\)
Series elements addShunt elements add
\(r=1\) circle\(g=1\) circle
Trap. The sign convention flips: a point in the upper half is inductive read as an impedance but capacitive read as an admittance. Both are the same physical point.
Immittance chart. The amber grid is the blue grid turned through \(180^\circ\); one location reads \(z = 0.5+j0.7\) on the impedance grid and \(y = 0.68-j0.95\) on the admittance grid. The faint point is where \(y\) would have to be read on a plain chart — a \(\lambda/4\) turn away.

column1: Why is impedance matching necessary? Compare the different impedance matching techniques
column4:
Why match
  • Maximum power transfer: a matched load absorbs all incident power; the fraction reflected is \(|\Gamma|^2\).
  • Protect the source: reflected power returning to a high-power amplifier or a magnetron causes heating, and can destroy it.
  • Remove standing waves: high VSWR means voltage peaks that cause dielectric breakdown and arcing, and current peaks that cause \(I^2R\) loss.
  • Preserve receiver sensitivity: mismatch at an LNA input degrades the noise figure directly.
  • Avoid distortion: multiple reflections on a long line arrive delayed, producing ghosting and intersymbol interference.
The matching network must be lossless
  • A resistive pad would “match” but dissipate the very power being matched.
  • So matching uses only reactive elements: line lengths, stubs, lumped \(L\) and \(C\).
The general problem: a lossless network between line \(Z_0\) and load \(Z_L\), chosen so the line sees \(Z_0\). Every technique in the table is one way to build the box. Pozar Fig 5.1.
Comparison of techniques
TechniqueHow it worksTrade-offs
Quarter-wave transformer\(\lambda/4\) of line with \(Z_{01}=\sqrt{Z_0 Z_L}\).Simplest, but needs a real \(Z_L\) — a complex load must first be walked to a \(V_{\max}\) or \(V_{\min}\). Narrowband.
L-section (lumped)Two reactances, series \(+\) shunt.Compact; fine below \(\sim\)1 GHz. Above that, component parasitics (§1.3) dominate.
Single stubOne shunt (or series) stub at a computed distance \(d\).Matches any load; only line, so no lumped parts. But \(d\) must move if the load changes — awkward to build as an adjustable tuner.
Double stubTwo stubs at fixed spacing; only the lengths are tuned.Positions are pre-set, so it makes a practical adjustable tuner. But a range of loads cannot be matched (the forbidden region).
Triple stubThree fixed stubs.Removes the forbidden region entirely; used in laboratory slide-screw tuners.
Advantages of double stub over single stub
  • Stub positions are fixed; matching is done by adjusting lengths only, so it can be built as a mechanical tuner with two sliding shorts.
  • No need to break into the line at a computed distance — the connection points are decided at manufacture.
  • Retunes for a new load without physically relocating anything.
  • Cost: a set of load admittances (the forbidden region) is unmatchable, and two stubs mean a slightly narrower bandwidth.

column1: Explain the design of a single-stub shunt tuner, stating all steps with reasoning. When is a short-circuited stub preferred over an open one?
column4:
Principle
  • Two degrees of freedom are needed to cancel a complex mismatch, and a single stub supplies exactly two: the distance \(d\) from the load to the stub, and the stub length \(\ell\).
  • Work in admittance, because a shunt stub adds its susceptance: \[ y_{in} = y(d) + y_{stub} = 1 + jb + (-jb) = 1 \]
  • Step 1 — choose \(d\) so the line admittance has unit conductance: \(y(d) = 1 + jb\). Geometrically, walk round the SWR circle until it cuts the \(g=1\) circle. It always cuts it twice, so there are always two solutions.
  • Step 2 — choose \(\ell\) so the stub presents \(-jb\), cancelling the residual susceptance and leaving \(y_{in}=1\), i.e. \(Z_{in}=Z_0\).
Design procedure on the chart
  1. Normalise \(z_L = Z_L/Z_0\) and plot it.
  2. Half-turn to \(y_L\) (or read it on the admittance grid). Note its WTG reading.
  3. Draw the SWR circle through \(y_L\).
  4. Move clockwise to each intersection with the \(g=1\) circle; call them \(y_1 = 1 - jb\) and \(y_2 = 1 + jb\). The WTG difference from \(y_L\) gives \(d_1\) and \(d_2\).
  5. The stub must supply \(+jb\) and \(-jb\) respectively.
  6. For the stub length, start at the termination point of the stub — the open-circuit point (\(y=0\)) for an open stub, the short-circuit point (\(y=\infty\)) for a shorted stub — and run clockwise round the rim to the required susceptance. That arc, read on the WTG scale, is \(\ell\).
Analytic check (use it to verify the chart)
  • With \(t = \tan\beta d\) and \(Z_L = R_L + jX_L\), the distance satisfies \[ t = \frac{X_L \pm \sqrt{R_L\big[(Z_0-R_L)^2 + X_L^2\big]/Z_0}}{R_L - Z_0} \] reducing to \(t = -X_L/2Z_0\) when \(R_L = Z_0\).
  • Then \(d/\lambda = \dfrac{1}{2\pi}\tan^{-1}t\) (add \(0.5\) if negative).
  • Stub length from the required susceptance \(b_s\): \[ \frac{\ell_{open}}{\lambda} = \frac{1}{2\pi}\tan^{-1}(b_s), \qquad \frac{\ell_{short}}{\lambda} = \frac{-1}{2\pi}\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{1}{b_s}\right) \] always reduced modulo \(0.5\lambda\).
Short-circuited or open-circuited stub?
StubWhen it is preferred
ShortCoax and waveguide. A shorting plate is exact and radiates nothing; an open coax end radiates and has fringing capacitance, so its electrical length is not its physical length. Also easier to make adjustable (sliding short).
OpenMicrostrip and other planar lines. Ending the strip is free; a true short needs a via drilled and plated through the substrate, which adds inductance and cost.
The two lengths differ by exactly \(\lambda/4\): \(\ell_{short} = \ell_{open} \pm \lambda/4\).
Which of the two solutions to build
  • Prefer the smaller \(d\): less line between load and stub means a shorter high-VSWR section, hence lower loss and wider bandwidth.
  • Prefer the shorter stub for the same reason, and for compactness.
  • A series stub is used when the line cannot be shunted (some waveguide and coaxial geometries); the construction is identical but done on the impedance grid against the \(r=1\) circle.
The circuit, which is what to draw
  • (a) Shunt stub: at distance \(d\) from the load the line admittance is \(Y = 1/Z = Y_0 + jB\); the stub of length \(\ell\), open or shorted, adds \(-jB\).
  • (b) Series stub: same two unknowns \(d\) and \(\ell\), but the stub is in series, so work in impedance: \(Z = Z_0 + jX\) at \(d\), stub supplies \(-jX\).
  • Mark \(d\) from the load and \(\ell\) from the stub's open or shorted end on the sketch: those are the two answers the question asks for.
  • Pozar Fig 5.4.

column1: Explain the steps for impedance matching of a load using a double-stub network. State the advantages over single-stub matching and the limitation of the technique
column4:
Principle
  • The two stubs sit at fixed positions a distance \(d\) apart — almost always \(\lambda/8\) or \(3\lambda/8\) in the papers. Only the two lengths \(\ell_1\) and \(\ell_2\) are adjusted, and those are the two degrees of freedom.
  • Stub 1 cannot change the conductance it sees — a shunt susceptance moves the point along its own constant-\(g\) circle. Its job is to land the point where the intervening \(d\) of line will carry it onto the \(g=1\) circle.
  • Stub 2 then simply cancels whatever susceptance is left, exactly as in single-stub matching.
The spacing circle — the key construction
  • Define the spacing circle as the \(g=1\) circle rotated \(d\) toward the load (anticlockwise).
  • Any point on it is carried onto \(g=1\) by \(d\) wavelengths of line.
  • So stub 1 must move the point from \(y_1\) to the intersection of its own constant-\(g\) circle with the spacing circle. There are generally two intersections, hence two solutions.
Design procedure
  1. Normalise \(z_L\), plot, half-turn to \(y_L\).
  2. If the first stub is offset from the load by \(d_1\), rotate \(y_L\) clockwise by \(d_1\) to get \(y_1\), the admittance just before stub 1.
  3. Draw the spacing circle (\(g=1\) rotated \(d\) toward the load).
  4. Follow the constant-\(g\) circle through \(y_1\) to its intersections with the spacing circle: \(y_a\) and \(y_a'\).
  5. \(b_1 = \operatorname{Im}(y_a) - \operatorname{Im}(y_1)\) — the susceptance stub 1 must add. Read \(\ell_1\) off the rim from the stub's termination point.
  6. Rotate \(y_a\) clockwise by \(d\) along its SWR circle; it lands on \(g=1\) at \(y_2 = 1 + jb_2'\).
  7. \(b_2 = -b_2'\); read \(\ell_2\) off the rim the same way. The network is matched.
Analytic check
  • With \(y_1 = g_1 + jb_L\) and \(t = \tan\beta d\), requiring \(\operatorname{Re}(y_2)=1\) after the spacing gives \[ \operatorname{Re}(y_2) = \frac{g_1(1+t^2)}{(1-tB)^2 + t^2g_1^2} = 1 \] \[ \Rightarrow \quad B = \frac{1 \pm \sqrt{g_1(1+t^2) - g_1^2t^2}}{t}, \qquad b_1 = B - b_L \] where \(B\) is the total susceptance after stub 1. Note the leading \(1\) in the numerator, not \(g_1\) — a common slip.
  • Then \(y_a = g_1 + jB\), and \(y_2 = \dfrac{y_a + jt}{1 + jt\,y_a}\), with \(b_2 = -\operatorname{Im}(y_2)\).
The forbidden region — always state this
  • The square root is real only if \[ g_1 \;\le\; \frac{1}{\sin^2\beta d} \]
  • For \(d = \lambda/8\) (\(\beta d = 45^\circ\)): \(g_1 \le 2\).
    For \(d = 3\lambda/8\): \(g_1 \le 2\) likewise.
    For \(d = \lambda/4\): \(g_1 \le 1\).
  • Loads whose conductance at the first stub exceeds this cannot be matched at all with that spacing. Graphically, their constant-\(g\) circle lies wholly inside the spacing circle and never cuts it.
  • The fix: add a length of line before the first stub (which moves \(g_1\)), or use a third stub.
  • This is why \(\lambda/4\) spacing is avoided in practice and \(\lambda/8\) or \(3\lambda/8\) is used — and why the examiner keeps specifying \(3\lambda/8\).
Trap. Stub spacings near \(\lambda/2\) make the two stubs nearly coincident and the tuner hopelessly narrowband, so practical spacings stay between \(\lambda/8\) and \(3\lambda/8\).
The circuit, which is what to draw
  • (a) load an arbitrary distance from the first stub: stub 1 (\(jB_1\), length \(\ell_1\)) nearer the load, stub 2 (\(jB_2\), \(\ell_2\)) a fixed \(d\) further toward the generator.
  • (b) the same tuner with that offset line absorbed into the load, now called \(Y_L'\). This is step 2 of the procedure: rotate \(y_L\) by \(d_1\) first, then design as if stub 1 sat at the load.
  • Only \(\ell_1\) and \(\ell_2\) are adjusted; \(d\) is fixed at manufacture, which is the whole advantage over one stub.
  • Pozar Fig 5.7.

column1: Prepare the scattering matrix of the network before and after matching
column4:
Before matching — a one-port
  • An unmatched load seen from the line is a one-port, so its scattering matrix is the single entry \[ [S] = \big[\,\Gamma_L\,\big] = \left[\frac{Z_L-Z_0}{Z_L+Z_0}\right] \]
  • Quote it in polar form, \(|\Gamma_L|\angle\theta^\circ\), and give the VSWR alongside — the examiner usually wants both.
After matching — an ideal two-port
  • A perfectly matched, lossless, reciprocal two-port has no reflection at either port, so \(S_{11} = S_{22} = 0\), and all power passes through, so \(|S_{12}| = |S_{21}| = 1\): \[ [S] = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \]
  • Keeping the electrical length \(\theta = \beta\ell\) of the through path: \[ [S] = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & e^{-j\theta} \\ e^{-j\theta} & 0 \end{bmatrix} \] Either answer earns the marks; state which convention you are using.
Justifying each property (this is where the marks are)
  • \(S_{11}=S_{22}=0\): that is the definition of a match — the tuner was designed to make \(Z_{in} = Z_0\) looking in at either port.
  • Reciprocity, \(S_{12} = S_{21}\): the network contains only passive, isotropic media (line and stubs), no ferrite and no active device, so \([S]\) is symmetric, \([S] = [S]^T\).
  • Lossless, so \([S]\) is unitary: \([S]^{*T}[S] = [I]\), giving \(\sum_k |S_{ki}|^2 = 1\) for every column. With \(S_{11}=0\) this forces \(|S_{21}| = 1\).
  • Reactive elements only means no power is dissipated, only redirected — so all incident power appears at the far port.
Worked shape of the answer
  • “Before: \(\Gamma_L = (Z_L-Z_0)/(Z_L+Z_0) = 0.45\angle60^\circ\), so \([S]=[\,0.45\angle60^\circ\,]\) and \(S = 2.64\).”
  • “After: the tuner makes \(Z_{in}=Z_0\), so \(S_{11}=S_{22}=0\); the network is reciprocal and lossless, so \(S_{12}=S_{21}\) with \(|S_{21}|=1\), giving \([S]=\left[\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right]\).”
S-parameter theory in full — properties, derivation, shifting reference planes — is Chapter 3. This band covers only the rider attached to stub questions.

column1: Sketch the physical diagram of the matched network using microstrips
column4:
From electrical length to millimetres
  • Microstrip is quasi-TEM, so the wave sees an effective permittivity between air and substrate: \[ \epsilon_{e} = \frac{\epsilon_r+1}{2} + \frac{\epsilon_r-1}{2} \frac{1}{\sqrt{1+12h/W}} \]
  • Guide wavelength, and hence every physical length: \[ \lambda_g = \frac{\lambda_0}{\sqrt{\epsilon_e}} = \frac{c}{f\sqrt{\epsilon_e}}, \qquad \ell_{\text{mm}} = \frac{\ell}{\lambda}\times\lambda_g \]
  • Strip width for a wanted \(Z_0\) (Hammerstad synthesis), with \(B = \dfrac{377\pi}{2Z_0\sqrt{\epsilon_r}}\) and \(W/h > 2\): \[ \frac{W}{h} = \frac{2}{\pi}\Big[B-1-\ln(2B-1) + \frac{\epsilon_r-1}{2\epsilon_r}\Big(\ln(B-1)+0.39-\frac{0.61}{\epsilon_r}\Big)\Big] \]
Layout rules the examiner looks for
  • Stubs are drawn as T-junctions off the main line, at the computed spacing.
  • Open stubs are drawn as a plain truncated strip; shorted stubs need a via to the ground plane, drawn as a filled circle.
  • Label \(W\) for the \(Z_0\) line, the stub lengths \(\ell_1\), \(\ell_2\) in mm, and the spacing \(d\) in mm.
  • State the substrate: e.g. RT/duroid 5880 (\(\epsilon_r=2.2\)), FR-4 (\(\epsilon_r=4.4\)), alumina (\(\epsilon_r=9.8\)), with \(h\).
Worked conversion — carry this shape into the exam
  • Take \(Z_0 = 50\,\Omega\) on FR-4, \(\epsilon_r = 4.4\), \(h = 1.6\) mm, \(f = 3\) GHz.
  • Synthesis gives \(W/h \approx 1.9\), so \(W \approx 3.0\) mm, and \(\epsilon_e \approx 3.33\).
  • \(\lambda_0 = c/f = 100\) mm, so \(\lambda_g = 100/\sqrt{3.33} \approx 54.8\) mm.
  • A stub of \(0.146\lambda\) is then \(0.146 \times 54.8 \approx \textbf{8.0 mm}\), and a \(3\lambda/8\) spacing is \(0.375 \times 54.8 \approx \textbf{20.5 mm}\).
Practical corrections worth a mark
  • Open-end fringing: an open stub behaves slightly longer than it is, by \(\Delta \ell \approx 0.3\text{--}0.4\,h\). Shorten the drawn stub by that much.
  • T-junction discontinuity: the junction adds shunt susceptance; the reference plane is not exactly the strip centreline.
  • Via inductance: a shorted stub's via is not a perfect short, which is the practical reason open stubs dominate in microstrip.
  • Radiation and dispersion rise with frequency; above about 10 GHz on FR-4 the losses make the design impractical, so low-loss substrates are used.

READ THIS FIRST
Every problem below is worked as a Smith chart construction, step by step — which circle to draw, which arc to follow, what to read off the rim — because that is what the examiner marks. The numbers were computed exactly from the transmission-line equations, so they are what a perfectly drawn chart would give; your hand-drawn readings will differ in the second decimal place and that is fine.

column1: M. The Three Methods, in Brief
column4:
M1 — Reading the chart (Problem 1)
  1. Normalise \(z_L = Z_L/Z_0\) and plot.
  2. Swing the SWR circle about the centre through that point. \(|\Gamma_L|\) is its radius; \(S\) is where it cuts the right-hand real axis.
  3. Moving along the line is rotation at constant radius: clockwise toward the generator, one lap \(=\lambda/2\). Read distances on the WTG rim scale.
  4. The circle crosses the horizontal axis twice per lap — those are the only purely resistive points, at \(V_{\max}\) (\(r=S\)) and \(V_{\min}\) (\(r=1/S\)).
M2 — Single-stub shunt tuner (Problems 2–7)
  1. Plot \(z_L\), half-turn to \(y_L\) (shunt stubs add susceptance, so all stub work is done in admittance).
  2. Rotate clockwise to the \(g=1\) circle. It is cut twice \(\rightarrow\) \(d_1\), \(d_2\).
  3. There \(y = 1 \pm jb\). The stub must supply \(\mp jb\).
  4. For the length, start at the stub's own termination — open stub at \(y=0\), short stub at \(y=\infty\) — and run clockwise round the rim to that susceptance. \(\ell_{short} = \ell_{open} \pm \lambda/4\).
M3 — Double-stub shunt tuner (Problems 8–24)
  1. Plot \(z_L\), half-turn to \(y_L\); if the first stub is offset, rotate clockwise to get \(y_1\), the admittance just before stub 1.
  2. Check \(g_1 \le 1/\sin^2\beta d\). If it fails, no length of stub can match this load at this spacing.
  3. Draw the spacing circle: the \(g=1\) circle rotated the stub spacing \(d\) toward the load.
  4. Stub 1 can only slide the point along its own constant-\(g\) circle. Follow that circle to its two intersections with the spacing circle \(\rightarrow\) \(y_a\), \(y_a'\). Then \(b_1 = \operatorname{Im}(y_a) - \operatorname{Im}(y_1)\).
  5. Rotate \(y_a\) clockwise by \(d\) on a new SWR circle. It lands on \(g=1\) at \(y_2 = 1 + jb\).
  6. Stub 2 supplies \(-jb\). Read both lengths off the rim as in M2.
Sign conventions that decide the answer
  • Clockwise \(=\) toward the generator. One full lap is \(\lambda/2\), so a quarter turn is \(\lambda/8\) and \(3\lambda/8\) is three quarter-turns.
  • On the admittance chart the terminations swap ends: \(y=0\) (open) is at the left, \(y=\infty\) (short) at the right — the mirror of the impedance chart. Getting this backwards corrupts every stub length by \(\lambda/4\).
  • Upper half \(= +b =\) capacitive; lower half \(= -b =\) inductive.
Analytic back-check
\[ B = \frac{1 \pm \sqrt{g_1(1+t^2) - g_1^2 t^2}}{t}, \quad t = \tan\beta d, \quad b_1 = B - b_L \] Note the leading \(1\) in the numerator, not \(g_1\).

column1: Problem 1 — Smith chart reading of a mismatched line
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 79 Ch [10]
A lossless \(50\,\Omega\) line is terminated by \(75+j100\,\Omega\). Using the Smith chart find (a) \(\Gamma_L\), (b) VSWR, (c) \(Z_{in}\) at \(0.375\lambda\) from the load, (d) the shortest length of line for which the impedance is purely resistive, and (e) the value of that resistance.
column4:
Given
  • \(Z_L = 75.00 + j100.00\,\Omega\), \(Z_0 = 50\,\Omega\).
Step 1 — normalise and plot \(z_L\)
  • \(z_L = Z_L/Z_0 = 75.00 + j100.00\) over \(50\) \(=1.50 + j2.00\).
  • Plot it where the \(r = 1.50\) circle cuts the \(x = +2.00\) arc; it reads \(0.198\lambda\) on the WTG scale.
  • \(\Gamma_L = (z_L-1)/(z_L+1) = 0.644\angle 37.3^\circ\), so \(|\Gamma_L| = 0.644\) sets the SWR-circle radius and \(S = 4.62\).
Step 2 — draw the SWR circle and read (a) and (b)
  • Centre the compass on the chart centre and swing a circle through \(z_L\). Its radius is \(|\Gamma_L| = 0.644\) of the chart radius.
  • (a) \(\Gamma_L = 0.644\angle 37.3^\circ\) — read the angle on the angle of reflection coefficient scale.
  • (b) The circle cuts the right-hand real axis at \(r = 4.62\), and on that axis \(r = S\), so \(\boxed{S = 4.62}\).
Step 3 — rotate \(0.375\lambda\) toward the generator for (c)
  • \(z_L\) reads \(0.198\lambda\) WTG. Add \(0.375\lambda\): \(0.198 + 0.375 = 0.573\), and since this exceeds \(0.5\), subtract half a turn \(\rightarrow 0.073\lambda\).
  • Staying on the SWR circle (the radius never changes on a lossless line), read \(z_{in} = 0.27 + j0.47\).
  • (c) \(Z_{in} = Z_0 z_{in} = 50 \times (0.27 + j0.47) = \boxed{13.33 + j23.33\,\Omega}\).
Step 4 — shortest purely resistive point, (d) and (e)
  • \(z\) is purely resistive wherever the SWR circle crosses the horizontal axis (\(x = 0\)) — which happens twice per lap, at the voltage maximum (right) and the voltage minimum (left).
  • Rotating clockwise from \(z_L\) at \(0.198\lambda\), the nearer crossing is the voltage maximum.
  • (d) \(\boxed{d = 0.052\lambda}\).
  • (e) At a voltage maximum the normalised resistance is \(r = S = 4.62\), so \(R = 50 \times 4.617 = \boxed{230.8\,\Omega}\).

QUESTION AS PRINTED 72 Ash [2+8]
Design single-stub shunt tuning networks (short-circuited and open-circuited) for \(Z_L = 80+j100\,\Omega\), and sketch the realisation in microstrip.
column4:
Given
  • \(Z_L = 80.00 + j100.00\,\Omega\), \(Z_0 = 50\,\Omega\).
Step 1 — normalise and plot \(z_L\)
  • \(z_L = Z_L/Z_0 = 80.00 + j100.00\) over \(50\) \(=1.60 + j2.00\).
  • Plot it where the \(r = 1.60\) circle cuts the \(x = +2.00\) arc; it reads \(0.200\lambda\) on the WTG scale.
  • \(\Gamma_L = (z_L-1)/(z_L+1) = 0.637\angle 35.7^\circ\), so \(|\Gamma_L| = 0.637\) sets the SWR-circle radius and \(S = 4.50\).
Step 2 — convert to admittance
  • Draw the diameter through \(z_L\) and read the opposite intersection — a \(\lambda/4\) half-turn. On an immittance chart read the amber grid in place and skip this step.
  • \(y_L = 1/z_L = 0.24 - j0.30\), at \(0.450\lambda\) on the WTG scale (exactly \(0.25\lambda\) from \(z_L\)).
Step 3 — walk to the \(g=1\) circle
  • Swing the SWR circle (radius \(|\Gamma_L| = 0.637\)) through \(y_L\).
  • Rotate clockwise (toward the generator) to each intersection with the \(g=1\) circle. There are always two:
    • \(y_1 = 1.00 + j1.65\) at \(0.180\lambda\) WTG, so \(d_1 = 0.180\lambda - 0.450\lambda = 0.230\lambda\).
    • \(y_2 = 1.00 - j1.65\) at \(0.320\lambda\) WTG, so \(d_2 = 0.320\lambda - 0.450\lambda = 0.370\lambda\).
  • Only the susceptance is left to cancel: the conductance is already 1.
Step 4 — read each stub length off the rim
  • The stub must present the negative of the residual susceptance. Start at the stub's own termination and run clockwise round the rim until you reach that value; the arc, read on the WTG scale, is the length.
  • Short-circuited stub — start at the short-circuit point (\(y=\infty\), the right of the chart):
    • needs \(b = -1.651\), giving \(\ell_1 = 0.087\lambda\).
    • needs \(b = +1.651\), giving \(\ell_2 = 0.413\lambda\).
  • Open-circuited stub — start at the open-circuit point (\(y=0\), the left of the chart):
    • needs \(b = -1.651\), giving \(\ell_1 = 0.337\lambda\).
    • needs \(b = +1.651\), giving \(\ell_2 = 0.163\lambda\).
Answer
QuantitySolution 1Solution 2
Stub distance \(d\)\(0.230\lambda\)\(0.370\lambda\)
Line admittance\(1.00 + j1.65\)\(1.00 - j1.65\)
Short stub \(\ell\)\(0.087\lambda\)\(0.413\lambda\)
Open stub \(\ell\)\(0.337\lambda\)\(0.163\lambda\)
Which to build
Solution 1 puts the stub closer to the load (\(0.230\lambda\) against \(0.370\lambda\)), so the high-VSWR section is shorter: lower loss and wider bandwidth. Prefer it unless the layout forbids it.
Microstrip realisation
  • Take FR-4, \(\epsilon_r = 4.4\), \(h = 1.6\text{ mm}\). Hammerstad synthesis for \(50\,\Omega\) gives \(W/h = 1.91\), i.e. \(W = 3.06\text{ mm}\), with \(\epsilon_e = 3.33\).
  • No frequency is given, so leave the answers in wavelengths; multiply by \(\lambda_g = \lambda_0/\sqrt{\epsilon_e}\) once \(f\) is fixed.
  • Draw the stubs as T-junctions off the \(W\)-wide main line. A shorted stub needs a plated via to the ground plane, drawn as a filled circle at the stub end.
  • Shorten each open stub by the fringing allowance \(\Delta\ell \approx 0.3h = 0.48\text{ mm}\).

Given

Step 1 — normalise and plot \(z_L\)
  • \(z_L = Z_L/Z_0 = 78.27 + j60.93\) over \(75\) \(=1.04 + j0.81\).
  • Plot it where the \(r = 1.04\) circle cuts the \(x = +0.81\) arc; it reads \(0.159\lambda\) on the WTG scale.
  • \(\Gamma_L = (z_L-1)/(z_L+1) = 0.370\angle 65.2^\circ\), so \(|\Gamma_L| = 0.370\) sets the SWR-circle radius and \(S = 2.17\).
Step 2 — convert to admittance
  • Draw the diameter through \(z_L\) and read the opposite intersection — a \(\lambda/4\) half-turn. On an immittance chart read the amber grid in place and skip this step.
  • \(y_L = 1/z_L = 0.60 - j0.46\), at \(0.409\lambda\) on the WTG scale (exactly \(0.25\lambda\) from \(z_L\)).
Step 3 — walk to the \(g=1\) circle
  • Swing the SWR circle (radius \(|\Gamma_L| = 0.370\)) through \(y_L\).

    • needs \(b = -0.796\), giving \(\ell_1 = 0.143\lambda\).
    • needs \(b = +0.796\), giving \(\ell_2 = 0.357\lambda\).

    • needs \(b = -0.796\), giving \(\ell_1 = 0.393\lambda\).
    • needs \(b = +0.796\), giving \(\ell_2 = 0.107\lambda\).

READ THIS FIRST
Chapter 3 is the cheapest 8 to 10 marks in the paper, because the same three asks recur:
  1. Why S-parameters, and how do they differ from h / Z / Y / ABCD? (13 papers) \(\rightarrow\) one reason list plus one comparison table, \(\S\)3.1.
  2. Derive the S-parameters of a two-port network (7 papers) \(\rightarrow\) the same six lines every time, \(\S\)3.2. Learn it as a script.
  3. Identify the passive device from this S-matrix (5 papers) \(\rightarrow\) in every one of the five it is the magic tee, in four different disguises. Learn the fingerprint in \(\S\)3.7 and the matrix in \(\S\)3.6.
Two more traps worth knowing before the paper starts:
  • The radar questions (“two transmitters, twice the power”, “half the power to the antenna via a duplexer”, 4 papers) are the same magic tee asked as a design problem, \(\S\)3.8. Nothing new has to be learnt for them.
  • An examiner who writes “3-port network” almost always wants the impossibility theorem (\(\S\)3.5), not just a \(3\times3\) matrix. Stating that a 3-port cannot be lossless, reciprocal and matched at the same time, and then naming the three escapes, is what separates a 4 from an 8.

column1: Why are S-parameters used in microwave network analysis? Compare S-parameters with h-parameters
column4:
What the low-frequency parameter sets need
  • All four classical sets relate total voltage and total current at the terminals:
    • \([V] = [Z][I]\), \(Z_{ij} = V_i/I_j\) with all other ports open, \(I_k = 0\).
    • \([I] = [Y][V]\), \(Y_{ij} = I_i/V_j\) with all other ports shorted, \(V_k = 0\).
    • h-parameters: mixed, \(h_{11}\) and \(h_{21}\) need a short on port 2, \(h_{12}\) and \(h_{22}\) need an open on port 1.
    • ABCD: cascade form, still defined on \(V\) and \(I\).
  • Two things are therefore assumed:
    • \(V\) and \(I\) are unique at a terminal pair (true only when \(d \ll \lambda\)).
    • Ideal open and short terminations are available.
  • Both assumptions fail above roughly \(1\,\)GHz.
What S-parameters do instead
  • Defined on travelling waves, not on totals:
    • \(a_i\) = wave incident on port \(i\), \(b_i\) = wave leaving port \(i\).
    • Normalised so \(|a_i|^2\) and \(|b_i|^2\) are powers, in watts.
  • Every port is terminated in \(Z_0\), a matched load:
    • Easy to build and broadband, unlike open or short.
    • No reflection back into the device \(\rightarrow\) no oscillation, no damage, bias undisturbed.
  • Measured with directional couplers plus a vector network analyser, which separate incident from reflected wave and read magnitude and phase directly.
  • Every practical figure of merit falls straight out: gain, return loss, insertion loss, isolation, VSWR, stability (\(\S\)3.4).
  • Valid at any frequency, so the same formalism covers DC to mmWave.
  • Cascadable after conversion to the transfer (T) form, so a chain of measured blocks can be multiplied out.
The five reasons they break at microwave
  1. No unique \(V\) and \(I\):
    • Circuit size is comparable to \(\lambda\), so voltage varies along the conductor.
    • In a waveguide there is no unique pair of conductors at all, so “the voltage” has no single definition.
  2. Open and short cannot be realised:
    • A physical short has series lead inductance, an open has fringing capacitance.
    • A short is a short at one frequency and one reference plane only: \(\lambda/4\) away it looks like an open.
  3. Total reflection is destructive:
    • \(|\Gamma| = 1\) sends all the power back into the device.
    • Transistors and negative-resistance diodes oscillate or burn out under open or short test conditions.
  4. No instrument measures RF \(V\) and \(I\):
    • Probes load the circuit and cannot follow GHz waveforms.
    • Power is what a microwave detector actually reads.
  5. Bias shifts:
    • Open and short terminations change the DC operating point and the junction capacitance of active devices, so the measurement is not of the device in use.

column1: Using a two-port network, define and derive the S-parameters
column4:
Step 1: the wave variables
  • At port \(i\) the line carries a forward wave \(V_i^{+}\) and a backward wave \(V_i^{-}\). Normalise both by \(\sqrt{Z_0}\): \[ a_i = \frac{V_i^{+}}{\sqrt{Z_0}}, \qquad b_i = \frac{V_i^{-}}{\sqrt{Z_0}} \]
  • The normalisation is chosen so that the squared magnitudes are powers: \[ P_i^{\text{inc}} = \tfrac{1}{2}|a_i|^2, \qquad P_i^{\text{ref}} = \tfrac{1}{2}|b_i|^2 \] (the \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) disappears if \(a\), \(b\) are taken as rms).
  • In terms of the total quantities: \[ V_i = \sqrt{Z_0}\,(a_i + b_i), \qquad I_i = \frac{a_i - b_i}{\sqrt{Z_0}} \] so nothing is lost, only re-expressed.
Port 1 and port 2 of a general two-port, each carrying an incident wave \(a\) and an emerging wave \(b\). Source: RF Pulchowk Ch3 deck.
Step 2: the defining matrix
  • The network is linear, so each outgoing wave is a weighted sum of all the incoming ones: \[ b_1 = S_{11}a_1 + S_{12}a_2, \qquad b_2 = S_{21}a_1 + S_{22}a_2 \] \[ \begin{bmatrix} b_1 \\ b_2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} S_{11} & S_{12} \\ S_{21} & S_{22} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} a_1 \\ a_2 \end{bmatrix} \quad\text{i.e.}\quad [b] = [S][a] \]
  • Subscript order: in \(S_{ij}\) the second index \(j\) is the port driven, the first index \(i\) is the port observed. \(S_{21}\) is “out of 2, in at 1”.
  • Written out, the matrix is the complete input-output description of the black box: knowing four numbers replaces solving for every internal voltage and current.
Step 3: isolate each parameter
  • Terminate the unused port in \(Z_0\). A matched load reflects nothing, so its incident wave vanishes and one column of the matrix survives at a time.
ParameterConditionMeaning
\(S_{11} = \dfrac{b_1}{a_1}\)\(a_2 = 0\)Input reflection coefficient, port 2 matched
\(S_{21} = \dfrac{b_2}{a_1}\)\(a_2 = 0\)Forward transmission (gain or insertion loss)
\(S_{12} = \dfrac{b_1}{a_2}\)\(a_1 = 0\)Reverse transmission (isolation, feedback)
\(S_{22} = \dfrac{b_2}{a_2}\)\(a_1 = 0\)Output reflection coefficient, port 1 matched
  • \(a_2 = 0\) means “port 2 terminated in \(Z_0\)”, never “port 2 open”. Writing “open circuit” here loses the mark, because it is exactly the condition S-parameters were invented to avoid.
Signal-flow graph of the same two-port: four branches, one per S-parameter. Useful when the question asks for a “flow diagram”.
Step 4: tie \(S_{11}\) back to impedance
  • With port 2 matched, port 1 simply sees the input impedance \(Z_{in}\), so \[ S_{11} = \Gamma_{in} = \frac{Z_{in} - Z_0}{Z_{in} + Z_0} \]
  • This is the bridge to Chapter 2: a one-port load has the single entry \([S] = [\,\Gamma_L\,]\), and a perfectly matched two-port has \([S] = \left[\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right]\) (\(\S\)2.8).
Step 5: generalise to \(n\) ports
  • \(b_i = \sum_{j=1}^{n} S_{ij}a_j\), an \(n \times n\) matrix with \(n^2\) entries: \[ S_{ij} = \left.\frac{b_i}{a_j}\right|_{a_k = 0,\ k \neq j} \]
  • Rows and columns both equal the port count, so a 3-port gives \(3\times3\) and a magic tee gives \(4\times4\).
  • Reference impedance: every entry is defined against the same \(Z_0\) (usually \(50\,\Omega\)), so a quoted matrix without its \(Z_0\) and its frequency is incomplete.

column1: State and justify the properties of the scattering matrix
column4:
P1. Zero diagonal \(\Leftrightarrow\) matched port
  • \(S_{ii} = 0\) means a wave arriving at port \(i\) is not reflected, so that port is matched to \(Z_0\).
  • “Matched at all ports” means the whole diagonal is zero.
P2. Symmetry \(\Leftrightarrow\) reciprocity
  • \(S_{ij} = S_{ji}\) for all \(i, j\), i.e. \([S] = [S]^{T}\).
  • Holds for networks built of passive, linear, isotropic media: lines, stubs, tees, couplers, resistors, capacitors, transformers.
  • Fails for magnetised ferrite (circulator, isolator, gyrator) and for active devices (amplifier, transistor), where \(S_{21} \neq S_{12}\) by design.
  • So a matrix that is not symmetric can never be a passive isotropic device.
P3. Unitary \(\Leftrightarrow\) lossless
  • A lossless network redirects power but never dissipates it, which forces \[ [S]^{*T}[S] = [I] \]
  • Reading that out column by column gives the two tests actually used in exams:
    • Column-sum test (each column carries unit power): \[ \sum_{k=1}^{n} |S_{ki}|^2 = 1 \quad \text{for every } i \]
    • Orthogonality test (distinct columns are orthogonal): \[ \sum_{k=1}^{n} S_{ki}\,S_{kj}^{*} = 0 \quad \text{for every } i \neq j \]
  • If a column sums to less than 1, the shortfall is the fraction of incident power the network dissipates, which is how “is it lossless?” is answered numerically (\(\S\)3.4 and Problem 1 of the companion).
P4. Shifting the reference plane multiplies by a phase
  • Move the reference plane of port \(i\) outward by an electrical length \(\theta_i = \beta \ell_i\). Then \[ S'_{ij} = S_{ij}\,e^{-j(\theta_i + \theta_j)} \]
  • Diagonal terms pick up \(e^{-2j\theta_i}\), because the wave travels the added length twice.
  • Magnitudes are unchanged: \(|S'_{ij}| = |S_{ij}|\). Return loss, insertion loss and VSWR do not depend on where the plane is drawn; only phase does.
  • This is why an S-parameter measurement is meaningless until the planes are declared, and why a VNA must be calibrated to a stated plane.
P5. Complex, frequency dependent, \(n^2\) entries
  • Each \(S_{ij}\) carries a magnitude and an angle, and both move with frequency, so a quoted set is meaningless without its \(f\) and its \(Z_0\).
  • An \(n\)-port has \(n^2\) coefficients; symmetry and structural zeros cut the number of independent ones sharply (the magic tee has 16 entries but only 2 distinct values).
P6. Symmetric and antimetric two-ports
  • Symmetric: reciprocal and \(S_{11} = S_{22}\). The network looks the same from either end.
  • Antimetric: \(S_{11} = -S_{22}\).
The four tests as an exam checklist
TestLook forConclusion
Diagonal\(S_{ii} = 0\)?That port is matched
Transpose\([S] = [S]^{T}\)?Reciprocal (passive) or not (ferrite / active)
Column sums\(\sum_k|S_{ki}|^2 = 1\)?Lossless, else lossy by the shortfall
Column dots\(\sum_k S_{ki}S_{kj}^{*} = 0\)?Confirms lossless, ties the phases
Run the four in this order on any matrix the examiner prints: they are enough to name the device (\(\S\)3.7) and to answer every “judge the condition” rider.

column1: Define return loss and insertion loss, and the losses associated with a two-port network
column4:
The three powers at a port
  • \(P_i\) incident, \(P_r\) reflected, \(P_t\) transmitted; whatever is left over is dissipated.
  • Everything below is a ratio of two of those, expressed in dB and rewritten in terms of \([S]\).
QuantityIn terms of \([S]\)What it tells you
Return loss\(RL = -20\log_{10}|S_{11}|\)How well port 1 is matched. Bigger is better
Insertion loss\(IL = -20\log_{10}|S_{21}|\)Power lost passing through. \(0\) dB is ideal
Isolation\(-20\log_{10}|S_{12}|\)Leakage backwards. Bigger is better
Forward gain\(G = 20\log_{10}|S_{21}|\)Same number as \(IL\), opposite sign, used for amplifiers
VSWR\(\dfrac{1+|S_{11}|}{1-|S_{11}|}\)The same match on a \(1\) to \(\infty\) scale
Reflection (mismatch) loss\(-10\log_{10}\!\left(1-|S_{11}|^2\right)\)The part of \(P_i\) that never enters the network
Dissipated fraction\(1 - \sum_k |S_{k1}|^2\)What the network eats. Zero for a lossless network
  • Useful anchors: \(|S_{11}| = 0.5 \rightarrow RL = 6\) dB, VSWR \(=3\); \(|S_{11}| = 0.1 \rightarrow RL = 20\) dB, VSWR \(= 1.22\); \(|S_{11}| = 0 \rightarrow\) perfect match, \(RL = \infty\).
What each S-parameter of a device under test is called in the lab. Source: RF Pulchowk Ch3 deck.
Sign conventions that cost marks
  • Return loss and insertion loss are quoted as positive dB for a passive device. The minus sign is already in the definition.
  • \(20\log\) for a ratio of waves (\(S\) is an amplitude ratio), \(10\log\) for a ratio of powers. Mixing the two is the commonest slip.
Reading a device off its numbers
  • Small \(|S_{11}|\), \(|S_{22}|\) \(\rightarrow\) well matched at both ends.
  • \(|S_{21}| > 1\) \(\rightarrow\) active: the device has gain.
  • \(|S_{21}| < 1\) with \(S_{12} = S_{21}\) \(\rightarrow\) passive and reciprocal: an attenuator, filter or line.
  • \(|S_{12}| \ll |S_{21}|\) \(\rightarrow\) unilateral: an amplifier or isolator; the smaller \(|S_{12}|\) is, the more stable the amplifier tends to be.
  • This is the whole method for 82 Bh, which prints two amplifier S-parameter sets and asks only for “the basic differences”. Problem 2 of the companion works it.
verified/added Correction to the source notes
  • The RF Pulchowk deck prints \(IL\,\text{(dB)} = 10\log\left(|a_1|^2/|b_1|^2\right)\).
  • \(|b_1|\) is the wave coming back out of port 1, so that expression is the return loss, not the insertion loss.
  • Insertion loss compares the incident wave with what leaves the far port: \[ IL = 10\log\frac{|a_1|^2}{|b_2|^2} = 20\log\frac{1}{|S_{21}|} \] which is what the deck's own next line prints. Use the \(|S_{21}|\) form.

column1: Analyse a three-port network using S-parameters. Write the properties of a 3-port network and define its characteristic parameters
column4:
The general 3-port
  • Nine coefficients: \[ [S] = \begin{bmatrix} S_{11} & S_{12} & S_{13} \\ S_{21} & S_{22} & S_{23} \\ S_{31} & S_{32} & S_{33} \end{bmatrix} \]
  • Characteristic parameters an examiner expects you to define:
    • Matching: \(S_{ii}\), hence return loss and VSWR at each port.
    • Coupling / division ratio: \(|S_{ij}|^2\), the fraction of the input power delivered to port \(i\).
    • Isolation: \(-20\log|S_{ij}|\) for the pair meant to be decoupled.
    • Phase relation: \(\arg S_{13}\) against \(\arg S_{23}\), i.e. whether the two output arms are in phase or in antiphase.
    • Insertion loss and bandwidth over which all of the above hold.
The non-reciprocal escape, drawn
(a) clockwise, (b) counterclockwise circulator with its \([S]\): zero diagonal (matched), one unit entry per column (lossless), and \([S] \neq [S]^T\). Pozar Fig 7.2.
The three escapes, and the device each one gives
Give upDeviceConsequence
LosslessResistive divider, matched 3-portAll ports matched and reciprocal, but power is burnt in the resistors
ReciprocalCirculator (ferrite)Matched and lossless, but \(S_{ij} \neq S_{ji}\); power circulates \(1\!\to\!2\!\to\!3\!\to\!1\)
Matched at every portE-plane tee, H-plane tee, T-junctionLossless and reciprocal, but only the side arm can be matched
  • Ideal circulator, matched and lossless but not reciprocal: \[ [S] = \begin{bmatrix} 0&0&1 \\ 1&0&0 \\ 0&1&0 \end{bmatrix} \] Terminate port 3 in a matched load and it becomes an isolator.
  • A 4-port escapes the trap entirely: a directional coupler and a magic tee are matched, lossless and reciprocal all at once, which is exactly why the exam favourite is a 4-port (\(\S\)3.6).
Theorem: no 3-port is lossless, reciprocal and matched at once
  • Assume all three. Matched gives \(S_{11}=S_{22}=S_{33}=0\), reciprocal gives \(S_{ij}=S_{ji}\), so \[ [S] = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & S_{12} & S_{13} \\ S_{12} & 0 & S_{23} \\ S_{13} & S_{23} & 0 \end{bmatrix} \]
  • Apply the orthogonality test to each pair of columns: \[ S_{13}^{*}S_{23} = 0, \qquad S_{12}^{*}S_{23} = 0, \qquad S_{12}^{*}S_{13} = 0 \] so at least two of \(S_{12}, S_{13}, S_{23}\) must be zero.
  • Apply the column-sum test: \[ |S_{12}|^2 + |S_{13}|^2 = 1, \quad |S_{12}|^2 + |S_{23}|^2 = 1, \quad |S_{13}|^2 + |S_{23}|^2 = 1 \] which requires all three to be non-zero.
  • The two demands contradict, so no such network exists. Give up exactly one of the three properties.
E-plane tee: the worked 3-port (\(\S\)3.6 has the full matrix)
  • Ports 1 and 2 collinear, port 3 the E-arm, assumed matched to the junction.
  • Three physical facts start the derivation:
    • An input at the E-arm splits into two outputs that are \(180^\circ\) out of phase: \(S_{23} = -S_{13}\).
    • Port 3 is matched: \(S_{33} = 0\).
    • The junction is passive and isotropic: \(S_{ij} = S_{ji}\).
  • Four unknowns are left, and the unitary property fixes all four (\(\S\)3.6, and Problem 5 of the companion works every line).
  • Ports 1 and 2 cannot be matched, and indeed the answer gives \(S_{11} = S_{22} = 1/2\), which is the theorem showing up in the arithmetic.

column1: Prepare the S-matrices of a perfectly working E-plane Tee, H-plane Tee and a Duplexer, and explore their uses
column4:
E-plane tee (series tee)
  • Side arm in the plane of the E field, so it excites the collinear arms in antiphase. \[ [S] = \begin{bmatrix} \tfrac{1}{2} & \tfrac{1}{2} & \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\[2pt] \tfrac{1}{2} & \tfrac{1}{2} & -\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\[2pt] \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 \end{bmatrix} \]
  • Fingerprint: the \(-1/\sqrt{2}\) in the third row / column.
  • Use: power splitting with a phase reversal; the difference arm of a magic tee.
  • Ports 1 and 2 are not matched (\(S_{11}=S_{22}=1/2\)), which is the 3-port theorem of \(\S\)3.5 showing up in the answer.
H-plane tee (shunt tee)
  • Side arm in the plane of the H field, so the collinear arms come out in phase. \[ [S] = \begin{bmatrix} \tfrac{1}{2} & -\tfrac{1}{2} & \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\[2pt] -\tfrac{1}{2} & \tfrac{1}{2} & \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\[2pt] \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 \end{bmatrix} \]
  • Fingerprint: the minus sign has moved to \(S_{12}\); the side-arm column is all positive.
  • Use: in-phase power divider or combiner; the sum arm of a magic tee.
  • E-tee vs H-tee in one line: same geometry, same magnitudes, opposite phase relation. The E-tee subtracts, the H-tee adds.
Magic tee (hybrid tee): the exam favourite
  • Ports 1 and 2 collinear, port 3 the E-arm (difference), port 4 the H-arm (sum). Four physical facts:
    • E-arm drive gives antiphase outputs: \(S_{23} = -S_{13}\).
    • H-arm drive gives in-phase outputs: \(S_{24} = +S_{14}\).
    • E-arm and H-arm are decoupled: \(S_{34} = S_{43} = 0\).
    • Ports 3 and 4 matched: \(S_{33} = S_{44} = 0\); and the collinear arms are decoupled, \(S_{12} = S_{21} = 0\).
  • The unitary property then forces \(S_{11} = S_{22} = 0\) as well, so the tee ends up matched at all four ports: \[ [S] = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \]
  • Fingerprint: an all-zero \(2\times2\) block on each diagonal, one column with a sign flip (E-arm), one without (H-arm).
Circulator, isolator, gyrator
  • Circulator: \([S]\) as in \(\S\)3.5, matched and lossless but not symmetric.
  • Isolator: a circulator with port 3 loaded, \([S] = \left[\begin{smallmatrix}0&0\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right]\); forward passes, reverse is absorbed.
  • Gyrator: \([S] = \left[\begin{smallmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right]\), a \(180^\circ\) phase difference between the two directions.
Directional coupler
  • Through arm \(\alpha\), coupled arm \(j\beta\), isolated arm 0, with \(\alpha^2 + \beta^2 = 1\): \[ [S] = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & \alpha & j\beta & 0 \\ \alpha & 0 & 0 & j\beta \\ j\beta & 0 & 0 & \alpha \\ 0 & j\beta & \alpha & 0 \end{bmatrix} \]
  • A \(3\) dB coupler has \(\alpha = \beta = 1/\sqrt{2}\), and is then a magic tee in quadrature form.
Duplexer
  • Circulator duplexer (the usual answer): port 1 transmitter, port 2 antenna, port 3 receiver. Ideally lossless, so all the transmitter power reaches the antenna and all the echo reaches the receiver, with the transmitter isolated from the receiver.
  • Magic-tee duplexer: transmitter on the H-arm, antenna and a matched dummy load on the collinear arms, receiver on the E-arm. Splits the transmitter power in half and keeps transmitter and receiver isolated. This is the version 76 Bh asks for (\(\S\)3.8).
Amplifier, attenuator, amplitude modulator
  • Matched amplifier: \([S] = \left[\begin{smallmatrix}0&S_{12}\\S_{21}&0\end{smallmatrix}\right]\) with \(|S_{21}| > 1 \gg |S_{12}|\). Not reciprocal, not lossless.
  • Matched attenuator of \(L\) dB: \([S] = \left[\begin{smallmatrix}0&\alpha\\ \alpha&0\end{smallmatrix}\right]\), \(\alpha = 10^{-L/20}\). Reciprocal but lossy.
  • Amplitude modulator (78 Ch): a matched, reciprocal two-port whose transmission is driven by the modulating signal, \[ [S] = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & \alpha(t) \\ \alpha(t) & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \alpha(t) = \alpha_0\left(1 + m\cos\omega_m t\right) \] Problem 6 of the companion derives it and evaluates the numbers.

column1: verified/added Magic tee with both E- and H-arms short-circuited
column4:
• Shorts at the junction reference plane give \(a_3 = -b_3\) and \(a_4 = -b_4\).
  • Substituting into the magic-tee equations collapses the 4-port to the two-port seen from ports 1 and 2: \[ [S]_{\text{shorted}} = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix} \]
  • Behaviour: each collinear arm reflects all of its incident power with a \(180^\circ\) phase reversal, and the two arms stay completely isolated from each other.
  • The E-arm and H-arm reflections add in the driven arm and cancel in the other one, which is why \(S_{21}\) stays zero.
  • Still lossless (each column sums to 1), still reciprocal. The tee has become a pair of independent short circuits, useful as a reflective phase shifter or a reference short.

column1: Identify and explain, with a neat diagram, the passive microwave device described by the given S-matrix
column4:
The six-step method
  1. Count the ports: the order of the matrix is the port count. \(4\times4\) narrows it to coupler, magic tee or hybrid ring immediately.
  2. Read the diagonal: zeros mark the matched ports. An all-zero diagonal on a 4-port means matched everywhere.
  3. Test the transpose: symmetric means passive and isotropic; asymmetric means ferrite or active.
  4. Test the columns: sums of 1 and orthogonal pairs mean lossless. A shortfall is dissipation.
  5. Map the zeros: an off-diagonal zero is an isolated pair. Which pairs are decoupled is the strongest single clue.
  6. Read the signs and the \(j\)'s: a sign flip down a column means an antiphase (difference, E) arm; matching signs mean an in-phase (sum, H) arm; a factor \(j\) means a quadrature coupled arm.
Answer skeleton
  • Name the device in the first line. Do not narrate the tests first.
  • Draw it: the 3D waveguide sketch with all arms labelled, plus the schematic.
  • Justify with the four tests, one line each.
  • Close with two uses and one limitation (the tee needs matching irises at the collinear arms to reach the ideal matrix in practice).
Fingerprint table
PatternDevice
\(2\times2\), \(S_{11}=S_{22}=0\), \(S_{12}=S_{21}=1\)Matched lossless line or ideal matched network
\(2\times2\), \(S_{12}=0\), \(S_{21}=1\)Isolator
\(2\times2\), \(|S_{21}|>1\), \(|S_{12}|\) tinyAmplifier (active, not reciprocal)
\(3\times3\), cyclic ones, not symmetricCirculator
\(3\times3\) with a \(\pm1/\sqrt{2}\) columnE-plane tee (\(-\)) or H-plane tee (\(+\))
\(4\times4\), zero diagonal, two zero \(2\times2\) blocks, one column sign-flippedMagic tee
\(4\times4\), zero diagonal, \(j\) on the coupled arm, one zero per rowDirectional coupler
The four matrices the papers actually print
  • 78 Ch 10, printed without its normalising factor: \[ [S] = \begin{bmatrix} 0&0&1&1 \\ 0&0&-1&1 \\ 1&-1&0&0 \\ 1&1&0&0 \end{bmatrix} \] Zero diagonal, symmetric, the \((1,2)\) and \((3,4)\) blocks zero, column 3 sign-flipped: magic tee. It is unitary only after dividing by \(\sqrt{2}\), and saying so earns the “judge the condition” mark.
  • 81 Bh 5 and 74 Bh 8, printed symbolically: \[ [S] = \begin{bmatrix} S_{11}&S_{12}&S_{13}&S_{14} \\ S_{12}&S_{22}&S_{13}&-S_{14} \\ S_{13}&S_{13}&0&0 \\ S_{14}&-S_{14}&0&0 \end{bmatrix} \] Column 3 in phase (H-arm), column 4 antiphase (E-arm), \(S_{33}=S_{44}=0\): the magic tee before the unitary property is applied. Finish the job and \(S_{11}=S_{22}=S_{12}=0\), \(S_{13}=S_{14}=1/\sqrt{2}\).
  • 75 Bh 6, the same device with the collinear isolation already written in: \[ [S] = \begin{bmatrix} S_{11}&0&S_{13}&S_{14} \\ 0&S_{22}&-S_{13}&S_{14} \\ S_{13}&-S_{13}&0&0 \\ S_{14}&S_{14}&0&0 \end{bmatrix} \] Here column 3 is the antiphase E-arm and column 4 the in-phase H-arm, the mirror of the previous labelling. Read the signs, not the port numbers.
  • 82 Bh 4 prints two amplifier sets instead, so steps 3 and 4 answer it: \(S_{12} \neq S_{21}\) and \(|S_{21}| > 1\) make both of them active and neither reciprocal (\(\S\)3.4, Problem 2).
Why the signs fall where they do
\(E\) in the collinear arms (2), (3) of a magic tee. (a) fed from the H-arm (Pozar's port 1, the sum port): the arms are driven in phase, the matching-sign column. (b) fed from the E-arm (4): antiphase, the sign-flipped column. Pozar numbers the arms differently from the papers, so label by E and H, not by number. Pozar Fig 7.50.

column1: Two identical radar transmitters must deliver twice the power to one antenna; and an ASR needs half the transmitter power at the antenna through a duplexer. Solve both with an S-matrix
column4:
Combining: two transmitters into one antenna
  • Device: magic tee (or a \(3\) dB hybrid coupler).
  • Connection: the two transmitters drive the collinear arms 1 and 2 in phase and at equal amplitude; the antenna hangs on the H-arm (port 4); the E-arm (port 3) carries a matched dummy load.
  • Mathematics, with \(a_1 = a_2 = a\) and \(a_3 = a_4 = 0\): \[ b_4 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(a_1 + a_2) = \sqrt{2}\,a \;\Rightarrow\; |b_4|^2 = 2|a|^2 \] \[ b_3 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(a_1 - a_2) = 0 \]
  • Result: the antenna receives \(2P\), twice what either transmitter can deliver, and the dummy load receives nothing.
  • Why the tee and not a plain T-junction: \(S_{12} = 0\), so the two transmitters are isolated and cannot pull or damage each other; and all four ports stay matched, so neither transmitter sees a VSWR.
  • Practical riders worth a mark each:
    • Phase must be equalised, so the two feed lines are cut to the same electrical length.
    • Amplitude imbalance \(\Delta\) shows up as \(|b_3|^2 \neq 0\): the dummy load absorbs exactly the mismatch, which is what protects the transmitters.
    • The dummy load must be rated for the full unbalanced power.
Splitting: half the transmitter power to the antenna
  • Device: the same magic tee, used as a duplexer, driven from the H-arm.
  • Connection: transmitter on port 4 (H-arm), antenna on port 1, matched load on port 2, receiver on port 3 (E-arm).
  • Mathematics, with \(a_4 = a\) and all other inputs zero: \[ b_1 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}a, \quad b_2 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}a \;\Rightarrow\; |b_1|^2 = |b_2|^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}|a|^2 \] \[ b_3 = 0 \]
  • Result: the antenna gets exactly \(P/2\), as 76 Bh requires, and the receiver on the E-arm gets none of the transmitter power, which is the whole point of a duplexer.
  • On receive, the echo arrives at port 1 alone and divides between the E-arm and the H-arm, so half of it reaches the receiver. The \(3\) dB penalty in each direction is the price of the magic-tee duplexer, and naming it shows you understand the device rather than reciting it.
  • Better answer for a real ASR: a ferrite circulator duplexer routes the full power \(1 \rightarrow 2\) and the full echo \(2 \rightarrow 3\) with no \(3\) dB loss. Quote it as the improvement whenever the question does not force the half-power split.
Answer skeleton for both
  • Name the device, draw it with every arm labelled and every termination named.
  • Write \([S]\) for the magic tee.
  • Write the drive vector \([a]\) the connection creates.
  • Multiply out, and read the answer off \(|b|^2\).
  • Close with the isolation and matching argument: that is the “sufficient explanation” the marks are for.
The schematic to draw beside the tee
  • A magic tee is a \(180^\circ\) hybrid: sum port \(\Sigma\) (the H-arm) and difference port \(\Delta\) (the E-arm), with outputs (2) and (3).
  • Combining: equal in-phase inputs at (2), (3) add at \(\Sigma\) and cancel at \(\Delta\), so the dummy load on \(\Delta\) sees nothing.
  • Splitting: drive \(\Sigma\) and (2), (3) each get half, in phase; \(\Delta\) stays isolated.
  • Pozar Fig 7.41.

column1: Chapter 3 numericals — which formulas does everything come from?
column4:
12 solved PYQ problems  \(\cdot\)  \(\approx\)100 marks across 11 papers  \(\cdot\)  2 numeric matrices, 3 derivations, 3 identifications, 3 design problems, 1 modulator
READ THIS FIRST
Chapter 3 numericals are not arithmetic problems. Every one of them is the same four tests of \(\S\)3.3 applied to a matrix, or the same five-step derivation run backwards to build one. Nothing here needs a calculator beyond \(\sqrt{2}\), a square and a \(\log\). Every number below was computed and asserted in src/sparam.py, which re-derives each device matrix from its stated properties rather than quoting it.
  • Always run the four tests in the same order, and always write them as a table. Examiners give a mark per test; a paragraph hides them.
  • A matrix that is not unitary is not wrong, it is lossy. Say so, and say how much: the shortfall in a column is the dissipated fraction.
  • Watch the normalising factor. Papers print magic-tee matrices without the \(1/\sqrt{2}\). Spotting that it is missing is worth a mark on its own.
  • Sign, not port number, names the arm. A column whose entries flip sign is the E-arm (difference); a column whose entries match is the H-arm (sum). Papers swap which port number carries which.
