column1: M. The Four Methods, in Brief
column4:
M1: the four tests (Problems 1, 6, 7, 8)
  1. Diagonal: which \(S_{ii} = 0\)? Those ports are matched.
  2. Transpose: is \(S_{ij} = S_{ji}\) for every pair? Yes means reciprocal (passive, isotropic); no means ferrite or active.
  3. Column sums: is \(\sum_k |S_{ki}|^2 = 1\) for every column? Yes means lossless; the shortfall is the dissipated fraction of the incident power.
  4. Column dots: is \(\sum_k S_{ki}S_{kj}^{*} = 0\) for every \(i \neq j\)? This is the phase half of the unitary condition.
Always write M1 as this table
TestComputationConclusion
Diagonalevery \(S_{ii}\)matched / not
Transpose\(S_{ij}\) vs \(S_{ji}\)reciprocal / not
Column sums\(\sum_k|S_{ki}|^2\)lossless, or lossy by the shortfall
Column dots\(\sum_k S_{ki}S_{kj}^{*}\)phases consistent / not
M2: build a device matrix from its physics (Problems 3, 4, 5)
  1. Write the blank \(n \times n\) matrix.
  2. Impose the phase facts: which arms come out in phase (\(S_{2k} = +S_{1k}\)) and which in antiphase (\(S_{2k} = -S_{1k}\)).
  3. Impose the matching facts: \(S_{kk} = 0\) for every port the question calls “perfectly matched to the junction”.
  4. Impose reciprocity, \(S_{ij} = S_{ji}\), and count what is left. Both a plane tee and a magic tee leave exactly 4 unknowns.
  5. Apply the unitary property \([S][S]^{*} = [I]\) and read off the equations row by row. Each row-column product gives one equation; solve.
M3: reduce an \(n\)-port by terminating ports (Problem 9)
  1. A termination on port \(k\) forces \(a_k = \Gamma_k b_k\), with \(\Gamma = -1\) for a short, \(+1\) for an open, \(0\) for a matched load, all measured at the junction reference plane.
  2. Write out \(b_i = \sum_j S_{ij}a_j\) for every port.
  3. Substitute the constraint for each terminated port and eliminate its \(a\) and \(b\).
  4. What is left is the smaller matrix seen from the remaining ports.
M4: power bookkeeping (Problems 1, 10, 11)
  1. Write the drive vector \([a]\) that the connection creates. One transmitter on port 1 alone is \([a] = [a_1, 0, 0, 0]^T\); two equal in-phase transmitters on ports 1 and 2 is \([a] = [a, a, 0, 0]^T\).
  2. Multiply: \([b] = [S][a]\).
  3. Power leaving port \(i\) is \(|b_i|^2\), in the same units as \(|a|^2\).
  4. Check the books: \(\sum_i |b_i|^2 \le \sum_j |a_j|^2\), with equality for a lossless network.
The conversions used throughout
  • \(RL = -20\log_{10}|S_{11}|\) dB,  \(IL = -20\log_{10}|S_{21}|\) dB.
  • \(G = +20\log_{10}|S_{21}|\) dB,   \(\text{VSWR} = \dfrac{1+|S_{11}|}{1-|S_{11}|}\).
  • \(P_{\text{ref}} = |S_{11}|^2 P_{\text{inc}}\),   \(P_{\text{trans}} = |S_{21}|^2 P_{\text{inc}}\).
  • \(P_{\text{diss}} = \left(1 - \sum_k |S_{k1}|^2\right) P_{\text{inc}}\).
  • \(1/\sqrt{2} = 0.7071\), and \(\left(1/\sqrt{2}\right)^2 = 0.5\): half the power.

column1: Problem 1: The four tests on a numeric two-port matrix
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 79 Bh [3+1+1+1+2]
Why are S-parameters used in high frequencies? The S-matrix of a certain microwave network is given as \([S] = \begin{bmatrix} 0.4+j0.5 & j0.6 \\ j0.6 & 0.4-j0.5 \end{bmatrix}\). (a) Is the network reciprocal? (b) Is the network lossless? (c) What is the return loss at the input? (d) If the input power to the network is 5 watts, what is the reflected power?
column4:
Given
  • \(S_{11} = 0.4+j0.5\),  \(S_{12} = S_{21} = j0.6\),  \(S_{22} = 0.4-j0.5\).
  • Input power \(P_{in} = 5\) W at port 1; port 2 terminated in \(Z_0\).
Step 0: the magnitudes, computed once and reused
  • \(|S_{11}| = \sqrt{0.4^2 + 0.5^2} = \sqrt{0.16+0.25} = \sqrt{0.41} = 0.6403\).
  • \(|S_{22}| = \sqrt{0.4^2 + (-0.5)^2} = \sqrt{0.41} = 0.6403\) (the same).
  • \(|S_{12}| = |S_{21}| = |j0.6| = 0.6\).
  • Squares, which is what every power test needs: \(|S_{11}|^2 = |S_{22}|^2 = 0.41\),  \(|S_{12}|^2 = |S_{21}|^2 = 0.36\).
Step 1: run the four tests
TestComputationResultConclusion
Diagonal\(S_{11} = 0.4+j0.5 eq 0\), \(S_{22} = 0.4-j0.5 eq 0\)both non-zeroNeither port is matched
Transpose\(S_{12} = j0.6\) and \(S_{21} = j0.6\)\(S_{12} = S_{21}\)(a) Reciprocal ✓
Column 1 sum\(|S_{11}|^2 + |S_{21}|^2 = 0.41 + 0.36\)\(0.77 eq 1\)(b) Not lossless
Column 2 sum\(|S_{12}|^2 + |S_{22}|^2 = 0.36 + 0.41\)\(0.77 eq 1\)Same shortfall at port 2
Column dot\(S_{11}S_{12}^{*} + S_{21}S_{22}^{*}\) \(= (0.4+j0.5)(-j0.6) + (j0.6)(0.4+j0.5)\) \(= (0.30 - j0.24) + (-0.30 + j0.24)\)\(0\)Phases are consistent; only the magnitudes fail
  • (a) \(S_{12} = S_{21} = j0.6\), so the network is \( oxed{ ext{reciprocal}}\): it is passive and contains no ferrite and no active device.
  • (b) Both columns sum to \(0.77\), not \(1\), so the network is \( oxed{ ext{not lossless}}\). It dissipates \(1 - 0.77 = 0.23\), i.e. 23% of whatever is fed into either port.
  • Worth adding: the column-dot test passes. A network can have the right phase relations and still be lossy, which is why both halves of the unitary condition must be checked.
Step 2: (c) return loss at the input
  • Return loss compares incident with reflected power at port 1, and \(S_{11}\) is an amplitude ratio, so the factor is \(20\): \[ RL = -20\log_{10}|S_{11}| = -20\log_{10}(0.6403) \]
  • \(\log_{10}(0.6403) = -0.19361\), so \(RL = -20 imes (-0.19361)\).
  • (c) \( oxed{RL = 3.87\ ext{dB}}\).
  • Sanity check: a low return loss means a bad match, and indeed VSWR \(= \dfrac{1+0.6403}{1-0.6403} = \dfrac{1.6403}{0.3597} = 4.56\), far from 1.
Step 3: (d) reflected power for 5 W in
  • Power scales as the square of the wave amplitude: \[ P_{ref} = |S_{11}|^2 \, P_{in} = 0.41 imes 5 \]
  • (d) \( oxed{P_{ref} = 2.05\ ext{W}}\).
Step 4: complete the power budget (free marks)
ComponentFormulaValueShare of 5 W
Reflected at port 1\(|S_{11}|^2 P_{in} = 0.41 imes 5\)\(2.05\) W\(41\%\)
Delivered to port 2\(|S_{21}|^2 P_{in} = 0.36 imes 5\)\(1.80\) W\(36\%\)
Dissipated inside\((1-0.77) imes 5\)\(1.15\) W\(23\%\)
Total\(\mathbf{5.00}\) W\(100\%\)
  • The three rows sum to the input, which is the arithmetic check that the whole answer is consistent.
  • Insertion loss, if asked: \(IL = -20\log_{10}(0.6) = oxed{4.44\ ext{dB}}\).
Answer to the theory rider (3 marks)
  • S-parameters are used at high frequencies because total \(V\) and \(I\) are not uniquely defined when the circuit is comparable to \(\lambda\), because open and short terminations cannot be realised broadband and would destroy or oscillate active devices, and because power is what microwave instruments actually measure. See \(\S\)3.1.

column1: Problem 2: Comparing two amplifier S-parameter sets
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 82 Bh [4]
Find the basic differences of the systems having the following sets of S-matrix.
(a) \(S_{11} = 0.65\angle146^\circ\), \(S_{12} = 0.12\angle46^\circ\), \(S_{21} = 2.30\angle44^\circ\), \(S_{22} = 0.17\angle{-172^\circ}\)
(b) \(S_{11} = 0.30\angle{-134^\circ}\), \(S_{12} = 0.03\angle46^\circ\), \(S_{21} = 2.20\angle44^\circ\), \(S_{22} = 0.10\angle{-172^\circ}\)
column4:
Given
  • Two two-port sets, quoted in polar form. Only the magnitudes matter for the comparison the question asks for; the angles matter only for \(\Delta\) and \(K\).
Step 1: what kind of device is each? (the two tests that decide it)
TestComputationResultConclusion
Transpose(a) \(|S_{12}| = 0.12\) vs \(|S_{21}| = 2.30\); (b) \(0.03\) vs \(2.20\)\(S_{12} \neq S_{21}\) in bothBoth are non-reciprocal
Column 1 sum(a) \(0.65^2 + 2.30^2 = 0.4225 + 5.29\); (b) \(0.30^2 + 2.20^2\)\(5.71\) and \(4.93\), both \(\gg 1\)Both are active: they add power
  • \(|S_{21}| > 1\) means the device has gain, so neither set can describe a passive component. Both are transistor amplifiers at the same frequency; the question is which is the better one.
Step 2: convert every magnitude into its engineering figure
QuantityFormulaSystem (a)System (b)Better
Forward gain\(20\log_{10}|S_{21}|\)\(7.23\) dB\(6.85\) dB(a), barely
Reverse isolation\(-20\log_{10}|S_{12}|\)\(18.42\) dB\(30.46\) dB(b), by 12 dB
Input return loss\(-20\log_{10}|S_{11}|\)\(3.74\) dB\(10.46\) dB(b)
Input VSWR\(\frac{1+|S_{11}|}{1-|S_{11}|}\)\(4.71\)\(1.86\)(b)
Output return loss\(-20\log_{10}|S_{22}|\)\(15.39\) dB\(20.00\) dB(b)
Output VSWR\(\frac{1+|S_{22}|}{1-|S_{22}|}\)\(1.41\)\(1.22\)(b)
  • Sample line, so the arithmetic is visible: \(-20\log_{10}(0.65) = -20 \times (-0.18709) = 3.74\) dB, and \(\text{VSWR} = (1+0.65)/(1-0.65) = 1.65/0.35 = 4.71\).
Step 3: stability, the one place the angles are needed
  • \(\Delta = S_{11}S_{22} - S_{12}S_{21}\), and \(K = \dfrac{1 - |S_{11}|^2 - |S_{22}|^2 + |\Delta|^2}{2|S_{12}S_{21}|}\).
  • System (a):
    • \(S_{11}S_{22} = (0.65)(0.17)\angle(146^\circ - 172^\circ) = 0.1105\angle{-26^\circ} = 0.0993 - j0.0484\).
    • \(S_{12}S_{21} = (0.12)(2.30)\angle(46^\circ + 44^\circ) = 0.276\angle90^\circ = j0.276\).
    • \(\Delta = 0.0993 - j0.0484 - j0.276 = 0.0993 - j0.3244\), so \(|\Delta| = 0.3393\).
    • \(K = \dfrac{1 - 0.4225 - 0.0289 + 0.1151}{2 \times 0.276} = \dfrac{0.6637}{0.552} = 1.202\).
  • System (b):
    • \(S_{11}S_{22} = (0.30)(0.10)\angle(-134^\circ - 172^\circ) = 0.03\angle54^\circ = 0.0176 + j0.0243\).
    • \(S_{12}S_{21} = (0.03)(2.20)\angle90^\circ = j0.066\).
    • \(\Delta = 0.0176 - j0.0417\), so \(|\Delta| = 0.0453\).
    • \(K = \dfrac{1 - 0.09 - 0.01 + 0.0021}{2 \times 0.066} = \dfrac{0.9021}{0.132} = 6.834\).
  • Both have \(K > 1\) and \(|\Delta| < 1\), so both are unconditionally stable, but (b) is stable by a wide margin and (a) only just.
Answer: the basic differences
  • Both are active, non-reciprocal two-ports, i.e. amplifiers of nearly the same gain (\(7.23\) dB against \(6.85\) dB, a difference of \(0.4\) dB that is within normal device spread).
  • The real difference is everywhere except the gain:
    • (b) is far better matched at the input: \(RL\) \(10.46\) dB against \(3.74\) dB, VSWR \(1.86\) against \(4.71\). System (a) reflects \(42\%\) of the drive power straight back at the source.
    • (b) is far better isolated: \(|S_{12}| = 0.03\) against \(0.12\), an extra \(12\) dB. System (b) is close to unilateral, so it can be designed with the simple unilateral equations; system (a) needs the full bilateral treatment.
    • (b) is more stable: \(K = 6.83\) against \(1.20\), and \(|\Delta| = 0.045\) against \(0.339\). System (a) sits near the edge of unconditional stability, so a mismatched load could push it into oscillation.
  • Verdict: \(\boxed{\text{(b) is the better amplifier}}\) at a cost of \(0.4\) dB of gain: better match, better isolation, much better stability margin.
  • Note for Chapter 6: the same paper then asks for the maximum unilateral and bilateral gains of set (a). For the record they are \(G_{TU,\max} = 9.75\) dB and \(G_{\max} = 10.11\) dB; the derivation belongs to the amplifier chapter.

column1: Problem 3: Derive the S-matrix of an E-plane Tee
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 80 Bh [4+4]
Briefly explain the need of S-parameters and their properties in microwave analysis. Explain three-port network parameters using an example of an E-plane Tee.
column4:
Given
  • An E-plane (series) tee: ports 1 and 2 are the collinear arms, port 3 is the E-arm side arm, assumed perfectly matched to the junction.
  • The junction is a passive, lossless, isotropic waveguide structure.
E-plane tee: 3D view and schematic, ports labelled as used below. Source: RF Pulchowk, S-parameter derivation sheets.
Step 1: write the blank matrix
  • A 3-port has \(3^2 = 9\) coefficients: \[ [S] = \begin{bmatrix} S_{11} & S_{12} & S_{13} \\ S_{21} & S_{22} & S_{23} \\ S_{31} & S_{32} & S_{33} \end{bmatrix} \tag{i} \]
Step 2: impose the three physical facts
Physical factEquationWhy
An input at the E-arm leaves ports 1 and 2 \(180^\circ\) out of phase\(S_{23} = -S_{13}\) (ii)The E-field of the side arm drives the two collinear arms in opposition
Port 3 is perfectly matched to the junction\(S_{33} = 0\) (iii)Nothing incident on the E-arm is reflected
The junction is passive and isotropic\(S_{ij} = S_{ji}\) (iv)Reciprocity: \(S_{12}=S_{21}\), \(S_{23}=S_{32}\), \(S_{31}=S_{13}\)
  • Substituting (ii), (iii) and (iv) into (i): \[ [S] = \begin{bmatrix} S_{11} & S_{12} & S_{13} \\ S_{12} & S_{22} & -S_{13} \\ S_{13} & -S_{13} & 0 \end{bmatrix} \tag{v} \]
  • Four unknowns remain: \(S_{11}\), \(S_{12}\), \(S_{22}\), \(S_{13}\). Four equations are needed, and the unitary property supplies them.
Step 3: apply the unitary (lossless) property
  • A lossless network satisfies \([S][S]^{*T} = [I]\), and since (v) is symmetric this is simply \([S][S]^{*} = [I]\): \[ \begin{bmatrix} S_{11} & S_{12} & S_{13} \\ S_{12} & S_{22} & -S_{13} \\ S_{13} & -S_{13} & 0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} S_{11}^{*} & S_{12}^{*} & S_{13}^{*} \\ S_{12}^{*} & S_{22}^{*} & -S_{13}^{*} \\ S_{13}^{*} & -S_{13}^{*} & 0 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1&0&0 \\ 0&1&0 \\ 0&0&1 \end{bmatrix} \]
Step 4: read off one equation per row-column product
ProductEquationWhat it gives
\(R_3 \cdot C_3\)\(|S_{13}|^2 + |S_{13}|^2 = 1 \Rightarrow 2|S_{13}|^2 = 1\)\(S_{13} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\) (vi)
\(R_3 \cdot C_1\)\(S_{13}S_{11}^{*} - S_{13}S_{12}^{*} + 0 = 0 \Rightarrow S_{11}^{*} = S_{12}^{*}\)\(S_{11} = S_{12}\) (vii)
\(R_1 \cdot C_1\)\(|S_{11}|^2 + |S_{12}|^2 + |S_{13}|^2 = 1\), and with (vi) and (vii) \(2|S_{11}|^2 = 1 - \tfrac{1}{2}\)\(|S_{11}|^2 = \tfrac{1}{4}\), so \(S_{11} = S_{12} = \tfrac{1}{2}\)
\(R_2 \cdot C_2\)\(|S_{12}|^2 + |S_{22}|^2 + |S_{13}|^2 = 1\), i.e. \(\tfrac{1}{4} + |S_{22}|^2 + \tfrac{1}{2} = 1\)\(|S_{22}|^2 = \tfrac{1}{4}\), so \(S_{22} = \tfrac{1}{2}\)
Answer
  • Substituting all four values back into (v): \[ \boxed{\;[S]_{\text{E-tee}} = \begin{bmatrix} \tfrac{1}{2} & \tfrac{1}{2} & \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\[3pt] \tfrac{1}{2} & \tfrac{1}{2} & -\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\[3pt] \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 \end{bmatrix}\;} \]
Reading the answer back (this is the “explain” half of the marks)
  • Power split: \(|S_{13}|^2 = |S_{23}|^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}\), so an input at the E-arm divides equally between the collinear arms.
  • Phase: \(S_{23} = -S_{13}\), so those two outputs are antiphase; this is what makes the E-tee a difference junction.
  • Matching: \(S_{33} = 0\) but \(S_{11} = S_{22} = \tfrac{1}{2}\), so the collinear arms are not matched: a quarter of the power incident on port 1 comes straight back. That is the 3-port theorem of \(\S\)3.5 appearing as arithmetic.
  • Isolation: \(S_{12} = \tfrac{1}{2} \neq 0\), so the collinear arms are not isolated from each other either. Adding the H-arm to fix both defects is exactly what turns a tee into a magic tee (Problem 5).
  • Check: every column sums to \(\tfrac{1}{4}+\tfrac{1}{4}+\tfrac{1}{2} = 1\) ✓lossless.

column1: Problem 4: Derive the S-matrix of an H-plane Tee
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 81 Ba [8]
Prepare S-matrices of a perfectly working E-plane Tee, H-plane Tee and a Duplexer, and explore their uses.
column4:
Given
  • An H-plane (shunt) tee: ports 1 and 2 collinear, port 3 the H-arm side arm, perfectly matched to the junction.
H-plane tee: the side arm lies in the plane of the magnetic field. Source: RF Pulchowk, S-parameter derivation sheets.
Step 1: the one fact that differs from Problem 3
  • In an H-plane tee an input at the side arm reaches the two collinear arms in phase: \[ S_{13} = S_{23} \tag{ii$'$} \]
  • Everything else is unchanged: \(S_{33} = 0\) (iii) and \(S_{ij} = S_{ji}\) (iv).
  • So the working matrix is \[ [S] = \begin{bmatrix} S_{11} & S_{12} & S_{13} \\ S_{12} & S_{22} & S_{13} \\ S_{13} & S_{13} & 0 \end{bmatrix} \tag{v$'$} \] with the same four unknowns.
Step 2: unitary property, row by row
ProductEquationWhat it gives
\(R_3 \cdot C_3\)\(|S_{13}|^2 + |S_{13}|^2 = 1\)\(S_{13} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\)
\(R_3 \cdot C_1\)\(S_{13}S_{11}^{*} + S_{13}S_{12}^{*} = 0 \Rightarrow S_{11}^{*} = -S_{12}^{*}\)\(S_{11} = -S_{12}\)
\(R_1 \cdot C_1\)\(|S_{11}|^2 + |S_{12}|^2 + \tfrac{1}{2} = 1 \Rightarrow 2|S_{11}|^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}\)\(S_{11} = \tfrac{1}{2}\), so \(S_{12} = -\tfrac{1}{2}\)
\(R_2 \cdot C_2\)\(\tfrac{1}{4} + |S_{22}|^2 + \tfrac{1}{2} = 1\)\(S_{22} = \tfrac{1}{2}\)
  • The sign moved. In the E-tee the minus sign sat in the side-arm column; here it sits in \(S_{12}\) instead. That single difference is the whole distinction between the two tees.
Answer, and the duplexer the same question asks for
  • H-plane tee: \[ \boxed{\;[S]_{\text{H-tee}} = \begin{bmatrix} \tfrac{1}{2} & -\tfrac{1}{2} & \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\[3pt] -\tfrac{1}{2} & \tfrac{1}{2} & \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\[3pt] \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 \end{bmatrix}\;} \]
  • Duplexer, taken as an ideal 3-port ferrite circulator with port 1 the transmitter, port 2 the antenna and port 3 the receiver: \[ \boxed{\;[S]_{\text{duplexer}} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\;} \] Matched at every port (\(S_{ii}=0\)), lossless (every column sums to 1) and deliberately non-reciprocal (\(S_{21}=1\) but \(S_{12}=0\)), which is the only way a 3-port can be both matched and lossless (\(\S\)3.5).
Uses, which the question asks for explicitly
DeviceBehaviourUses
E-plane teeEqual split, outputs in antiphase; difference junctionBalanced mixers, phase comparators, the difference arm of a magic tee, feeding balanced antennas
H-plane teeEqual split, outputs in phase; sum junctionIn-phase power dividers and combiners, feeding two antennas from one source, the sum arm of a magic tee
DuplexerOne antenna shared by transmitter and receiver, with the receiver isolated from the transmitterRadar, and any single-antenna transceiver; protects the sensitive receiver front end from the transmit pulse

column1: Problem 5: Derive the S-matrix of a Magic Tee
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED The device behind five identification questions
Describe the operational principles of a magic tee based on its S-parameters, and derive its scattering matrix.
column4:
Given
  • A hybrid (magic) tee: ports 1 and 2 are the collinear arms, port 3 is the E-arm and port 4 is the H-arm. Both side arms are perfectly matched to the junction.
Magic tee: an E-plane tee and an H-plane tee sharing the same junction. Source: RF Pulchowk, S-parameter derivation sheets.
Step 1: write the blank \(4\times4\)
\[ [S] = \begin{bmatrix} S_{11}&S_{12}&S_{13}&S_{14} \\ S_{21}&S_{22}&S_{23}&S_{24} \\ S_{31}&S_{32}&S_{33}&S_{34} \\ S_{41}&S_{42}&S_{43}&S_{44} \end{bmatrix} \tag{i} \]
Step 2: impose the five physical facts
Physical factEquationWhy
It contains an E-plane tee, so an input at the E-arm (port 3) leaves ports 1 and 2 antiphase\(S_{23} = -S_{13}\) (ii)Same argument as Problem 3
It contains an H-plane tee, so an input at the H-arm (port 4) leaves ports 1 and 2 in phase\(S_{24} = +S_{14}\) (iii)Same argument as Problem 4
An input at the E-arm produces no output at the H-arm, and the reverse\(S_{34} = S_{43} = 0\) (iv)The two side arms are geometrically orthogonal; the E-arm excites an antisymmetric field, the H-arm a symmetric one
Both side arms are perfectly matched to the junction\(S_{33} = S_{44} = 0\) (v)Stated in the question
No output at port 2 for an input at port 1, and the reverse\(S_{12} = S_{21} = 0\) (vi)The collinear arms are decoupled, which is the “magic”
  • With reciprocity \(S_{ij} = S_{ji}\) (vii), equations (ii) to (vii) reduce (i) to \[ [S] = \begin{bmatrix} S_{11} & 0 & S_{13} & S_{14} \\ 0 & S_{22} & -S_{13} & S_{14} \\ S_{13} & -S_{13} & 0 & 0 \\ S_{14} & S_{14} & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \tag{viii} \]
  • Four unknowns: \(S_{11}\), \(S_{22}\), \(S_{13}\), \(S_{14}\).
Step 3: unitary property, row by row
ProductEquationWhat it gives
\(R_3 \cdot C_3\)\(|S_{13}|^2 + |{-}S_{13}|^2 + 0 + 0 = 1\), i.e. \(2|S_{13}|^2 = 1\)\(S_{13} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\)
\(R_4 \cdot C_4\)\(|S_{14}|^2 + |S_{14}|^2 + 0 + 0 = 1\), i.e. \(2|S_{14}|^2 = 1\)\(S_{14} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\)
\(R_1 \cdot C_1\)\(|S_{11}|^2 + 0 + |S_{13}|^2 + |S_{14}|^2 = 1\), i.e. \(|S_{11}|^2 + \tfrac{1}{2} + \tfrac{1}{2} = 1\)\(|S_{11}|^2 = 0\), so \(\mathbf{S_{11} = 0}\)
\(R_2 \cdot C_2\)\(0 + |S_{22}|^2 + |S_{13}|^2 + |S_{14}|^2 = 1\)\(\mathbf{S_{22} = 0}\)
  • This is the striking result: matching the two side arms and decoupling the collinear pair forces the collinear arms to be matched as well. Nothing was assumed about \(S_{11}\) or \(S_{22}\); the unitary condition produced them.
Answer
\[ \boxed{\;[S]_{\text{magic tee}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\;} \]
Operational principles, read straight off the matrix
DriveOutputsConsequence
E-arm (port 3)\(b_1 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}a_3\), \(b_2 = -\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}a_3\), \(b_4 = 0\)Equal split, antiphase, nothing into the H-arm
H-arm (port 4)\(b_1 = b_2 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}a_4\), \(b_3 = 0\)Equal split, in phase, nothing into the E-arm
Port 1\(b_3 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}a_1\), \(b_4 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}a_1\), \(b_2 = 0\)Splits into both side arms, nothing reaches port 2
Ports 1 and 2 together\(b_4 \propto (a_1+a_2)\), \(b_3 \propto (a_1-a_2)\)H-arm is the sum arm, E-arm the difference arm
  • Why “magic”: all four ports are matched and two pairs (\(1\)–\(2\) and \(3\)–\(4\)) are completely isolated, which a 3-port can never achieve.
  • Uses: power combining and splitting (\(\S\)3.8), balanced mixers, duplexers, impedance bridges, monopulse radar comparators.
  • In practice the ideal matrix needs matching posts or irises at the junction; without them \(S_{11}\) and \(S_{22}\) are not zero.

column1: Problem 6: Identify the device from a numeric 4-port matrix
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 78 Ch [10]
Identify and explain the properties of a microwave passive device having the following S-matrix, with necessary diagram. \([S] = \begin{bmatrix} 0&0&1&1 \\ 0&0&-1&1 \\ 1&-1&0&0 \\ 1&1&0&0 \end{bmatrix}\)
column4:
Given
  • A \(4\times4\) matrix, so the device has four ports.
  • The paper prints the first row as “0 .0 1 1”; the stray point is a scanner artefact over a zero, and the matrix is the standard form.
Step 1: run the four tests
TestComputationResultConclusion
Diagonal\(S_{11}=S_{22}=S_{33}=S_{44}=0\)all zeroMatched at every port
Transpose\(S_{13}=S_{31}=1\), \(S_{23}=S_{32}=-1\), \(S_{14}=S_{41}=1\), \(S_{24}=S_{42}=1\)\([S]=[S]^{T}\)Reciprocal, so passive and non-ferrite
Column sums\(|0|^2+|0|^2+|1|^2+|1|^2 = 2\) for every column\(2 \neq 1\)Not unitary as printed: the \(1/\sqrt{2}\) factor has been omitted
Column dots\(C_1 \cdot C_2^{*} = (0)(0)+(0)(0)+(1)(-1)+(1)(1) = 0\); \(C_3 \cdot C_4^{*} = (1)(1)+(-1)(1)+0+0 = 0\)all zeroPhases are consistent; only the scale is wrong
  • Judging the condition: divide the printed matrix by \(\sqrt{2}\). Then every column sums to \(\tfrac{1}{2}+\tfrac{1}{2} = 1\) and the device is lossless. Say this explicitly: it is the “judge the condition” mark.
Step 2: map the zeros and read the signs
  • Zero blocks: \(S_{12} = S_{21} = 0\), so ports 1 and 2 are isolated; \(S_{34} = S_{43} = 0\), so ports 3 and 4 are isolated. Two isolated pairs on a matched, lossless, reciprocal 4-port.
  • Column 3 reads \((1, -1)\) down the collinear ports: the signs flip, so port 3 is the difference (E) arm.
  • Column 4 reads \((1, 1)\): the signs match, so port 4 is the sum (H) arm.
  • Equal magnitudes everywhere off the zero blocks, so every split is \(50/50\).
Answer
  • \(\boxed{\text{The device is a magic tee (hybrid tee)}}\), with ports 1 and 2 the collinear arms, port 3 the E-arm and port 4 the H-arm. Normalised: \[ [S] = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix} 0&0&1&1 \\ 0&0&-1&1 \\ 1&-1&0&0 \\ 1&1&0&0 \end{bmatrix} \]
  • Diagram: reproduce the 3D sketch of Problem 5 with all four arms labelled.
Properties, one line each
  • Matched at all four ports, so no port reflects: \(S_{ii}=0\), return loss infinite in the ideal case.
  • Reciprocal, \([S]=[S]^{T}\): passive waveguide, no ferrite, no gain.
  • Lossless once normalised: all incident power is redistributed, none dissipated.
  • Two isolated pairs: \(1\)–\(2\) and \(3\)–\(4\). Two sources on ports 1 and 2 cannot see each other, and the E-arm and H-arm are decoupled.
  • Equal power division, \(|S_{13}|^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}\): every drive splits in half, i.e. a \(3\) dB hybrid.
  • Phase: E-arm drive gives antiphase outputs, H-arm drive gives in-phase outputs.
  • Uses: power combiner and splitter, duplexer, balanced mixer, monopulse comparator, impedance bridge.

column1: Problem 7: Identify and complete a symbolic 4-port matrix
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 81 Bh [5]  and  74 Bh [8]
Identify and explain, along with a neat diagram, the properties of the passive microwave device described by the following S-matrix: \([S] = \begin{bmatrix} S_{11}&S_{12}&S_{13}&S_{14} \\ S_{12}&S_{22}&S_{13}&-S_{14} \\ S_{13}&S_{13}&0&0 \\ S_{14}&-S_{14}&0&0 \end{bmatrix}\)
column4:
Step 1: read the structure before doing any algebra
FeatureWhereWhat it means
\(S_{33} = S_{44} = 0\)bottom-right blockPorts 3 and 4 are matched to the junction
\(S_{34} = S_{43} = 0\)bottom-right blockPorts 3 and 4 are isolated from each other
Column 3 is \((S_{13}, S_{13})\)signs matchPort 3 drives the collinear arms in phase: the H-arm
Column 4 is \((S_{14}, -S_{14})\)signs flipPort 4 drives them in antiphase: the E-arm
\([S] = [S]^{T}\)everywhereReciprocal, hence passive and isotropic
  • Four ports, two matched side arms, one sum arm and one difference arm: this is a magic tee. Note that the port labels are the reverse of Problem 6: here port 3 is the H-arm and port 4 the E-arm. Read the signs, not the numbers.
Step 2: finish the job the printed matrix leaves undone
  • The matrix still carries \(S_{11}\), \(S_{12}\), \(S_{22}\), \(S_{13}\), \(S_{14}\) as unknowns. Apply the unitary property exactly as in Problem 5:
ProductEquationResult
\(R_3 \cdot C_3\)\(|S_{13}|^2 + |S_{13}|^2 = 1\)\(S_{13} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\)
\(R_4 \cdot C_4\)\(|S_{14}|^2 + |{-}S_{14}|^2 = 1\)\(S_{14} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\)
\(R_3 \cdot C_4\)\(S_{13}S_{14}^{*} - S_{13}S_{14}^{*} = 0\)satisfied identically, no new information
\(R_1 \cdot C_2\)\(S_{11}S_{12}^{*} + S_{12}S_{22}^{*} + |S_{13}|^2 - |S_{14}|^2 = 0\), and the last two cancel\(S_{11}S_{12}^{*} + S_{12}S_{22}^{*} = 0\)
\(R_1 \cdot C_1\)\(|S_{11}|^2 + |S_{12}|^2 + \tfrac{1}{2} + \tfrac{1}{2} = 1\)\(|S_{11}|^2 + |S_{12}|^2 = 0\), so \(\mathbf{S_{11} = S_{12} = 0}\)
\(R_2 \cdot C_2\)\(|S_{12}|^2 + |S_{22}|^2 + \tfrac{1}{2} + \tfrac{1}{2} = 1\)\(\mathbf{S_{22} = 0}\)
Answer
  • \(\boxed{\text{Magic tee}}\), with the completed matrix \[ [S] = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix} 0&0&1&1 \\ 0&0&1&-1 \\ 1&1&0&0 \\ 1&-1&0&0 \end{bmatrix} \] which is Problem 6's matrix with columns 3 and 4 interchanged, as the port labelling demands.
  • The strongest single line in this answer: nothing was assumed about \(S_{11}\), \(S_{12}\) or \(S_{22}\), yet all three came out zero. Matching the two side arms of a 4-port forces the collinear arms to be matched and isolated. That is precisely what a 3-port cannot do (\(\S\)3.5).
  • Properties and uses: as listed in Problem 6.

column1: Problem 8: Judge the condition of a given S-matrix
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 75 Bh [6]
Which passive microwave device is explained by this S-matrix? Judge the condition and explain its characteristics. \([S] = \begin{bmatrix} S_{11}&0&S_{13}&S_{14} \\ 0&S_{22}&-S_{13}&S_{14} \\ S_{13}&-S_{13}&0&0 \\ S_{14}&S_{14}&0&0 \end{bmatrix}\)
column4:
Step 1: identify
  • Four ports; \(S_{33} = S_{44} = 0\) and \(S_{34} = S_{43} = 0\), so ports 3 and 4 are matched and mutually isolated.
  • \(S_{12} = S_{21} = 0\) is already written in, so ports 1 and 2 are isolated too: the collinear pair.
  • Column 3 is \((S_{13}, -S_{13})\), signs flipping \(\rightarrow\) E-arm. Column 4 is \((S_{14}, S_{14})\), signs matching \(\rightarrow\) H-arm.
  • \([S] = [S]^{T}\) \(\rightarrow\) reciprocal, so passive.
  • \(\boxed{\text{Magic tee}}\), with the port labelling of Problem 6.
Step 2: judge the condition (what the question actually rewards)
TestComputationResultConclusion
Diagonal\(S_{11}\), \(S_{22}\) left as unknowns; \(S_{33}=S_{44}=0\)side arms matchedCollinear match not yet stated
Transposeevery \(S_{ij} = S_{ji}\)symmetricReciprocal
Column 3 sum\(|S_{13}|^2 + |{-}S_{13}|^2 = 1\)\(S_{13} = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\)Equal, antiphase split from the E-arm
Column 4 sum\(|S_{14}|^2 + |S_{14}|^2 = 1\)\(S_{14} = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\)Equal, in-phase split from the H-arm
Column 1 sum\(|S_{11}|^2 + 0 + \tfrac{1}{2} + \tfrac{1}{2} = 1\)\(S_{11} = 0\)Port 1 is matched after all
Column 2 sum\(0 + |S_{22}|^2 + \tfrac{1}{2} + \tfrac{1}{2} = 1\)\(S_{22} = 0\)Port 2 likewise
  • The condition: the matrix describes a lossless, reciprocal, matched-at-all-four-ports device, and this is consistent only because it has four ports. The same set of demands on a 3-port is impossible (\(\S\)3.5).
  • Completed: \[ [S] = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix} 0&0&1&1 \\ 0&0&-1&1 \\ 1&-1&0&0 \\ 1&1&0&0 \end{bmatrix} \]
Characteristics
  • \(3\) dB equal division: \(|S_{13}|^2 = |S_{14}|^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}\), so every input splits half and half.
  • Double isolation: \(1\)–\(2\) and \(3\)–\(4\). Two transmitters on the collinear arms cannot load each other; the E-arm and H-arm cannot leak into each other.
  • Phase discrimination: sum at the H-arm, difference at the E-arm, which is what makes it usable as a comparator.
  • Bidirectional: being reciprocal, it combines as readily as it splits.
  • Limitation: the ideal matrix assumes matching irises at the junction and holds over a limited bandwidth.

column1: Problem 9: Magic tee with both E- and H-arms short-circuited
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 82 Bh [4+4]
Design a model of a three-port network and define its characteristic parameters. Prepare the S-matrix of a rectangular magic tee having both E- and H-arms shorted, and explain how it behaves.
column4:
Given
  • The ideal magic tee of Problem 5, with ports 3 (E-arm) and 4 (H-arm) short-circuited at the junction reference plane.
  • A short reflects with \(\Gamma = -1\), so \(a_3 = -b_3\) and \(a_4 = -b_4\).
Step 1: write out the four scattering equations
  • From \([b] = [S][a]\) with the magic-tee matrix: \[ b_1 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(a_3 + a_4), \qquad b_2 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(-a_3 + a_4) \] \[ b_3 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(a_1 - a_2), \qquad b_4 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(a_1 + a_2) \]
Step 2: substitute the short-circuit conditions
  • \(a_3 = -b_3 = -\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(a_1 - a_2)\).
  • \(a_4 = -b_4 = -\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(a_1 + a_2)\).
Step 3: eliminate and collect
  • Into the expression for \(b_1\): \[ b_1 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left[-\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(a_1-a_2) - \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(a_1+a_2)\right] = -\tfrac{1}{2}\left[(a_1-a_2) + (a_1+a_2)\right] = -\tfrac{1}{2}(2a_1) = -a_1 \]
  • Into the expression for \(b_2\): \[ b_2 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left[+\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(a_1-a_2) - \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(a_1+a_2)\right] = \tfrac{1}{2}\left[(a_1-a_2) - (a_1+a_2)\right] = \tfrac{1}{2}(-2a_2) = -a_2 \]
  • The \(a_2\) terms cancel in \(b_1\) and the \(a_1\) terms cancel in \(b_2\): the two reflections arriving from the shorted arms add in the driven arm and subtract in the other one.
Answer
  • Seen from the two collinear arms, the shorted magic tee is the two-port \[ \boxed{\;[S]_{\text{shorted}} = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix}\;} \]
How it behaves
  • Total reflection: \(|S_{11}| = |S_{22}| = 1\), so every watt fed into port 1 comes back out of port 1. Return loss \(= 0\) dB, VSWR \(= \infty\).
  • Phase reversal: the \(-1\) is a \(180^\circ\) shift, exactly what an ideal short does. The tee behaves as a pair of independent short circuits, one at each collinear arm.
  • Complete isolation survives: \(S_{12} = S_{21} = 0\), so the two arms still cannot see each other even though both are totally reflecting.
  • Still lossless: each column sums to \(|-1|^2 = 1\); nothing is dissipated, everything is returned.
  • Still reciprocal: \([S] = [S]^{T}\).
  • Use: a reflective phase shifter or a calibration short. Moving the shorts a distance \(\ell\) out from the junction changes \(\Gamma\) from \(-1\) to \(-e^{-2j\beta\ell}\), and the same algebra then gives \(S_{11} = S_{22} = -e^{-2j\beta\ell}\) with \(S_{12}\) still zero, so a tunable phase with a constant unity magnitude.

column1: Problem 10: Two radar transmitters, twice the power into one antenna
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 73 Bh [8]  and  74 Ma [6]
Suppose there are two identical radar transmitters and a few passive devices in equipment stock. A particular application requires twice more input power to an antenna than either transmitter can deliver. As an RF engineer, give your appropriate solution with necessary figures, mathematics and sufficient explanation.
column4:
Given
  • Two identical transmitters, each able to deliver \(P\) watts.
  • One antenna, which must receive \(2P\) watts.
Step 1: choose the device, and say why
  • Choice: a magic tee used as a power combiner (a \(3\) dB hybrid coupler works identically).
  • Why not a simple T-junction or Y-junction:
    • A plain junction gives \(S_{12} \neq 0\), so each transmitter drives power into the other one: mutual loading, pulling of the oscillators, and possible damage.
    • Its collinear ports are not matched (\(S_{11} = S_{22} = \tfrac{1}{2}\) for a tee, Problem 3), so both transmitters see a high VSWR.
  • The magic tee cures both: \(S_{12} = 0\) (perfect isolation) and \(S_{ii} = 0\) (matched at every port).
Step 2: the connection
PortConnected toReason
1 (collinear)Transmitter AIsolated from port 2
2 (collinear)Transmitter BIsolated from port 1
3 (E-arm)Matched dummy loadTakes the difference, which is zero when the drives are balanced
4 (H-arm)AntennaTakes the sum of the two drives
  • The two feed lines must be cut to the same electrical length, so that the transmitters arrive in phase.
Step 3: the mathematics
  • Both transmitters equal and in phase, nothing incident on the side arms: \[ [a] = \begin{bmatrix} a & a & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}^{T}, \qquad |a|^2 = P \]
  • Multiply \([b] = [S][a]\) with the magic-tee matrix: \[ b_3 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(a_1 - a_2) = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(a - a) = 0 \] \[ b_4 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(a_1 + a_2) = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(2a) = \sqrt{2}\,a \] \[ b_1 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(a_3 + a_4) = 0, \qquad b_2 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(-a_3 + a_4) = 0 \]
Step 4: read the powers
PortWavePowerMeaning
4, antenna\(b_4 = \sqrt{2}\,a\)\(|b_4|^2 = 2|a|^2 = 2P\)The requirement, met exactly
3, dummy load\(b_3 = 0\)\(0\)Nothing wasted when the drives are balanced
1 and 2, transmitters\(b_1 = b_2 = 0\)\(0\)No reflection back into either transmitter
Total out\(\mathbf{2P}\)Equals the total in, as a lossless network requires
Answer
  • \(\boxed{\text{Feed the two transmitters into the collinear arms of a magic tee, antenna on the H-arm, matched load on the E-arm}}\). The antenna then receives \(2P\) watts, twice what either transmitter alone can deliver.
Explanation, which carries the remaining marks
  • Why the sum appears at the H-arm: an H-plane junction excites the two collinear arms in phase, so by reciprocity two in-phase drives add there.
  • Why the dummy load matters: if the transmitters are unequal or out of phase, \(b_3 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(a_1 - a_2) \neq 0\) and the imbalance is absorbed by the load instead of being reflected into the transmitters. The load must be rated for the worst-case imbalance, i.e. the full power of one transmitter.
  • Phase error costs power: with a phase error \(\phi\) between the drives, the antenna receives \(2P\cos^2(\phi/2)\) and the load takes the rest. A \(20^\circ\) error already loses \(0.13\) dB.
  • Alternatives: a \(3\) dB branch-line or rat-race hybrid does the same job in microstrip; a Wilkinson combiner does it with an isolation resistor when the device must be planar.

column1: Problem 11: ASR duplexer delivering half the transmitter power
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 76 Bh [10]  and  73 Ma [8]
A radar installation engineer is given the responsibility of installing an Airport Surveillance Radar that requires half the input power to the antenna than the transmitter can deliver, using a duplexer. Prepare its S-matrix.  (73 Ma: choose a suitable passive microwave device to split power in half and explain its properties.)
column4:
Given
  • A transmitter delivering \(P\) watts.
  • The antenna must receive \(P/2\) watts, and the receiver must share the same antenna while staying isolated from the transmitter.
Step 1: choose the device
  • Choice: a magic tee used as a duplexer. It is the only passive device that splits power exactly in half and provides the transmitter-to-receiver isolation a duplexer must have.
  • A resistive splitter would also halve the power but would burn the other half and give no isolation.
Step 2: the connection
PortConnected toReason
4 (H-arm)TransmitterDrives both collinear arms equally and in phase
1 (collinear)AntennaReceives half the transmitter power
2 (collinear)Matched dummy loadAbsorbs the other half, and balances the bridge
3 (E-arm)ReceiverIsolated from the H-arm, so the transmit pulse never reaches it
Step 3: transmit path
  • Drive vector \([a] = \begin{bmatrix} 0&0&0&a \end{bmatrix}^{T}\) with \(|a|^2 = P\).
  • From \([b]=[S][a]\): \[ b_1 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}a_4 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}a, \qquad b_2 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}a_4 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}a, \qquad b_3 = 0 \]
  • Powers: \[ |b_1|^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}|a|^2 = \frac{P}{2}, \qquad |b_2|^2 = \frac{P}{2}, \qquad |b_3|^2 = 0 \]
  • The antenna receives exactly \(P/2\), which is the requirement, and the receiver on the E-arm receives nothing from the transmitter, which is the point of a duplexer.
Step 4: receive path
  • The echo arrives at port 1 alone: \([a] = \begin{bmatrix} a_1&0&0&0 \end{bmatrix}^{T}\) with \(|a_1|^2 = P_{echo}\).
  • \(b_3 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}a_1\) and \(b_4 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}a_1\), so \[ |b_3|^2 = \frac{P_{echo}}{2} \quad\text{to the receiver}, \qquad |b_4|^2 = \frac{P_{echo}}{2} \quad\text{back into the transmitter} \]
  • Nothing reaches port 2, since \(S_{21} = 0\).
Answer
  • The duplexer is the magic tee, whose S-matrix is \[ \boxed{\;[S] = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\;} \] with port 4 the transmitter, port 1 the antenna, port 2 the matched load and port 3 the receiver.
Properties and the honest limitation
  • Equal split: \(|S_{14}|^2 = |S_{24}|^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}\), a \(3\) dB hybrid.
  • Isolation: transmitter (port 4) to receiver (port 3) is \(S_{34} = 0\), so the receiver front end is protected from the full transmit pulse.
  • Matched at every port, so neither the transmitter nor the antenna sees a standing wave.
  • The \(3\) dB penalty is real and should be stated: half the transmit power goes into the dummy load, and half the echo goes back to the transmitter. The magic-tee duplexer therefore costs \(3\) dB in each direction.
  • Better in practice: a ferrite circulator duplexer, \([S] = \left[\begin{smallmatrix}0&0&1\\1&0&0\\0&1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right]\), routes the whole transmit power to the antenna and the whole echo to the receiver, with no \(3\) dB loss. Quote it as the improvement whenever the question does not explicitly demand the half-power split, as 76 Bh does.

column1: Problem 12: Evaluate the S-matrix of an amplitude modulator
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 78 Ch [3+7]
Elaborate the importance of S-parameters for microwave frequencies. Evaluate the S-matrix of an Amplitude Modulator.
column4:
Step 1: model the modulator as a two-port
  • A microwave amplitude modulator sits in the RF path: the carrier enters port 1 and the modulated carrier leaves port 2. The modulating signal is a control input, applied as bias, not as a third RF port.
  • Physically it is a PIN-diode variable attenuator: the diode's RF resistance is set by its DC bias, so the modulating waveform steers the transmission through the device.
  • Both RF ports are designed to stay matched across the modulation swing, otherwise the modulation would pull the source and produce incidental phase modulation.
Step 2: impose the three properties
PropertyEquationWhy
Matched at both ports\(S_{11} = S_{22} = 0\)The attenuator is built as a matched pad at every bias point
Reciprocal\(S_{12} = S_{21} = \alpha\)Passive, no ferrite and no gain: a diode resistance is bilateral
Lossy, and time varying\(0 \le \alpha(t) \le 1\)The power removed from the carrier is dissipated in the diode
  • Hence \[ \boxed{\;[S] = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & \alpha(t) \\ \alpha(t) & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \alpha(t) = \alpha_0\left(1 + m\cos\omega_m t\right)\;} \] with \(\alpha_0\) the carrier-level transmission, \(m\) the modulation index and \(\omega_m\) the modulating frequency.
Step 3: check the condition
  • Column sum: \(|S_{11}|^2 + |S_{21}|^2 = \alpha^2\), which equals 1 only when \(\alpha = 1\).
  • So the modulator is never lossless except at full transmission: the dissipated fraction is \(1 - \alpha^2(t)\), and this is unavoidable. An amplitude modulator works by throwing power away in step with the modulating signal.
  • It is reciprocal and matched, so the only non-ideal property is the loss.
Step 4: evaluate with numbers
  • Take \(\alpha_0 = 0.5\) and \(m = 0.6\), a typical shallow modulation.
Instant\(\alpha(t)\)\([S]\)\(IL\) and \(P_{out}\) for \(1\) W in
Peak, \(\cos\omega_m t = +1\)\(0.5(1+0.6) = 0.80\)\(\left[\begin{smallmatrix}0&0.8\\0.8&0\end{smallmatrix}\right]\)\(IL = -20\log 0.8 = 1.94\) dB; \(P_{out} = 0.64\) W
Carrier, \(\cos\omega_m t = 0\)\(0.5\)\(\left[\begin{smallmatrix}0&0.5\\0.5&0\end{smallmatrix}\right]\)\(IL = 6.02\) dB; \(P_{out} = 0.25\) W
Trough, \(\cos\omega_m t = -1\)\(0.5(1-0.6) = 0.20\)\(\left[\begin{smallmatrix}0&0.2\\0.2&0\end{smallmatrix}\right]\)\(IL = 13.98\) dB; \(P_{out} = 0.04\) W
  • Recovering the modulation index from the matrix, which is the check the examiner is looking for: \[ m = \frac{|S_{21}|_{\max} - |S_{21}|_{\min}}{|S_{21}|_{\max} + |S_{21}|_{\min}} = \frac{0.80 - 0.20}{0.80 + 0.20} = \frac{0.60}{1.00} = 0.6 \checkmark \]
  • Modulation depth in dB: the transmission swings over \(13.98 - 1.94 = 12.04\) dB.
Notes worth adding
  • Balanced realisation: build the modulator on a magic tee, carrier into the H-arm, matched PIN diodes in the two collinear arms and the modulating bias on the E-arm. The two diodes reflect equally, the reflections recombine into the E-arm and the output amplitude follows the bias. The device is then a magic tee with two variable terminations, and the algebra is Problem 9 with \(\Gamma\) set by the bias instead of fixed at \(-1\).
  • \(S_{11}\) is the figure of merit: a good modulator keeps \(S_{11}\) small at every bias point. If it does not, the source sees a varying load and the output picks up incidental phase modulation.
  • Contrast with an ideal switch: \(\alpha\) toggling between \(1\) and \(0\) makes the same matrix an on-off (ASK) modulator, with \(m = 1\).

READ THIS FIRST
Chapter 4 has the biggest question count in the paper, but three scripts answer most of it:
  1. Field equations of a rectangular waveguide, TE or TM (14 papers, up to 10 marks) \(\rightarrow\) \(\S\)4.1. One six-step script covers both modes: only the boundary condition in step 4 changes. Learn TM first; TE is the same page with \(\sin\) and \(\cos\) swapped.
  2. Mode questions (9 papers, 1 to 5 marks each): dominant, degenerate, “prove TM\(_{01}\) cannot exist”, “show TM\(_{11}\) is the lowest TM mode” \(\rightarrow\) \(\S\)4.2. Every one is the cut-off formula plus one sentence.
  3. Magic tee (9 papers) \(\rightarrow\) \(\S\)4.5 for construction and the derivation, \(\S\)3.6 for the matrix. The combinations (two tees joined, arms terminated) are worked in the numerical companion.
Two more things worth knowing before the paper starts:
  • Circular waveguide (4 papers, 7 to 10 marks) is the rectangular script again in cylindrical coordinates, with Bessel functions in place of sines. The only new fact to memorise is the root table of \(\S\)4.3.

column1: Derive the field equations and characteristic parameters of a rectangular waveguide operating in TE / TM mode
column2: 457+388+210
column4:
Set-up
  • Hollow metal pipe, inner broad wall \(a\) along \(x\), narrow wall \(b\) along \(y\), propagation along \(+z\), \(a > b\).
  • Lossless dielectric \((\mu, \epsilon)\) inside, perfectly conducting walls.
  • Every field component carries \(e^{-\gamma z}\), \(\gamma = \alpha + j eta\).
  • Notation used throughout (Gangaju):
    • \(k = \omega\sqrt{\mu\epsilon}\), the free-space wave number of the filling.
    • \(h^2 = \gamma^2 + k^2 = k_x^2 + k_y^2\), the cut-off wave number squared (Pozar writes \(k_c^2\)).
  • No TEM mode. With \(E_z = H_z = 0\) every transverse component below is zero. Physically, a closed \(H\) loop in the cross-section needs an axial current, and a single hollow conductor has no centre conductor to carry it.
Co-ordinates of the rectangular guide. Source: Gangaju, Ch-4 deck, slide 12.
Step 1: transverse fields from the longitudinal ones (Maxwell's curl equations)
  • Write \( abla imes E = -j\omega\mu H\) and \( abla imes H = j\omega\epsilon E\) in components with \(\partial/\partial z ightarrow -\gamma\), and solve the four transverse equations for \(E_x, E_y, H_x, H_y\):
\[ egin{aligned} E_x &= - rac{\gamma}{h^2} rac{\partial E_z}{\partial x} - rac{j\omega\mu}{h^2} rac{\partial H_z}{\partial y}, & E_y &= - rac{\gamma}{h^2} rac{\partial E_z}{\partial y} + rac{j\omega\mu}{h^2} rac{\partial H_z}{\partial x}, \[3pt] H_x &= - rac{\gamma}{h^2} rac{\partial H_z}{\partial x} + rac{j\omega\epsilon}{h^2} rac{\partial E_z}{\partial y}, & H_y &= - rac{\gamma}{h^2} rac{\partial H_z}{\partial y} - rac{j\omega\epsilon}{h^2} rac{\partial E_z}{\partial x}. \end{aligned} \]
  • This block is the whole trick: find \(E_z\) (TM) or \(H_z\) (TE) and the other four components follow by differentiation.
Step 2: the wave equation for the longitudinal component
  • Helmholtz: \( abla^2 E_z + k^2 E_z = 0\), i.e. \(\dfrac{\partial^2 E_z}{\partial x^2} + \dfrac{\partial^2 E_z}{\partial y^2} + \dfrac{\partial^2 E_z}{\partial z^2} + \omega^2\mu\epsilon E_z = 0\).
  • The same equation holds for \(H_z\).
Step 3: separation of variables
  • Put \(E_z = X(x)\,Y(y)\,Z(z)\) and divide by \(XYZ\): \(\dfrac{X''}{X} + \dfrac{Y''}{Y} + \dfrac{Z''}{Z} = -k^2\).
  • Each ratio must be a constant:
    • \(X''/X = -k_x^2 \Rightarrow X = C_1\cos k_x x + C_2\sin k_x x\).
    • \(Y''/Y = -k_y^2 \Rightarrow Y = C_3\cos k_y y + C_4\sin k_y y\).
    • \(Z''/Z = \gamma^2 \Rightarrow Z = C_5 e^{\gamma z} + C_6 e^{-\gamma z}\); a wave along \(+z\) only \(\Rightarrow C_5 = 0\).
  • Adding the constants back: \(-k_x^2 - k_y^2 + \gamma^2 = -k^2\), so \( oxed{h^2 = k_x^2 + k_y^2 = \gamma^2 + k^2}\).
  • General solution: \(E_z = (A_1\cos k_x x + A_2\sin k_x x)(A_3\cos k_y y + A_4\sin k_y y)\,e^{-\gamma z}\).
  • \(H_z\) has the same form with its own constants \(B_1, B_2, B_3, B_4\); the working below reuses the letters \(A\) for brevity.
Step 4 (TM): \(H_z = 0\), apply \(E_z = 0\) on the walls
  • \(E_z\) is tangential to every wall, so it must vanish there.
  • \(x = 0\): \(E_z = 0 \Rightarrow A_1 = 0\).
  • \(y = 0\): \(E_z = 0 \Rightarrow A_3 = 0\).
  • \(x = a\): \(\sin k_x a = 0 \Rightarrow k_x = m\pi/a\).
  • \(y = b\): \(\sin k_y b = 0 \Rightarrow k_y = n\pi/b\).
\[ E_z = E_0 \sin rac{m\pi x}{a}\,\sin rac{n\pi y}{b}\,e^{-\gamma z} \]
Step 4 (TE): \(E_z = 0\), apply \(E_x, E_y = 0\) on the walls
  • With \(E_z = 0\): \(E_x \propto \partial H_z/\partial y\), \(E_y \propto \partial H_z/\partial x\).
  • \(x = 0\): \(E_y = 0 \Rightarrow \partial H_z/\partial x = 0 \Rightarrow A_2 = 0\).
  • \(y = 0\): \(E_x = 0 \Rightarrow \partial H_z/\partial y = 0 \Rightarrow A_4 = 0\).
  • \(x = a\): \(\sin k_x a = 0 \Rightarrow k_x = m\pi/a\).
  • \(y = b\): \(\sin k_y b = 0 \Rightarrow k_y = n\pi/b\).
\[ H_z = H_0 \cos rac{m\pi x}{a}\,\cos rac{n\pi y}{b}\,e^{-\gamma z} \] Deck slide 18 prints \(k_y = n\pi/a\) in the last line; it is \(n\pi/b\).
Step 5: substitute into Step 1 (write \(e^{-\gamma z}\) on every line in the exam)
TM\(_{mn}\)  (\(H_z = 0\)) \[ egin{aligned} E_x &= - rac{\gamma}{h^2} rac{m\pi}{a}E_0\cos rac{m\pi x}{a}\sin rac{n\pi y}{b} \ E_y &= - rac{\gamma}{h^2} rac{n\pi}{b}E_0\sin rac{m\pi x}{a}\cos rac{n\pi y}{b} \ H_x &= \phantom{-} rac{j\omega\epsilon}{h^2} rac{n\pi}{b}E_0\sin rac{m\pi x}{a}\cos rac{n\pi y}{b} \ H_y &= - rac{j\omega\epsilon}{h^2} rac{m\pi}{a}E_0\cos rac{m\pi x}{a}\sin rac{n\pi y}{b} \end{aligned} \]
TE\(_{mn}\)  (\(E_z = 0\)) \[ egin{aligned} E_x &= \phantom{-} rac{j\omega\mu}{h^2} rac{n\pi}{b}H_0\cos rac{m\pi x}{a}\sin rac{n\pi y}{b} \ E_y &= - rac{j\omega\mu}{h^2} rac{m\pi}{a}H_0\sin rac{m\pi x}{a}\cos rac{n\pi y}{b} \ H_x &= \phantom{-} rac{\gamma}{h^2} rac{m\pi}{a}H_0\sin rac{m\pi x}{a}\cos rac{n\pi y}{b} \ H_y &= \phantom{-} rac{\gamma}{h^2} rac{n\pi}{b}H_0\cos rac{m\pi x}{a}\sin rac{n\pi y}{b} \end{aligned} \]
All eight components are checked in src/wg.py against both curl equations and against tangential \(E = 0\) on all four walls; a single flipped sign fails the check.

Definitions
  • Mode: one allowed field pattern, labelled by the integers \(m, n\) = number of half-cycle variations across \(a\) and across \(b\).
  • Dominant mode: the mode with the lowest cut-off frequency.
    • Rectangular guide (\(a > b\)): TE\(_{10}\), \(f_c = c/2a\), \(\lambda_c = 2a\).
    • Circular guide: TE\(_{11}\), \(f_c = 1.841\,c/2\pi r\) (\(\S\)4.3).
    • Between \(f_{c,10}\) and the next cut-off only the dominant mode propagates \(\rightarrow\) single-mode operation, the reason guides are sized this way.
E and H field of TE\(_{10}\), TE\(_{20}\), TE\(_{01}\): one, two and one half-cycles across the walls. Source: Gangaju, slide 20.
  • Degenerate modes: different field patterns with the same cut-off frequency.
    • TE\(_{mn}\) and TM\(_{mn}\) for every \(m, n \ge 1\): same \(f_c\) formula.
    • Square guide (\(a = b\)): TE\(_{10}\) and TE\(_{01}\) as well.
    • Circular guide: TE\(_{01}\) and TM\(_{11}\) (both root 3.832).
    • Unwanted, because power can couple between them at any discontinuity.
Cut-off ladder, Gangaju slide 22 (from Sadiku). The slide's caption says \(a = 2.5\) cm, \(b = 1\) cm; the arrows (TE\(_{10}\) at 3 GHz, TE\(_{20}\) at 6, TE\(_{50}\) and TE\(_{02}\) at 15) are those of a 5 cm \(\times\) 2 cm guide. column1: Field equations of a circular waveguide in TE / TM mode; TE vs TM; dominant mode
column4:
Set-up
  • Hollow circular pipe of inner radius \(a\), co-ordinates \((\rho, \phi, z)\), fields \(\propto e^{-j\beta z}\); \(k_c^2 = k^2 - \beta^2\), with \(k = \omega\sqrt{\mu\epsilon}\).
  • Step 1, the cylindrical version of the transverse equations (Waveguide.pdf p8, Pozar \(\S\)3.4):
\[ \begin{aligned} E_\rho &= -\frac{j}{k_c^2}\left(\beta\frac{\partial E_z}{\partial\rho} + \frac{\omega\mu}{\rho}\frac{\partial H_z}{\partial\phi}\right), & E_\phi &= -\frac{j}{k_c^2}\left(\frac{\beta}{\rho}\frac{\partial E_z}{\partial\phi} - \omega\mu\frac{\partial H_z}{\partial\rho}\right), \\ H_\rho &= \phantom{-}\frac{j}{k_c^2}\left(\frac{\omega\epsilon}{\rho}\frac{\partial E_z}{\partial\phi} - \beta\frac{\partial H_z}{\partial\rho}\right), & H_\phi &= -\frac{j}{k_c^2}\left(\omega\epsilon\frac{\partial E_z}{\partial\rho} + \frac{\beta}{\rho}\frac{\partial H_z}{\partial\phi}\right). \end{aligned} \]
Cylindrical co-ordinates. The figure is a circular cavity (a guide closed at both ends, \(\S\)4.8); the guide itself is the same cylinder, open along \(z\). Source: Gangaju, slide 93.
Step 2 and 3: separate the Helmholtz equation
  • \(\dfrac{\partial^2 h_z}{\partial\rho^2} + \dfrac{1}{\rho}\dfrac{\partial h_z}{\partial\rho} + \dfrac{1}{\rho^2}\dfrac{\partial^2 h_z}{\partial\phi^2} + k_c^2 h_z = 0\).
  • \(h_z = R(\rho)P(\phi)\):
    • \(P'' + n^2 P = 0 \Rightarrow P = A\sin n\phi + B\cos n\phi\); \(n\) an integer because the field repeats every \(2\pi\).
    • \(\rho^2R'' + \rho R' + (k_c^2\rho^2 - n^2)R = 0\): Bessel's equation \(\Rightarrow R = C J_n(k_c\rho) + D Y_n(k_c\rho)\).
    • \(Y_n \rightarrow \infty\) at \(\rho = 0\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(D = 0\).
TE\(_{nm}\): \(E_z = 0\)
  • \(H_z = (A\sin n\phi + B\cos n\phi)\,J_n(k_c\rho)\,e^{-j\beta z}\).
  • Boundary: \(E_\phi(\rho = a) = 0\). Since \(E_\phi \propto \partial H_z/\partial\rho\): \(J_n'(k_c a) = 0 \Rightarrow \boxed{k_c = p'_{nm}/a}\), \(p'_{nm}\) = \(m\)-th root of \(J_n'\).
\[ \begin{aligned} E_\rho &= \frac{-j\omega\mu n}{k_c^2\rho}(A\cos n\phi - B\sin n\phi)J_n(k_c\rho) \\ E_\phi &= \frac{j\omega\mu}{k_c}(A\sin n\phi + B\cos n\phi)J_n'(k_c\rho) \\ H_\rho &= \frac{-j\beta}{k_c}(A\sin n\phi + B\cos n\phi)J_n'(k_c\rho) \\ H_\phi &= \frac{-j\beta n}{k_c^2\rho}(A\cos n\phi - B\sin n\phi)J_n(k_c\rho) \end{aligned} \]
  • \(f_{c} = \dfrac{p'_{nm}}{2\pi a\sqrt{\mu\epsilon}}\),   \(Z_{TE} = \dfrac{E_\rho}{H_\phi} = \dfrac{\omega\mu}{\beta} = \dfrac{\eta k}{\beta}\).
TM\(_{nm}\): \(H_z = 0\)
  • \(E_z = (A\sin n\phi + B\cos n\phi)\,J_n(k_c\rho)\,e^{-j\beta z}\).
  • Boundary: \(E_z(\rho = a) = 0\) directly: \(J_n(k_c a) = 0 \Rightarrow \boxed{k_c = p_{nm}/a}\), \(p_{nm}\) = \(m\)-th root of \(J_n\).
\[ \begin{aligned} E_\rho &= \frac{-j\beta}{k_c}(A\sin n\phi + B\cos n\phi)J_n'(k_c\rho) \\ E_\phi &= \frac{-j\beta n}{k_c^2\rho}(A\cos n\phi - B\sin n\phi)J_n(k_c\rho) \\ H_\rho &= \frac{j\omega\epsilon n}{k_c^2\rho}(A\cos n\phi - B\sin n\phi)J_n(k_c\rho) \\ H_\phi &= \frac{-j\omega\epsilon}{k_c}(A\sin n\phi + B\cos n\phi)J_n'(k_c\rho) \end{aligned} \]
  • \(f_{c} = \dfrac{p_{nm}}{2\pi a\sqrt{\mu\epsilon}}\),   \(Z_{TM} = \dfrac{E_\rho}{H_\phi} = \dfrac{\beta}{\omega\epsilon} = \dfrac{\eta\beta}{k}\).
  • Sign: Waveguide.pdf p11 prints \(E_\phi\) with a \(+\); it is \(-\). wg.py fails the curl equation with the \(+\). verified/added

column1: Explain the magic tee with a neat diagram and derive its S-matrix; E-plane vs H-plane tee
column4:
Magic tee: collinear ports 1, 2; E-arm 3; H-arm 4.
Construction
  • A hybrid of the two simple tees on one junction:
    • E-plane (series) tee: side arm on the broad wall, its axis parallel to the main guide's E field. Port 3.
    • H-plane (shunt) tee: side arm on the narrow wall, in the plane of H. Port 4.
  • Collinear arms 1 and 2 are symmetric about both side arms.
  • A post and iris inside the junction match ports 3 and 4; without them the junction is simply a “hybrid tee” and is poorly matched.
  • It is called magic because a matched 4-port with this symmetry turns out to be matched at all ports and isolates the two pairs, which nothing in its shape makes obvious.
Derivation of the S-matrix, the 4-mark version asked in 80 Bh and 72 Ma
  1. 4 ports \(\Rightarrow\) a \(4\times4\) matrix \([S]\); write all sixteen \(S_{ij}\) out, \(i, j\) from 1 to 4.
  2. H-arm symmetry: input at 4 reaches 1 and 2 equally and in phase \(\Rightarrow S_{14} = S_{24}\).
  3. E-arm antisymmetry: input at 3 reaches 1 and 2 equally and in antiphase \(\Rightarrow S_{13} = -S_{23}\).
  4. E and H arms are orthogonal: an E-arm wave cannot excite the H-arm mode \(\Rightarrow S_{34} = S_{43} = 0\).
  5. Matched side arms (post and iris) \(\Rightarrow S_{33} = S_{44} = 0\).
  6. Reciprocity \(\Rightarrow S_{ij} = S_{ji}\).
  7. Unitary, column 3: \(|S_{13}|^2 + |S_{23}|^2 = 1\), with \(|S_{13}| = |S_{23}| \Rightarrow S_{13} = 1/\sqrt{2}\). Same for column 4: \(S_{14} = 1/\sqrt{2}\).
  8. Unitary, column 1: \(|S_{11}|^2 + |S_{12}|^2 + \tfrac{1}{2} + \tfrac{1}{2} = 1 \Rightarrow S_{11} = S_{12} = 0\); column 2 gives \(S_{22} = 0\).
  9. Result: \(\;[S] = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left[\begin{smallmatrix} 0&0&1&1\\ 0&0&-1&1\\ 1&-1&0&0\\ 1&1&0&0 \end{smallmatrix}\right]\), matched at all four ports, lossless, reciprocal.
Properties (read straight off the matrix)
  • Into H-arm (4): equal halves at 1 and 2, in phase; nothing at 3.
  • Into E-arm (3): equal halves at 1 and 2, antiphase; nothing at 4.
  • Into collinear port 1: halves at 3 and 4; nothing at 2.
  • Equal in-phase signals at 1 and 2: sum emerges at 4, nothing at 3.
  • Equal antiphase signals at 1 and 2: difference emerges at 3, nothing at 4.
  • All four ports matched: no reflection anywhere.
Applications
  • Power combiner, e.g. two radar transmitters into one antenna (\(\S\)3.8).
  • Duplexer: transmitter and receiver on the isolated E and H arms (\(\S\)3.6).
  • Balanced mixer: signal on one side arm, local oscillator on the other.
  • Impedance bridge / measurement: unknown and standard on 1 and 2, null detector on 3.
  • Monopulse radar comparator: sum and difference channels.

• Hybrid tee with a terminated arm (82 Ba, 70 Ma): a matched load simply deletes that row and column.

  • Two magic tees joined E-arm to E-arm (77 Ch): a matched, lossless, reciprocal 6-port. The difference signal of one tee crosses to the other and re-appears in antiphase; the sum signal stays in its own H-arm. Joined H to H (78 Ch), the roles swap.

column1: Explain directional couplers and the four parameters used to describe their performance
column4:
What it is
  • A 4-port junction that samples power travelling in one direction only.
  • Main guide: port 1 (input) to port 2 (through).
  • Auxiliary guide: port 4 (coupled) and port 3 (isolated), Gangaju's numbering.
  • Ideal, all ports matched:
    • \(1 \rightarrow 2\) passes almost all the power.
    • \(1 \rightarrow 4\) a known small fraction.
    • \(1 \rightarrow 3\) nothing.
  • Uses: power monitoring, reflectometers and VSWR measurement (one coupler each way), network analysers, signal injection, and as a 3 dB hybrid.
  • S-matrix: \(\S\)3.6. Note \(\S\)3.6 labels the coupled port 3; the numbering varies by text, the physics does not.
Block view, Gangaju slide 54.
The four parameters (\(P_i\) = power at port \(i\), input at 1)
ParameterDefinitionMeasures
Coupling \(C\)\(10\log\dfrac{P_1}{P_4}\) dBhow much is sampled
Directivity \(D\)\(10\log\dfrac{P_4}{P_3}\) dBforward vs backward discrimination
Isolation \(I\)\(10\log\dfrac{P_1}{P_3}\) dBleakage to isolated port
Insertion loss\(10\log\dfrac{P_1}{P_2}\) dBloss on the main line
  • \(\boxed{I = C + D}\). Example: \(P_1 = 10\) mW, \(P_4 = 1\) mW, \(P_3 = 0.1\,\mu\)W \(\Rightarrow C = 10\) dB, \(D = 40\) dB, \(I = 50\) dB.
  • Good coupler: \(D\) of 30 to 40 dB, VSWR near 1.
Two-hole coupler, Gangaju slide 57.
Two-hole coupler: why it is directional
  • Two small holes in the common wall, spaced \(d = (2n+1)\lambda_g/4\).
  • Each hole radiates a small wave into the auxiliary guide, both ways.
  • Forward waves (towards port 4) travel equal total paths \(\rightarrow\) in phase \(\rightarrow\) add.
  • Backward waves (towards port 3) differ by \(2d = (2n+1)\lambda_g/2\) \(\rightarrow\) \((2n+1)\pi\) out of phase \(\rightarrow\) cancel.
  • Exact only at one frequency; more holes with tapered sizes widen the band.

column1: Explain the microwave circulator
column4:
Circulator
  • A non-reciprocal multi-port in which power entering port \(n\) leaves only by port \(n+1\): \(1 \rightarrow 2 \rightarrow 3 \rightarrow 1\) (3-port), or round four ports.
  • Ideal: matched at every port and lossless, but \(S_{ij} \ne S_{ji}\). 3-port form (matrix of \(\S\)3.5): \([S] = \left[\begin{smallmatrix}0&0&1\\1&0&0\\0&1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right]\).
  • Non-reciprocity comes from a magnetised ferrite.
  • Faraday rotation: a plane wave along a ferrite rod in an axial magnetic field has its polarisation rotated by an angle set by the field strength and the rod length, and in the same absolute sense whichever way it travels. A return trip therefore doubles the rotation instead of undoing it.
  • Four-port construction (slide 62): two 3 dB side-hole couplers, a primary and a secondary guide, and a non-reciprocal ferrite phase shifter in each.
    • Port 1 \(\rightarrow\) port 2: both paths arrive with the same phase \(\rightarrow\) add.
    • Port 1 \(\rightarrow\) port 4: the paths differ by 180\(^\circ\) \(\rightarrow\) cancel.
    • The phase shifters behave differently in the reverse direction, so port 2 feeds port 3, port 3 feeds 4, port 4 feeds 1.
Four-port circulator: two 3 dB couplers plus ferrite phase shifters. Gangaju slide 62.
Applications
  • Duplexer: transmitter port 1, antenna 2, receiver 3 (\(\S\)3.6).
  • Reflection amplifiers (tunnel diode, parametric): separate input from output.
  • An isolator, by loading one port.
Isolator (uniline)
  • Passes power one way, absorbs it the other way: \([S] = \left[\begin{smallmatrix}0&0\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right]\).
  • Circulator with port 3 matched-terminated, or a Faraday-rotation isolator:
    • Input E vertical; ferrite rotates it \(45^\circ\); output guide twisted \(45^\circ\) to accept it.
    • Reflection from the load is rotated a further \(45^\circ\) in the same sense \(\rightarrow\) \(90^\circ\) from the input orientation \(\rightarrow\) absorbed by a resistive vane.
  • Use: between a klystron or magnetron and its load, so a mismatch cannot reflect back and pull the oscillator frequency.
Phase shifter (syllabus, not yet asked)
  • Changes the phase of the transmitted wave by \(\Delta\phi = 2\pi l/\lambda_g\), either by changing the length \(l\) or the guide wavelength \(\lambda_g\).
  • Mechanical: telescoping coaxial line; dielectric vane moved across the guide (more dielectric in the high-E centre, smaller \(\lambda_g\), more phase).
  • Electrical: ferrite under a variable bias field; PIN-diode switched lines.
  • Uses: phased-array beam steering, phase discriminators, power-amplifier linearisation.

column1: Explain microwave cavity resonators
column4:
What and why
  • A closed metal enclosure that stores EM energy at discrete resonant frequencies: a section of waveguide shorted at both ends.
  • Microwave replacement for the LC tank: lumped L and C fail above a few hundred MHz (radiation, skin effect, lead parasitics).
  • Circuit analogue: stored E energy \(\rightarrow\) C, stored H energy \(\rightarrow\) L, wall loss \(\rightarrow\) R.
  • Types: rectangular, circular, re-entrant (the klystron cavity, Ch 5).
  • Infinitely many modes; the lowest is the dominant mode.
Rectangular cavity \(a \times b \times d\). Gangaju slide 90.
Rectangular cavity: resonant frequency
  • Standing wave along \(z\): the guide length must hold \(p\) half guide-wavelengths, \(d = p\lambda_g/2 \Rightarrow \beta = p\pi/d\).
  • \(k^2 = k_c^2 + \beta^2\) gives \[ f_{mnp} = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{\mu\epsilon}}\sqrt{\left(\frac{m}{a}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{n}{b}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{p}{d}\right)^2} \]
  • Allowed indices:
    • TE\(_{mnp}\): \(p \ge 1\), \(m\) and \(n\) not both zero.
    • TM\(_{mnp}\): \(m, n \ge 1\), \(p \ge 0\).
  • Dominant for \(b < a < d\): TE\(_{101}\), \(f_{101} = \frac{c}{2}\sqrt{\frac{1}{a^2} + \frac{1}{d^2}}\). Example \(2 \times 1 \times 3\) cm: \(9.01\) GHz, next TE\(_{102}\) at \(12.5\) GHz.
  • Circular cavity, radius \(a\), length \(d\): \(f = \dfrac{c}{2\pi}\sqrt{\left(\dfrac{p'_{nm}}{a}\right)^2 + \left(\dfrac{l\pi}{d}\right)^2}\) (TE), with \(p_{nm}\) for TM.
Quality factor
  • \(Q = \omega\,\dfrac{\text{energy stored}}{\text{power lost}}\).
  • Cavities reach \(10^4\) to \(10^6\); a lumped LC circuit about \(10^2\).
  • Losses add as reciprocals: \[ \frac{1}{Q_L} = \frac{1}{Q_c} + \frac{1}{Q_d} + \frac{1}{Q_{ext}} \]
    • \(Q_c\): wall conduction loss.
    • \(Q_d = 1/\tan\delta\): dielectric filling.
    • \(Q_{ext}\): power taken by the coupling; \(Q_L\) is the loaded Q.
  • Coupling (probe, loop, aperture) is under-, critically or over-coupled; at critical coupling the input is matched.
Applications
  • Klystron and magnetron cavities; wavemeters; filters; oscillator stabilisation; TR cells in duplexers.

column1: Gunn diode
column4:
• Transferred-electron device (TED): bulk n-type GaAs (or InP), no p-n junction; “diode” only because it has two terminals.
  • Construction: n\(^+\) contact / lightly doped n active layer (epitaxial, about 6 to 18 \(\mu\)m) / n\(^+\) substrate, metal contacts, heat sink.
  • Two-valley model (Ridley-Watkins-Hilsum):
    • GaAs conduction band has a lower valley (light electrons, high mobility) and an upper satellite valley about \(0.36\) eV higher (heavy, low mobility).
    • Low field: electrons stay in the lower valley, current rises with voltage.
    • Above a threshold field (about \(3.2\) kV/cm) electrons gain enough energy to transfer to the upper valley \(\rightarrow\) average mobility falls \(\rightarrow\) drift velocity falls as field rises.
    • That is negative differential resistance between the peak and the valley of the I-V curve.
  • Oscillation: a high-field domain forms at the cathode, drifts to the anode at \(v_d \approx 10^5\) m/s, and a new one forms when it arrives: \[ f = \frac{v_d}{L} \quad\text{e.g. } \frac{10^5}{10\,\mu\text{m}} = 10\ \text{GHz} \]
  • Correction to the deck (slide 72): it says the low-field current rises because electrons move from the valence band to the conduction band. It does not; the carriers are already conduction electrons in the lower valley. verified/added
Construction and the peak-valley characteristic. Gangaju slides 69 and 73.
(+) and (-)
  • (+) small, cheap, low noise, wide band, reliable, 1 to 100+ GHz.
  • (-) low efficiency (a few %), poor temperature stability, high bias current.
Applications
  • Local oscillators, police and door-opening radar sensors, low-power transmitters, microwave relay links.

column1: MASER
column4:
• Microwave Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation: the microwave ancestor of the laser (Townes, 1954).
  • A quantum device working on energy levels of atoms or molecules. The deck's “semiconductor device” is wrong. verified/added
  • Three-level principle:
    • Pump at \(f_{13}\) lifts particles from level 1 to 3.
    • They decay without radiating to the metastable level 2 and accumulate \(\rightarrow\) population inversion between 2 and 1.
    • An incoming signal at \(f_{21} = (E_2 - E_1)/h\) stimulates emission of identical photons (same frequency, phase, direction) \(\rightarrow\) coherent amplification.
  • Types: ammonia gas maser (23.87 GHz, the first), hydrogen maser (1.42 GHz, frequency standard), solid-state ruby maser (Cr\(^{3+}\) in Al\(_2\)O\(_3\), tuned by a magnetic field, cooled to a few kelvin).
  • Key property: extremely low noise.
  • Applications: radio-telescope and deep-space receivers, satellite ground stations, atomic clocks.
Pump to level 3, relax to 2, stimulated transition 2 to 1. Gangaju slide 78.
Microwave transistors (syllabus, not yet asked)
  • Differ from low-frequency parts in geometry and packaging: interdigitated, overlay and matrix layouts cut lead inductance and junction capacitance.
  • Si BJT: up to a few GHz. HBT (heterojunction, e.g. SiGe, InGaP/GaAs): higher \(f_T\), amplifiers and MMICs.
  • GaAs MESFET: Schottky-barrier gate on an n-channel; high electron mobility \(\rightarrow\) well above 5 GHz; low noise, depletion-mode.
  • HEMT: AlGaAs/GaAs heterojunction confines a 2-D electron gas in undoped GaAs, away from donor scattering \(\rightarrow\) even higher mobility, beyond 20 GHz, lowest noise.
MESFET (left) and HEMT (right) cross-sections. Gangaju slides 85 and 86.

column1: Microstrips
column4:
• Strip of width \(W\) on a substrate of thickness \(h\) and permittivity \(\epsilon_r\), ground plane underneath, air above.
  • Quasi-TEM: the field lives partly in air and partly in the substrate, so it sees an effective permittivity \(\epsilon_{\text{eff}} = \dfrac{\epsilon_r + 1}{2} + \dfrac{\epsilon_r - 1}{2}\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 + 12h/W}}\), \(1 < \epsilon_{\text{eff}} < \epsilon_r\).
  • \(v_p = c/\sqrt{\epsilon_{\text{eff}}}\), \(\lambda_g = \lambda_0/\sqrt{\epsilon_{\text{eff}}}\); \(Z_0\) falls as \(W/h\) rises.
  • (+) planar, cheap photolithography, components mount on top, MMIC friendly.
  • (-) radiation at bends, dispersion, lower Q and power than waveguide, crosstalk.
Attenuators and terminations (syllabus, not yet asked)
  • Attenuator: reduces power by a set amount with low VSWR; a resistive (carbon) vane or flap in the guide absorbs power through induced currents.
    • Fixed: lossy vane, or lossy walls.
    • Variable: flap lowered through a slot in the centre of the broad wall (deeper \(=\) more loss, since E is strongest there), vane moved from side wall to centre, or rotary vane in a circular guide.
  • Matched termination: absorbs all incident power; a guide section ending in a tapered absorbing wedge so the impedance changes gradually and nothing reflects.
  • Reference short: a metal plate; sliding short: movable, sets a reactance.
Flap and rotating-vane attenuators. Gangaju slide 39.
Windows, posts and screws (waveguide matching)
  • Inductive window: diaphragms from the side walls \(\rightarrow\) shunt L.
  • Capacitive window: from top and bottom \(\rightarrow\) shunt C; limits power (breakdown).
  • Resonant window: both \(\rightarrow\) parallel LC, transparent at resonance.
  • Post / screw: part-way in \(\rightarrow\) capacitive; right through \(\rightarrow\) inductive; \(\lambda/4\) deep \(\rightarrow\) series resonance.
  • Waveguide equivalent of a stub (\(\S\)2.6).

column1: Chapter 4 numericals — which formulas does everything come from?
column4:
8 solved PYQ problems  \(\cdot\)  46 marks across 8 papers  \(\cdot\)  2 guide-parameter sets, 1 cut-off family, 2 mode rankings, 3 junction networks
READ THIS FIRST
Chapter 4 numericals come in two kinds, and neither needs more than a calculator's square root.
  • Waveguide arithmetic (Problems 1 to 5). Everything hangs off one number, the factor \(F = \sqrt{1 - (f_c/f)^2}\). Compute it once, write it in a box, and every other quantity is a multiplication or a division by it: \[ \lambda_g = \frac{\lambda}{F}, \quad v_p = \frac{c}{F}, \quad v_g = cF, \quad Z_{TE} = \frac{\eta_0}{F}, \quad Z_{TM} = \eta_0 F. \] Always start by naming the dominant mode and checking \(f > f_c\); a guide below cut-off has no \(\lambda_g\) or \(v_p\) to find.
  • Junction networks (Problems 6 to 8). Treat each tee as its \(\S\)3.6 matrix and follow one unit wave through: out of one tee, into the next, out again. A matched termination deletes a row and column; a connection hands a leaving wave to the other tee as an arriving one. Column power sums are the self-check.
  • Constants used by the papers and here: \(c = 3\times10^8\) m/s, \(\eta_0 = 120\pi = 376.99\,\Omega\). Every answer is asserted in src/wg.py.

column1: Problem 1: Full parameter set of an air-filled rectangular guide
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 80 Ba [6+4]
For an air-filled rectangular waveguide with a width of 3 cm and a desired frequency of operation of 6 GHz (for dominant mode), determine cut-off frequency, cut-off wavelength, group velocity, phase velocity, propagation wavelength in the waveguide and the characteristic impedance. Explain the four basic parameters used to describe the performance of a directional coupler.
column4:
Given
  • Air filling: \(v = c = 3\times10^8\) m/s, \(\eta = \eta_0 = 120\pi\,\Omega\).
  • Width (broad wall) \(a = 3\) cm \(= 0.03\) m; \(f = 6\) GHz.
  • Dominant mode of a rectangular guide: TE\(_{10}\) (\(m = 1\), \(n = 0\)), so \(b\) is not needed.
Step 1: cut-off frequency and wavelength of TE\(_{10}\)
  • \(f_c = \dfrac{c}{2}\sqrt{\left(\dfrac{1}{a}\right)^2 + 0} = \dfrac{c}{2a} = \dfrac{3\times10^8}{2 \times 0.03} = \boxed{5\ \text{GHz}}\).
  • \(\lambda_c = 2a = \boxed{6\ \text{cm}}\)  (check: \(c/f_c = 3\times10^8/5\times10^9 = 0.06\) m).
  • \(f = 6\) GHz \(> f_c = 5\) GHz \(\Rightarrow\) the guide propagates, so the remaining quantities exist.
Step 2: the factor, computed once

  • \(F = \sqrt{0.30556} = \boxed{0.55277}\)  (exactly \(\sqrt{11}/6\)).
  • Free-space wavelength \(\lambda = c/f = 3\times10^8/6\times10^9 = 5\) cm.

column1: Problem 3: Does the guide pass the signal? Cut-off checks
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 70 Bh [7+3]
Define expressions for various field components of a rectangular waveguide in TE mode. Show that a 1 GHz signal cannot propagate in TE\(_{10}\) made in a rectangular waveguide with a wall separation of 5 cm.
QUESTION AS PRINTED 80 Bh [1+1+2]
What is dominant mode in a waveguide? What are the dominant modes for rectangular and circular waveguides? Does a rectangular waveguide of width 2.254 cm support the propagation of a signal having frequency 6 GHz?
column4:
Method
  1. Name the mode (TE\(_{10}\), the dominant one) and read the broad-wall width \(a\).
  2. \(f_c = c/2a\).
  3. Compare: \(f > f_c\) propagates; \(f < f_c\) is evanescent.
  4. For “show that”, add the attenuation: \(\gamma = \alpha = \sqrt{k_c^2 - k^2}\) is real.
70 Bh worked: \(a = 5\) cm, \(f = 1\) GHz
  • \(f_c = \dfrac{3\times10^8}{2\times0.05} = 3\times10^9\) Hz \(= \boxed{3\ \text{GHz}}\).
  • \(f = 1\) GHz \(< f_c = 3\) GHz \(\Rightarrow\) below cut-off.
  • Confirm with \(\gamma\):
    • \(k_c = \pi/a = \pi/0.05 = 62.832\) rad/m,  \(k_c^2 = 3947.8\).
    • \(k = 2\pi f/c = 2\pi\times10^9/3\times10^8 = 20.944\) rad/m,  \(k^2 = 438.6\).
    • \(\gamma^2 = k_c^2 - k^2 = 3947.8 - 438.6 = 3509.2 > 0\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(\gamma\) is real: \(\gamma = \alpha = \sqrt{3509.2} = 59.24\) Np/m, \(\beta = 0\).
  • The field decays as \(e^{-59.24z}\): to \(1/e\) in \(1/59.24 = 1.69\) cm, i.e. \(20\log_{10}e \times 59.24 = 514.5\) dB/m. No wave travels: the 1 GHz signal cannot propagate.
Both instances

column1: Problem 6: Two magic tees joined at their E-arms
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 77 Ch [10]
Explain the properties of two Magic Tees if one connects their E-arms and derive its S-matrix.
column4:
Given: the two tees
  • Each tee, ports (1, 2) collinear, 3 = E-arm, 4 = H-arm, \(r = 1/\sqrt{2}\) (\(\S\)3.6): \([S_T] = r\left[\begin{smallmatrix} 0&0&1&1\\ 0&0&-1&1\\ 1&-1&0&0\\ 1&1&0&0 \end{smallmatrix}\right]\).
  • Tee A ports \(1, 2, 3, 4\); tee B ports \(1', 2', 3', 4'\). The E-arms \(3\) and \(3'\) are joined, so they disappear as external ports.
  • Joining means: the wave leaving arm 3 enters arm 3', and vice versa: \(a_{3'} = b_3\), \(a_3 = b_{3'}\).
  • External ports left: \(1, 2, 4\) (tee A) and \(1', 2', 4'\) (tee B) \(\Rightarrow\) a 6-port, \(6\times6\) matrix.
Step 1: drive port 1 with a unit wave (\(a_1 = 1\), all other inputs zero)
  • Inside tee A: \(b_3 = S_{31} = r\),  \(b_4 = S_{41} = r\),  \(b_2 = S_{21} = 0\).
  • \(b_3 = r\) enters tee B's E-arm: \(a_{3'} = r\).
  • Inside tee B: \(b_{1'} = S_{13}\,a_{3'} = r\cdot r = \tfrac{1}{2}\),   \(b_{2'} = S_{23}\,a_{3'} = -r\cdot r = -\tfrac{1}{2}\),   \(b_{4'} = S_{43}\,a_{3'} = 0\).
  • Nothing reflects back into arm 3, because \(S_{3'3'} = 0\) (matched E-arm).
  • Column for port 1: \((b_1, b_2, b_4, b_{1'}, b_{2'}, b_{4'}) = (0,\ 0,\ r,\ \tfrac12,\ -\tfrac12,\ 0)\).
  • Power check: \(\tfrac12 + \tfrac14 + \tfrac14 = 1\) ✓.
Step 2: the other drives, same way
  • Port 2: \(b_3 = S_{32} = -r\), \(b_4 = r\); tee B receives \(-r\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(b_{1'} = -\tfrac12\), \(b_{2'} = +\tfrac12\).
  • Port 4 (H-arm A): \(b_1 = b_2 = r\), and \(b_3 = S_{34} = 0\) \(\Rightarrow\) nothing crosses to tee B.
  • Ports \(1', 2', 4'\): mirror images, by symmetry of the connection.
Step 3: the 6-port S-matrix
\[ [S] = \begin{array}{c} \\ 1 \\ 2 \\ 4 \\ 1' \\ 2' \\ 4' \end{array} \!\!\begin{array}{c} \begin{array}{cccccc} 1 & 2 & 4 & 1' & 2' & 4' \end{array} \\ \left[\begin{array}{cccccc} 0 & 0 & r & \tfrac12 & -\tfrac12 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & r & -\tfrac12 & \tfrac12 & 0 \\ r & r & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ \tfrac12 & -\tfrac12 & 0 & 0 & 0 & r \\ -\tfrac12 & \tfrac12 & 0 & 0 & 0 & r \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & r & r & 0 \end{array}\right] \end{array} \] \(r = 1/\sqrt{2}\). Identical to the connect() result in wg.py.
Step 4: properties
  • Matched: all six diagonal entries are 0.
  • Reciprocal: \([S] = [S]^T\).
  • Lossless: every column's powers sum to 1.
  • Collinear isolation kept: \(S_{12} = S_{1'2'} = 0\).
  • H-arms isolated from each other and from the far tee: \(S_{44'} = 0\).
  • Difference channel crosses: an antiphase pair at \((1, 2)\) appears entirely at \((1', 2')\), again antiphase.
  • Sum channel stays: an in-phase pair at \((1, 2)\) leaves entirely by \(4\).
  • Use: a sum/difference separator, e.g. two monopulse channels feeding a common difference path.

column1: Problem 7: Hybrid tee with a terminated arm
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 82 Ba [4+4+2]
Using proper S-Matrices, mention the properties of a Hybrid-Tee in the situation of (a) terminated E-arm, (b) terminated H-arm and (c) terminated co-planner arms.
column4:
Step 0: what “terminated” does to a matrix
  • Terminated = a matched load, \(\Gamma = 0\): whatever leaves that arm is absorbed, nothing comes back, so \(a_k = 0\).
  • Therefore row \(k\) and column \(k\) simply drop out; the rest of the matrix is unchanged.
  • Start from the magic tee, ports 1, 2 collinear (the co-planar arms), 3 = E, 4 = H.
  • If the paper meant a short, \(\Gamma = -1\), the answer is different; that is the 82 Bh case, \(\S\)3.6.
CaseReduced S-matrixProperties
(a) E-arm terminated, ports \((1, 2, 4)\)\(\left[\begin{smallmatrix} 0&0&r\\ 0&0&r\\ r&r&0 \end{smallmatrix}\right]\)Matched and reciprocal. From the H-arm: equal, in-phase halves at 1 and 2, no loss. Ports 1 and 2 isolated. From port 1: only half reaches port 4, the other half is absorbed in the E-arm load, so the 3-port is not lossless. An in-phase power divider.
(b) H-arm terminated, ports \((1, 2, 3)\)\(\left[\begin{smallmatrix} 0&0&r\\ 0&0&-r\\ r&-r&0 \end{smallmatrix}\right]\)Matched and reciprocal. From the E-arm: equal, antiphase halves at 1 and 2. Ports 1 and 2 isolated. From port 1: half to port 3, half lost in the H-arm load. An antiphase (180\(^\circ\)) power divider.
(c) Both co-planar arms terminated, ports \((3, 4)\)\(\left[\begin{smallmatrix} 0&0\\ 0&0 \end{smallmatrix}\right]\)E and H arms both matched and completely isolated. Any power entering either side arm splits into the two loads and nothing comes out anywhere: the tee acts as a matched termination for both.
  • Why (a) and (b) must be lossy: they are matched, reciprocal 3-ports, and \(\S\)3.5 proves no such 3-port can be lossless. The load is where the missing half goes.
  • Column check, (a): column 1 \(= 0 + 0 + \tfrac12 = \tfrac12\) (half absorbed); column 4 \(= \tfrac12 + \tfrac12 = 1\) (lossless from the H-arm).

column1: Problem 8: Two magic tees connected in the H-plane
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 78 Ch [5]
Write short notes on: Combitional effect of two magic fees connected in H-plane.
column4:
The paper's typos (“Combitional”, “magic fees”) are reproduced as printed; read “combinational effect of two magic tees”.
Step 1: join H-arm 4 to H-arm 4' (\(a_{4'} = b_4\), \(a_4 = b_{4'}\)) and follow port 1

  • From port 2: \(b_4 = S_{42} = +r\) as well, so tee B again gets \(+\tfrac12, +\tfrac12\).
Step 2: the 6-port S-matrix
\[ [S] = \begin{array}{c} \\ 1 \\ 2 \\ 3 \\ 1' \\ 2' \\ 3' \end{array} \!\!\begin{array}{c} \begin{array}{cccccc} 1 & 2 & 3 & 1' & 2' & 3' \end{array} \\ \left[\begin{array}{cccccc} 0 & 0 & r & \tfrac12 & \tfrac12 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -r & \tfrac12 & \tfrac12 & 0 \\ r & -r & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ \tfrac12 & \tfrac12 & 0 & 0 & 0 & r \\ \tfrac12 & \tfrac12 & 0 & 0 & 0 & -r \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & r & -r & 0 \end{array}\right] \end{array} \]
