READ THIS FIRST
Chapter 5 is descriptive, with no numerical PYQ in 24 papers, and the questions come in a fixed shape: a 2-mark definition, then a 6 to 8 mark “construction and working”.
  1. The 2-mark riders (bunching, density modulation, transit time, cross-field effect, slow-wave structure) \(\rightarrow\) each has a boxed two-line answer below. Bunching alone is asked in 9 papers.
  2. Klystrons (two-cavity, multicavity, reflex; 9 papers) \(\rightarrow\) \(\S\)5.3 and \(\S\)5.4. One figure (the Applegate diagram) explains all three.
  3. Magnetron (9 papers) \(\rightarrow\) \(\S\)5.5. The “45\(^\circ\) / 60\(^\circ\) / 90\(^\circ\) phase shift between adjacent cavities” versions are the same answer plus one formula, \(\phi = 2\pi n/N\).
Two things worth knowing before the paper starts:
  • Every tube here does the same three things: velocity-modulate a beam, let it bunch, and decelerate the bunches in a field that takes their energy. Say this in the first line of any tube answer and the structure of the answer follows.
  • Linear-beam (O-type) tubes: klystron, reflex klystron, TWT, BWO. Crossed-field (M-type) tubes: magnetron, crossed-field amplifier. An examiner who writes “field effect” or “cross-field” wants the M-type family.

column1: How is the output of conventional tubes reduced at microwaves? What is transit-time effect?
column4:
Why triodes and pentodes fail above about 1 GHz
  • Inter-electrode capacitance \(C_{gp}, C_{gk}, C_{pk}\):
    • Reactance \(1/\omega C\) falls with frequency \(\rightarrow\) shorts the input and output \(\rightarrow\) gain falls.
    • Cure (spread electrodes, smaller area) raises transit time: a compromise.
  • Lead inductance: \(\omega L\) grows \(\rightarrow\) degenerative feedback; cure: short leads (disk-seal tubes).
  • Transit-time effect (below).
  • Cathode emission: more current needs a bigger cathode, which adds capacitance; filament voltage and temperature are limited.
  • Power losses: skin-effect resistance grows as \(\sqrt{f}\); dielectric loss in the glass envelope; radiation from leads.
Inter-electrode capacitances of a triode. Karkee, Ch-5 deck, slide 4.
Transit-time effect: the 2-mark answer 2
  • Transit time = time an electron takes from cathode to anode. Transit-time effect: when this becomes a significant fraction of one RF cycle, the grid voltage changes while the electron is in flight \(\rightarrow\) plate current lags the grid voltage \(\rightarrow\) efficiency and gain collapse.
  • Numbers: \(\tau = 1\) ns is \(0.001\) cycle at 1 MHz but a whole cycle at 1 GHz. Above about \(0.1\) cycle the loss is serious.
  • Estimate: 100 V gives \(v = \sqrt{2eV/m} = 5.93\times10^6\) m/s; a 1 mm gap then takes \(3.4\times10^{-10}\) s, i.e. \(0.34\) cycle at 1 GHz.
  • Cure in a conventional tube: closer electrodes and higher voltage (fights the capacitance). Cure in a microwave tube: exploit it. Klystrons, TWTs and magnetrons turn transit time into velocity modulation and bunching.

column1: What is bunching effect (density modulation)? Explain velocity modulation and bunching
column4:
2-mark answer. Velocity modulation: an RF voltage across a gap speeds up electrons crossing in one half-cycle and slows those crossing in the other. Bunching (= density modulation): in the field-free drift space beyond, fast electrons catch up with slow ones sent earlier, so the uniform beam gathers into bunches once per RF cycle. The beam current is now modulated at the RF frequency and can drive a second cavity.
The equations (for the 5 and 10 mark versions)
  • Beam accelerated by \(V_0\): \(v_0 = \sqrt{2eV_0/m} = 0.593\times10^{6}\sqrt{V_0}\) m/s.
  • Buncher gap voltage \(V_1\sin\omega t\). Leaving at \(t_1\): \[ v(t_1) = v_0\left[1 + \frac{\beta_i V_1}{2V_0}\sin\omega t_1\right] \] \(\beta_i = \dfrac{\sin(\theta_g/2)}{\theta_g/2}\), the beam coupling coefficient; \(\theta_g = \omega d/v_0\) the gap transit angle.
  • Three reference electrons: #2 crosses at zero voltage (unchanged), #3 on the rising half (accelerated), #1 before it (decelerated). #1 and #3 converge on #2.
  • Arrival at the catcher, drift length \(L\): \(t_2 = t_1 + L/v(t_1)\).
  • Bunching parameter \[ X = \frac{\beta_i V_1}{2V_0}\,\theta_0, \qquad \theta_0 = \frac{\omega L}{v_0} \]
  • Catcher current: \(i_2 = I_0 + \sum_n 2I_0 J_n(nX)\cos n\omega(t_2 - \tau_0)\).
  • Fundamental \(2I_0 J_1(X)\) peaks at \(X = 1.841\), where it is \(1.164\,I_0\) \(\rightarrow\) optimum drift length.
Applegate diagram: each line is one electron's distance vs time; steep lines are fast. Lines converge (a bunch) around the electron that crossed at zero gap voltage. Karkee deck, PDF p22.
  • Checked by simulation in tubes.py: electrons launched with this velocity law and drifted ballistically give a fundamental of exactly \(2J_1(X)\).
  • Too short a drift (\(X < 1.84\)): weak bunches. Too long: electrons overtake and the bunch spreads again (debunching).

column1: Describe the construction and operation of a two-cavity / multicavity klystron amplifier or oscillator
column4:
Construction (two-cavity amplifier)
  • Electron gun: heated cathode, focusing electrode, anode at \(+V_0\) forms a narrow beam; an axial magnetic field keeps it focused.
  • Buncher cavity (input): re-entrant cavity with grids across the beam; RF in via coaxial loop.
  • Drift space: field-free tube of length \(L\).
  • Catcher cavity (output): identical cavity, RF out via loop.
  • Collector: absorbs the spent beam.
  • Cavities and collector at the same dc potential, so the beam drifts at constant mean speed.
Two-cavity klystron. Karkee deck, slide 14.
Operation
  1. Weak RF in the buncher sets up \(V_1\sin\omega t\) across its gap.
  2. Velocity modulation: electrons crossing are accelerated or decelerated (\(\S\)5.2).
  3. Bunching in the drift space: velocity modulation becomes density modulation.
  4. Bunches reach the catcher once per cycle and induce RF current in it. Its field builds up to oppose the bunches: they are decelerated and give up kinetic energy, while the thin stream between bunches is accelerated and takes back only a little.
  5. Net energy flows from beam to RF \(\rightarrow\) amplified output. The beam leaves slower and is collected.
  • Correction to the source (PDF p23): it says “all the kinetic energy is converted”. Only part is; the beam still reaches the collector with most of its speed. Theoretical maximum efficiency is \(\tfrac{1}{2}\times 1.164 = \) 58% (at \(X = 1.841\), catcher voltage equal to \(V_0\)); practical about 40%. verified/added
  • Gain of two cavities is low (about 10 dB) \(\rightarrow\) multicavity.
Multicavity klystron. Karkee deck, slide 19.
Multicavity klystron (amplifier)
  • One or more intermediate cavities between buncher and catcher, not externally driven.
  • Weak bunches from cavity 1 excite cavity 2 \(\rightarrow\) its larger gap voltage re-modulates the beam \(\rightarrow\) tighter bunches \(\rightarrow\) and so on.
  • Each stage adds gain: 30 to 70 dB overall.
  • Stagger tuning the cavities slightly apart widens the bandwidth.
  • Higher efficiency and power: up to MW pulsed, kW CW.
  • Uses: UHF TV and troposcatter transmitters, satellite ground stations, radar transmitters, linear accelerators.
Klystron oscillator
  • Feed part of the catcher output back to the buncher with the right phase (feedback loop, slide 18) \(\rightarrow\) self-sustained oscillation. Multicavity oscillator: the same loop around a multicavity tube (72 Ash).
  • Tuned by the cavities; for a single-cavity, voltage-tuned oscillator use the reflex klystron (\(\S\)5.4).

column1: Explain velocity modulation and bunching in a reflex klystron with neat diagrams and equations
column4:
Karkee deck, PDF p29.
Electrons \(e_e, e_r, e_l\) return together: the bunch arrives \(n + \tfrac34\) cycles later. PDF p30.
Construction
  • Electron gun, one re-entrant anode cavity at \(+V_0\), and a repeller electrode at \(-V_R\) beyond it.
  • Output via a coaxial loop from the same cavity.
Operation
  1. Noise starts a small RF voltage across the cavity gap.
  2. Electrons crossing it are velocity-modulated.
  3. In the retarding repeller field they stop and turn back. A faster electron goes deeper and takes longer: round trip \(T' = \dfrac{2mLv}{e(V_R + V_0)}\).
  4. So an early (fast) electron, the reference and a late (slow) one return together: the bunch forms in the repeller space.
  5. The bunch re-crosses the gap. If the gap field then opposes it, it gives energy to the cavity and oscillation grows.
Condition for oscillation
  • The bunch forms round the electron that left at zero gap voltage (going positive), and must return when the field most strongly retards it: \[ \boxed{T' = \left(n + \tfrac{3}{4}\right)\text{ cycles}}, \quad n = 0, 1, 2 \]
  • Power returned to the gap \(\propto -J_1(X)\sin\theta_0\): positive for \(\theta_0\) in the second half-cycle, largest at \(\tfrac34\). tubes.py scans \(\theta_0\) with simulated electrons and finds the peak at \(1.750\) cycles.
  • Electronic tuning: changing \(V_R\) changes \(T'\) and pulls the frequency a few percent; modes are the different \(n\).
  • Efficiency: maximum \(\dfrac{2X'J_1(X')}{2\pi n + 3\pi/2}\) with \(X' = 2.405\): 53% for \(n = 0\) (not practical), 22.7% for \(n = 1\). The deck's 22.78% is this, with \(X'\) rounded to 2.408. Practical 10 to 20%.
  • Performance: 4 to 200 GHz, 1 mW to 2.5 W. Uses: local oscillator in receivers, signal source for bench tests, portable links, pump for parametric amplifiers.

column1: Describe the construction and working of a cavity magnetron; magnetron with 45 / 60 / 90 degree phase shift between adjacent cavities
column4:
2-mark answer: cross-field effect (72 Ma, 78 Ch, 81 Bh). An electron in perpendicular dc electric and magnetic fields feels \(\vec F = -e(\vec E + \vec v\times\vec B)\). It does not go straight to the anode: it follows a cycloidal path and drifts at \(v = E/B\), perpendicular to both fields. Crossed-field (M-type) tubes use this drift to keep electrons in step with an RF wave for a long interaction.
Construction
  • Thick cylindrical cathode on the axis (radius \(a\)).
  • Copper anode block (radius \(b\)) with \(N\) (typically 8) resonant cavities cut into it, opening onto the interaction space.
  • Radial dc field from anode voltage \(V_0\); axial magnetic field from a permanent magnet, so \(E \perp B\).
  • Output: coupling loop in one cavity to a coaxial line or waveguide.
  • Straps join alternate anode segments to hold the tube in the \(\pi\)-mode.
Cavity magnetron cross-section and axial flux. PDF p55.
Electron paths and the Hull cut-off
  • \(B = 0\): straight radial path to the anode.
  • Small \(B\): curved path, still reaches the anode.
  • \(B = B_c\): path just grazes the anode (cut-off).
  • \(B > B_c\): electron returns to the cathode without collecting.
  • Hull cut-off field: \[ B_c = \frac{\sqrt{8mV_0/e}}{b\left(1 - a^2/b^2\right)} \]
  • Checked by integrating electron trajectories in tubes.py: for \(V_0 = 10\) kV, \(a = 5\) mm, \(b = 10\) mm the grazing field is \(0.0899\) T, equal to the formula. verified/added
  • The magnetron works just above \(B_c\): without RF no electron reaches the anode.
(b) normal operation, (c) at cut-off. PDF p61.
\(\pi\)-mode spoke pattern. Deck slide 50.
Operation (oscillator)
  1. Noise excites the cavities; RF fringing fields appear at the vane tips, alternating round the anode.
  2. Electrons circling the cathode meet these fields. Those in a retarding RF field slow down, feel less \(v\times B\) force, and drift outwards, giving energy to the RF on the way.
  3. Those in an accelerating field curl back to the cathode (back-bombardment heats it, often enough to switch the heater off).
  4. The result is phase focusing: the electron cloud forms rotating spokes, each sitting in a retarding field. This is the magnetron's bunching.
  5. On the next half-cycle the field pattern reverses and the spokes rotate one cavity on, staying in step: sustained oscillation. Efficiency 40 to 70%.

column1: The phase-shift versions: 45, 60, 90 degrees between adjacent cavities
column4:
• Around a ring of \(N\) cavities the total phase must be a whole number of turns: \[ \phi = \frac{2\pi n}{N}, \quad n = 0, \pm1, \pm2 \text{ up to } \pm\frac{N}{2} \]
  • \(n = N/2\): \(\phi = 180^\circ\), the \(\pi\)-mode, normal operation. \(n = 0\): zero mode, no RF between anode and cathode, unused.
  • The RF pattern repeats every \(360^\circ/\phi\) cavities, so there is one spoke per that many cavities:
    • \(45^\circ\): 8 cavities per wavelength (in an 8-cavity tube \(n = 1\), one spoke).
    • \(60^\circ\): 6 cavities per wavelength (\(N = 6\), \(n = 1\)).
    • \(90^\circ\): 4 cavities per wavelength (\(N = 8\) gives \(n = 2\), two spokes).
    • \(180^\circ\): 2 cavities, \(N/2\) spokes.
  • Synchronism: the spokes rotate at the RF pattern's angular velocity \(\omega/n\); set \(V_0\) and \(B\) so the electron drift (\(E/B\)) matches it.
  • As a power amplifier (80 Ba, 72 Ma): break the ring, feed RF in at one cavity and take it out several cavities later. The phase shift per cavity sets the wave's speed along the anode, \(v_p = \omega p/\phi\) (\(p\) = cavity pitch), and the beam drift is matched to it. That is the crossed-field amplifier of \(\S\)5.6.
  • Write the sketch with the cavities marked \(+\) / \(-\) according to \(\phi\) and draw the spokes in the retarding cavities; that sketch carries most of the marks.
  • Uses: radar transmitters, microwave ovens (2.45 GHz), industrial heating, linear accelerators.

column1: Explain the working principle of a circular-beam type microwave cavity-controlled crossed-field amplifier
column4:
• A crossed-field amplifier (CFA), also amplitron or platinotron: magnetron geometry, \(E \perp B\), but with an RF input and an RF output.
  • Circular-beam (re-entrant beam): the electron stream circulates round the cathode continuously, as in a magnetron.
  • Cavity-controlled (non-re-entrant RF circuit): the anode cavities form a slow-wave line from input to output; between output and input sits an RF absorber / insulator, so the wave cannot circulate and the tube does not oscillate.
  • Working:
    • The input wave travels along the anode at \(v_p = \omega p/\phi\).
    • Electrons drift at \(E/B\); matched to \(v_p\) they bunch into spokes in the retarding phase of the wave (\(\S\)5.5).
    • Spokes move with the wave and give up energy cavity by cavity \(\rightarrow\) the wave grows \(\rightarrow\) amplified output.
    • Left-over electrons carry little RF past the absorber and re-enter the input region.
  • Performance: high efficiency (up to about 70%), broad band (about 10%), low gain (10 to 15 dB), high power.
  • Use: final power stage of radar transmitters, driven by a TWT.
Circular CFA: input, output, absorber, spiralling electron flow. Student presentation 2078.

column1: Describe the construction and operation of a travelling wave tube (TWT)
column4:
Construction
  • Electron gun: cathode, focusing plate, anode.
  • Helix: a wire coil round the beam, the slow-wave structure; RF in at the gun end, out at the collector end.
  • Attenuator midway along the helix: absorbs reflected waves so the tube cannot oscillate.
  • Focusing magnets (solenoid or periodic permanent magnets) along the tube.
  • Collector: collects the spent beam.
  • No resonant cavities \(\rightarrow\) very wide bandwidth.
TWT construction. Student presentation 2078.
Operation
  1. RF on the helix travels round the turns at about \(c\), but along the axis only at \(v_p \approx c\,\dfrac{\text{pitch}}{2\pi r}\) (a few percent of \(c\)).
  2. The beam voltage is set so the electrons move slightly faster than \(v_p\).
  3. The axial RF field velocity-modulates the beam \(\rightarrow\) bunches form, and because beam and wave travel together the interaction lasts the whole length.
  4. Being slightly faster, the bunches sit in the retarding field and give energy to the wave, which grows exponentially \(\rightarrow\) gain 30 to 60 dB.
  • Correction to the source (PDF p38): the beam does not move at the velocity of light; the whole point of the helix is to slow the wave down to the beam. Example (tubes.py): pitch 1 mm, radius 2 mm gives \(v_p = 0.079c\), matched by a beam of about 1.6 kV; a 1 kV beam moves at \(0.063c\). verified/added
  • Performance: 0.5 to 95 GHz, octave bandwidth, 5 to 20% efficiency, mW to 10 MW pulsed. Uses: satellite transponders (long life), broadband receivers, radar, troposcatter links, EW jammers.

column1: What is bunching effect? Explain the working principle of a BWO with neat diagrams
column4:
• BWO (carcinotron): a TWT-family tube used as an oscillator, microwave up to terahertz.
  • Electron gun, slow-wave structure (helix or folded line), collector, magnetic focusing. No RF input.
  • The beam interacts with a backward space harmonic: its phase velocity is along the beam (so they stay in step) but its group velocity, the direction energy flows, is towards the gun.
  • Bunches give energy to this wave; the energy travels back to the gun end, where it velocity-modulates newly arriving electrons: built-in feedback \(\rightarrow\) self-sustained oscillation.
  • Output is taken at the gun end; the collector end is matched.
  • Frequency is tuned electronically by the beam voltage (it sets which backward harmonic is in step): very wide tuning range.
  • M-type BWO: crossed fields with a negative sole electrode (lower figure).
  • Uses: swept signal generators, THz spectroscopy and imaging, jammers.
  • Not a klystron: some student notes describe buncher and catcher cavities and a feedback conductor; a BWO has none.
O-type BWO: output near the gun. Deck slide 40.

column1: What do you mean by a slow (backward) wave structure?
column4:
• A slow-wave structure is a periodic RF circuit that makes the wave's axial phase velocity much smaller than \(c\), so an electron beam of practical voltage can keep in step with it: helix, folded-back line, ring-bar, interdigital line, coupled cavities.
  • It is backward when the space harmonic used has phase and group velocity in opposite directions: energy flows against the beam, as the BWO needs.

column1: Explain the construction and working principle of an LNA
column4:
• Purpose: the first amplifier after the antenna. Its noise figure sets the whole receiver's, by Friis: \[ F = F_1 + \frac{F_2 - 1}{G_1} + \frac{F_3 - 1}{G_1G_2} \quad\text{(one more term per stage)} \] e.g. a 1 dB, 20 dB-gain LNA before an 8 dB mixer gives 1.18 dB overall; the mixer first would give 8.02 dB (tubes.py).
  • Construction:
    • Low-noise device: GaAs FET / HEMT (historically a parametric amplifier, maser or low-noise TWT).
    • Input matching network: presents the source reflection \(\Gamma_{opt}\) for minimum noise figure, not conjugate match.
    • Output matching network: conjugate match for gain.
    • Bias network with RF chokes and bypass capacitors; stabilising resistors so \(K > 1\).
  • Working: the signal is amplified with gain 10 to 20 dB while adding as little noise as possible (NF 0.5 to 2 dB); trade-off between minimum NF and maximum gain drawn as noise circles and gain circles on the Smith chart (Ch 6).

column1: Why are microwave filters designed using the insertion loss method? How is a Butterworth / Chebyshev LPF prototyped?
column2: 452+63+56+2810
column4:
Filters, and the two design methods
  • Filter: two-port that passes a frequency band and attenuates the rest: LPF, HPF, BPF, BSF.
  • Image parameter method (1930s): cascade simple sections with the right cut-off and attenuation.
    • Cannot specify the whole response; needs repeated iteration.
  • Insertion loss method (ILM): network synthesis from a specified power loss ratio over all frequencies.
Power loss ratio
\[ P_{LR} = \frac{P_{\text{available}}}{P_{\text{load}}} = \frac{1}{1 - |\Gamma(\omega)|^2} = 1 + \frac{M(\omega^2)}{N(\omega^2)} \]
  • \(|\Gamma|^2\) is even in \(\omega\), so \(M\), \(N\) are polynomials in \(\omega^2\).
  • Insertion loss \(IL = 10\log P_{LR}\) dB; matched both ends: \(P_{LR} = 1/|S_{21}|^2\).
Why the insertion loss method (the 2 to 3 mark answer)
  • Response is completely specified and met exactly, no trial and error.
  • Explicit trade-offs: binomial for minimum passband loss, Chebyshev for sharpest cut-off, linear phase for low distortion.
  • Order \(N\) follows from the stopband requirement.
  • Starts from normalised low-pass prototypes (\(R_0 = 1\,\Omega\), \(\omega_c = 1\) rad/s), so one table serves every filter after scaling.
  • Designs improve systematically with \(N\); CAD tools implement it directly.
\(N = 3\): equal-ripple is sharper, maximally flat is smoother. Gangaju Ch-6 deck, slide 11.
The three standard responses
  • Maximally flat (Butterworth, binomial): \(P_{LR} = 1 + k^2(\omega/\omega_c)^{2N}\).
    • Band-edge loss \(1 + k^2\); \(k = 1\) gives \(-3\) dB.
    • Beyond cut-off rises \(20N\) dB/decade; flattest possible passband.
  • Equal ripple (Chebyshev): \(P_{LR} = 1 + k^2T_N^2(\omega/\omega_c)\).
    • Ripple of amplitude \(1 + k^2\) in the passband.
    • Also \(20N\) dB/decade, but \(\dfrac{2^{2N}}{4}\) times more attenuation than Butterworth well beyond cut-off.
  • Linear phase: \(\phi = A\omega[1 + p(\omega/\omega_c)^{2N}]\), maximally flat group delay; poorer selectivity.
Low-pass prototype and element values
The two dual ladder forms, \(g_0 = 1\) source, \(g_{N+1}\) load. Deck slide 7 (Pozar p.403).
  • Butterworth (\(k = 1\)): \(g_k = 2\sin\dfrac{(2k-1)\pi}{2N}\), \(g_{N+1} = 1\).
  • Chebyshev, ripple \(L_r\) dB: \(\beta = \ln\coth\frac{L_r}{17.37}\), \(\gamma = \sinh\frac{\beta}{2N}\), \(a_k = \sin\frac{(2k-1)\pi}{2N}\), \(b_k = \gamma^2 + \sin^2\frac{k\pi}{N}\); \(g_1 = \dfrac{2a_1}{\gamma}\), \(g_k = \dfrac{4a_{k-1}a_k}{b_{k-1}g_{k-1}}\); \(g_{N+1} = 1\) for odd \(N\), \(\coth^2\frac{\beta}{4}\) for even \(N\).
  • Order (Butterworth): smallest \(N\) with \(10\log\left[1 + (\omega/\omega_c)^{2N}\right] \ge\) required stopband loss.

column1: Why are Butterworth and Chebyshev common to prototype two-port filters?
column4:
• Both power loss ratios are polynomials in \(\omega^2\) that give a realisable lossless LC ladder with closed-form element values.
  • They sit at the two ends of the useful trade-off: flattest passband (Butterworth) vs sharpest cut-off for a given \(N\) (Chebyshev).
  • Tabulated, normalised values mean a designer only scales; the same table gives LPF, HPF, BPF and BSF by transformation (\(\S\)6.2).
  • Ladders map directly onto transmission-line sections, so both are practical in microstrip (\(\S\)6.3).

column1: Explain the steps of microwave filter design; how is a LPF prototype converted to other filters?
column4:
The procedure (write it as four boxes)
  1. Specifications: type, cut-off \(f_c\) (or band \(f_1\) to \(f_2\)), passband loss or ripple, stopband attenuation at a stated frequency, \(R_0\).
  2. Low-pass prototype: choose response, find \(N\), read \(g_1\) to \(g_{N+1}\) (\(R_0 = 1\), \(\omega_c = 1\)).
  3. Scaling and conversion: impedance-scale by \(R_0\), frequency-scale to \(\omega_c\), and transform LP \(\rightarrow\) HP / BP / BS.
  4. Implementation: lumped (below about 5 GHz) or distributed microstrip: stepped impedance, Richards' stubs, Kuroda identities (\(\S\)6.3).
Impedance and frequency scaling (LPF)
\[ L'_k = \frac{R_0L_k}{\omega_c}, \qquad C'_k = \frac{C_k}{R_0\omega_c}, \qquad R'_s = R'_L = R_0 \]
Element transformations, \(\Delta = (\omega_2 - \omega_1)/\omega_0\), \(\omega_0 = \sqrt{\omega_1\omega_2}\). Deck slide 19 (Pozar p.414).
Conversion rules
  • LPF \(\rightarrow\) HPF, \(\omega \rightarrow -\omega_c/\omega\): series L becomes series C \(= \dfrac{1}{R_0\omega_cL_k}\); shunt C becomes shunt L \(= \dfrac{R_0}{\omega_cC_k}\).
  • LPF \(\rightarrow\) BPF: series L \(\rightarrow\) series LC (\(L_k R_0/\omega_0\Delta\), \(\Delta/\omega_0L_kR_0\)); shunt C \(\rightarrow\) shunt LC (\(\Delta R_0/\omega_0C_k\), \(C_k/\omega_0\Delta R_0\)).
  • LPF \(\rightarrow\) BSF: the reverse pairing (series arms become parallel LC, shunt arms series LC).

column1: Implement the filter using microstrip: LPF \(\pi\) / double \(\pi\), double-pad T-type, double-section shunt-arm or series-arm, HPF, single-section series-arm BPF
column2: 233+55+37+38+210
column4:
Why microstrip, and the two methods
  • Lumped L, C work to about 5 GHz; above that their size and spacing are no longer small in wavelengths.
  • Microstrip: planar, cheap, light, easy to mount active devices; but lossier, lower power, radiates and couples.
  • Stepped impedance (Hi-Z / Low-Z): alternate very high and very low impedance short lines.
  • Stubs (Richards' transformation): inductor \(\rightarrow\) short-circuited stub, capacitor \(\rightarrow\) open-circuited stub, each \(\lambda/8\) long at \(f_c\); Kuroda identities separate series stubs.
Why a short line is an L or a C
  • T-model of a line length \(l\): series \(X/2 = Z_0\tan(\beta l/2)\), shunt \(B = \sin(\beta l)/Z_0\).
  • High \(Z_0\), short: \(X \approx Z_h\beta l\), \(B \approx 0\) \(\rightarrow\) a series inductor.
  • Low \(Z_0\), short: \(B \approx \beta l/Z_l\), \(X \approx 0\) \(\rightarrow\) a shunt capacitor.
  • Design lengths: \[ \beta l = \frac{g_kR_0}{Z_h}\ \text{(inductor)}, \qquad \beta l = \frac{g_kZ_l}{R_0}\ \text{(capacitor)} \] Keep \(\beta l < 45^\circ\); typically \(Z_h \approx 100\) to \(120\,\Omega\), \(Z_l \approx 20\,\Omega\).
Stepped-impedance LPF and its layout. Deck slide 26.
Elliptic LPF with capacitive stubs alternating sides to cut cross-talk. Deck slide 27.
  • Checked: filt.py reproduces the deck's example table (\(N = 6\), \(Z_h = 120\), \(Z_l = 20\,\Omega\), \(\epsilon_r = 4.2\), \(h = 1.58\) mm): \(\beta l = 11.8, 33.8, 44.3, 46.1, 32.4, 12.3^\circ\), \(W = 11.3\) and \(0.43\) mm.
Vocabulary the papers use
  • Pad: a wide, low-\(Z\) section = a shunt capacitor.
  • Series arm: an element in the signal path (series L in an LPF, series C in an HPF). Shunt arm: an element to ground (shunt C as a pad or open stub; shunt L as a shorted stub).
  • \(\pi\)-section: shunt, series, shunt (C-L-C for a LPF). T-section: series, shunt, series (L-C-L).
  • Double / triple: two or three such sections cascaded.
The layouts below are drawn to scale by filt.py from computed dimensions for one assumed specification, which is what a paper that says “illustrate an example” expects: Butterworth, \(f_c = 2.5\) GHz, \(R_0 = 50\,\Omega\), \(Z_h = 120\,\Omega\), \(Z_l = 20\,\Omega\), \(\epsilon_r = 4.2\), \(h = 1.58\) mm (\(W_{50} = 3.13\) mm).
LPF \(\pi\)-section, \(N = 3\) (79 Bh, 73 Ma, 74 Ma, 72 Ash)
  • \(g = 1, 2, 1\): pads \(\beta l = 22.9^\circ\) (4.04 mm), line \(47.7^\circ\) (9.44 mm).
Double \(\pi\)-section, \(N = 5\) (76 Bh)
  • \(g = 0.618, 1.618, 2, 1.618, 0.618\): three pads, two high-\(Z\) lines.
Double-pad T-type, \(N = 5\) (81 Ba; series-arm, 78 Ch)
  • L-C-L-C-L: the series arms are the three high-\(Z\) lines, the two pads the shunt capacitors. A “double-section series-arm” filter is this layout.
Double-section shunt-arm LPF, \(N = 4\) (80 Ba)
  • Shunt capacitors as open stubs, \(\lambda/8\) at \(f_c\) with \(Z = R_0/g_k\) (Richards): 65 and 27 \(\Omega\); series inductors as high-\(Z\) lines.
HPF \(\pi\)-section (74 Bh, 80 Bh, 82 Ba)
  • From the C-L-C prototype: shunt \(L = 3.18\) nH, series \(C = 0.637\) pF.
  • Series capacitor = a gap (or interdigital) in the strip; shunt inductor = a short-circuited stub through a via: \(Z_s\tan\beta l = \omega_cL\) gives 5.19 mm of \(100\,\Omega\) line.
  • Triple-pad series-arm HPF (82 Ba): three pads separated by two gaps (the series capacitors) with shorted stubs from the pads.
  • 80 Bh's “second-order \(\pi\)”: one series gap between two stubbed pads.
Single-section series-arm BPF (81 Bh)
  • The series LC arm of a BPF is a half-wave resonator coupled by a gap at each end: resonant at \(f_0\) (series-resonant, passes), capacitively coupled (blocks DC and low frequencies).
  • \(l = \lambda_g/2\) at \(f_0\): 37.2 mm on 50 \(\Omega\) at 2.25 GHz.
  • More sections (more resonators) sharpen the skirts.

column1: Draw the design flowchart of a microwave amplifier; stability analysis; stability synthesis on the Smith chart; amplifier vs oscillator
column2: 453+85+56+4810
column4:
Reflection coefficients seen by the device
\[ \Gamma_{in} = S_{11} + \frac{S_{12}S_{21}\Gamma_L}{1 - S_{22}\Gamma_L} = \frac{S_{11} - \Delta\Gamma_L}{1 - S_{22}\Gamma_L} \] \[ \Gamma_{out} = S_{22} + \frac{S_{12}S_{21}\Gamma_S}{1 - S_{11}\Gamma_S} = \frac{S_{22} - \Delta\Gamma_S}{1 - S_{11}\Gamma_S} \] \(\Delta = S_{11}S_{22} - S_{12}S_{21}\). From \(b_2 = S_{21}a_1 + S_{22}\Gamma_Lb_2\) (deck slides 33 to 34).
Three power gains
  • Transducer \(G_T = P_L/P_{avs}\) (the one the papers use).
  • Available \(G_A = P_{avn}/P_{avs}\); operating \(G_P = P_L/P_{in}\).
\[ G_T = \frac{1 - |\Gamma_S|^2}{|1 - \Gamma_{in}\Gamma_S|^2}\,|S_{21}|^2\, \frac{1 - |\Gamma_L|^2}{|1 - S_{22}\Gamma_L|^2} \]
  • Unilateral (\(S_{12} \approx 0\)): \(G_{TU} = G_S\,G_0\,G_L\) with \(G_0 = |S_{21}|^2\); maximum at \(\Gamma_S = S_{11}^*\), \(\Gamma_L = S_{22}^*\): \[ G_{TU,max} = \frac{1}{1 - |S_{11}|^2}\,|S_{21}|^2\,\frac{1}{1 - |S_{22}|^2} \]
  • Unilateral figure of merit \(M = \dfrac{|S_{11}||S_{12}||S_{21}||S_{22}|}{(1 - |S_{11}|^2)(1 - |S_{22}|^2)}\); error bound \(\dfrac{1}{(1 + M)^2} < \dfrac{G_T}{G_{TU}} < \dfrac{1}{(1 - M)^2}\). Unilateral is acceptable if the bound is a few tenths of a dB.
  • Bilateral maximum (simultaneous conjugate match, \(\Gamma_S = \Gamma_{in}^*\), \(\Gamma_L = \Gamma_{out}^*\)), only if unconditionally stable: \[ \Gamma_S = \frac{B_1 - \sqrt{B_1^2 - 4|C_1|^2}}{2C_1}, \quad \Gamma_L = \frac{B_2 - \sqrt{B_2^2 - 4|C_2|^2}}{2C_2} \] \(B_1 = 1 + |S_{11}|^2 - |S_{22}|^2 - |\Delta|^2\), \(C_1 = S_{11} - \Delta S_{22}^*\) (and \(1 \leftrightarrow 2\)). Then \(G_{T,max} = \dfrac{|S_{21}|}{|S_{12}|}\left(K - \sqrt{K^2 - 1}\right)\).
Stability
  • Oscillation is possible if \(|\Gamma_{in}| > 1\) or \(|\Gamma_{out}| > 1\) (negative resistance at a port).
  • Unconditionally stable: \(|\Gamma_{in}|, |\Gamma_{out}| < 1\) for every passive source and load. Test (Rollett): \[ K = \frac{1 - |S_{11}|^2 - |S_{22}|^2 + |\Delta|^2}{2|S_{12}S_{21}|} > 1 \ \text{and}\ |\Delta| < 1 \] or the single test \(\mu = \dfrac{1 - |S_{11}|^2}{|S_{22} - \Delta S_{11}^*| + |S_{12}S_{21}|} > 1\).
  • Conditionally (potentially) stable: some \(\Gamma_S\) or \(\Gamma_L\) cause oscillation. Find them with stability circles: \[ C_L = \frac{(S_{22} - \Delta S_{11}^*)^*}{|S_{22}|^2 - |\Delta|^2}, \quad R_L = \left|\frac{S_{12}S_{21}}{|S_{22}|^2 - |\Delta|^2}\right| \] \[ C_S = \frac{(S_{11} - \Delta S_{22}^*)^*}{|S_{11}|^2 - |\Delta|^2}, \quad R_S = \left|\frac{S_{12}S_{21}}{|S_{11}|^2 - |\Delta|^2}\right| \]
  • On the output circle \(|\Gamma_{in}| = 1\); on the input circle \(|\Gamma_{out}| = 1\). Each is a boundary, not a region.
Deck slides 45 to 46: \(S_{11} = 0.65\angle{-95^\circ}\) etc. at 800 MHz, \(K = 0.547\): \(C_S = 1.79\angle122^\circ\), \(R_S = 1.04\); \(C_L = 1.30\angle48^\circ\), \(R_L = 0.45\). Hatched overlaps are the unstable \(\Gamma\). Reproduced exactly in amp.py.
Which side of the circle is stable (synthesis on the Smith chart)
  1. Plot \(C_L\), \(R_L\) (and \(C_S\), \(R_S\)) on the chart.
  2. Test the centre \(\Gamma_L = 0\): there \(|\Gamma_{in}| = |S_{11}|\).
  3. If \(|S_{11}| < 1\) the centre is stable, so the stable region is the side of the circle that contains the centre:
    • \(|C_L| > R_L\) (centre outside) \(\Rightarrow\) stable outside the circle.
    • \(|C_L| < R_L\) (centre inside) \(\Rightarrow\) stable inside.
  4. Same for the source circle with \(|S_{22}|\).
  5. Circle entirely outside the unit chart (or enclosing it on the stable side) \(\Rightarrow\) unconditionally stable. Circle cutting the chart \(\Rightarrow\) conditionally stable; choose \(\Gamma_S\), \(\Gamma_L\) well inside the stable part.
73 Bh, 74 Bh, 75 Bh give a sketched chart; 71 Bh gives the circles directly. Worked: companion Problem 7.
Amplifier design flowchart (write as boxes joined by arrows)
  1. Specify \(f\), gain, noise figure, \(Z_0\); choose a transistor (GaAs FET / HEMT / BJT) and bias; read its S-parameters.
  2. Stability: compute \(\Delta\), \(K\) (or \(\mu\)).
  3. \(K > 1\), \(|\Delta| < 1\)? Yes \(\rightarrow\) step 4. No \(\rightarrow\) draw stability circles, restrict \(\Gamma_S\), \(\Gamma_L\) to the stable region (or add resistive loading / feedback), then step 4.
  4. Unilateral check: compute \(M\) and the error bound.
    • Small \(\rightarrow\) \(\Gamma_S = S_{11}^*\), \(\Gamma_L = S_{22}^*\) (or gain circles for a specified gain).
    • Large \(\rightarrow\) bilateral: \(\Gamma_S\), \(\Gamma_L\) from \(B\), \(C\).
  5. Gain: \(G_{TU,max}\) or \(G_{T,max}\); compare with the specification.
  6. Matching networks: realise \(\Gamma_S\) and \(\Gamma_L\) from \(50\,\Omega\) with a line plus a stub (Smith chart, Ch 2).
  7. Bias network, DC blocks, RF chokes; layout in microstrip; simulate, build, measure, tune.
Final amplifier: input network, transistor, output network. Deck slide 58.

column1: Microwave oscillator theory
column4:
Feedback view
  • Gain \(A\) with positive feedback \(\beta\): \(\dfrac{e_o}{e_i} = \dfrac{A}{1 - A\beta}\).
  • \(A\beta = 1\) \(\rightarrow\) finite output with no input: Barkhausen condition. To start, \(A\beta \approx 1.1\) to \(1.2\); oscillation grows from noise until gain compression brings \(A\beta\) back to 1.
Negative-resistance view (the microwave one)
  • A device port with \(|\Gamma_{out}| > 1\) has negative resistance.
  • One-port oscillator: device \(Z_{out} = R_{out} + jX_{out}\) with \(R_{out} < 0\), load \(Z_L\). Loop condition \(\Gamma_{out}\Gamma_L = 1\) gives \[ R_L + R_{out} = 0, \qquad X_L + X_{out} = 0 \]
  • To start oscillation the circuit must have net negative resistance: \(R_L < |R_{out}|\). The deck's rule \(|R_{out}| \ge 1.2R_L\) (Pozar uses \(R_L = |R_{out}|/3\)).
  • Two-port oscillator: transistor with a generator tuning network (\(\Gamma_S\)) and a load network (\(\Gamma_L\)). Conditions:
    1. \(K < 1\): device potentially unstable.
    2. \(\Gamma_{in}\Gamma_S = 1\).
    3. \(\Gamma_{out}\Gamma_L = 1\) (equivalent to 2, shown by substituting \(\Gamma_{in}\)).
Positive feedback. Deck slide 60.
Two-port oscillator. Deck slide 62.
One-port: negative-resistance device and load. Deck slide 65.
Two-port design steps
  1. From the S-parameters find \(K\); need \(K < 1\) (use a common-gate / common-base configuration or series feedback to make it so).
  2. Draw the input stability circle.
  3. Choose \(\Gamma_S\) inside the unstable region, usually on the rim for the largest \(|\Gamma_{out}|\); realise it with an inductor or shorted stub.
  4. \(\Gamma_{out} = S_{22} + \dfrac{S_{12}S_{21}\Gamma_S}{1 - S_{11}\Gamma_S}\), \(|\Gamma_{out}| > 1\) \(\rightarrow\) \(Z_{out} = R_{out} + jX_{out}\) with \(R_{out} < 0\).
  5. Choose \(R_L = |R_{out}|/3\) (start-up margin), \(X_L = -X_{out}\); design the load matching network.
Worked: Gunn diode one-port (deck slide 66, checked in amp.py)
  • \(\Gamma_{out} = 1.24\angle30^\circ\) at 10 GHz. Plot \(1/\Gamma_{out}^* = 0.806\angle30^\circ\), read \(z\) and negate the real part: \(Z_{out} = -68.9 + j159.0\,\Omega\) (deck reads \(-70 + j160\)).
  • Resonance: \(X_L = -159\,\Omega\), a capacitor \(C = 1/(2\pi f\cdot159) = 0.100\) pF.
  • Start-up: the deck picks \(R_L = 60\,\Omega\), which breaks its own rule: \(|R_{out}| \ge 1.2R_L\) needs \(R_L \le 57.5\,\Omega\). Use \(R_L = 23\,\Omega\) (Pozar's \(|R_{out}|/3\)) or at most \(57\,\Omega\). verified/added
\(\Gamma_S\) chosen inside the input stability circle. Deck slide 67.

  • Frequency stability: high-Q resonator in the tuning network; isolator at the output (Ch 4).

column1: Mixer theory / microwave mixer
column4:
• Mixer: a nonlinear three-port (diode or FET) that multiplies an RF signal \(f_{RF}\) with a local oscillator \(f_{LO}\) to translate it in frequency.
  • Square-law principle: \(i = a v^2\) with \(v = V_{RF}\cos\omega_{RF}t + V_{LO}\cos\omega_{LO}t\) contains \(aV_{RF}V_{LO}\cos(\omega_{RF} \pm \omega_{LO})t\): sum and difference (checked by FFT in amp.py).
  • Down-conversion: keep \(f_{IF} = |f_{RF} - f_{LO}|\) with a filter; the superheterodyne receiver then amplifies at a fixed IF.
  • Up-conversion (transmitters): keep \(f_{RF} = f_{LO} + f_{IF}\).
  • Image frequency: \(f_{IM} = f_{LO} \pm f_{IF}\) on the other side of the LO also lands on \(f_{IF}\) \(\rightarrow\) reject it with an RF pre-filter or an image-reject mixer.
  • Figures of merit: conversion loss \(L_c = 10\log(P_{RF}/P_{IF})\) (typically 4 to 7 dB for diode mixers), noise figure, LO-RF and LO-IF isolation, 1 dB compression, intermodulation.
  • Types:
    • Single-ended diode: one Schottky diode; simple, poor isolation.
    • Balanced: two diodes fed through a 90\(^\circ\) or 180\(^\circ\) hybrid (magic tee, rat race, Ch 4): cancels LO AM noise, better isolation, better input match.
    • Double-balanced: diode ring with two baluns: suppresses even harmonics and both RF and LO at the IF port.
    • FET mixers: conversion gain instead of loss.
(a) up-conversion, (b) down-conversion, each with its output spectrum: both \(f_{LO} \pm f_{IF}\) (or \(f_{RF} \pm f_{LO}\)) appear and a filter keeps one. Pozar Fig 13.24.
(a) single-ended diode mixer: RF and LO combined in a diplexing coupler, DC-biased diode, low-pass filter to the IF port; (b) its ideal equivalent, \(v_{RF} + v_{LO}\) across the diode. Pozar Fig 13.25.

column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 72 Ash [5+5]
Justify that a transistor having following S-parameters S\(_{11}\) = 0.894 \(\angle\) -60.6\(^\circ\), S\(_{12}\) = 0.020 \(\angle\) 62.4\(^\circ\), S\(_{21}\) = 3.122 \(\angle\) 123.6\(^\circ\) and S\(_{22}\) = 0.781 \(\angle\) -27.6\(^\circ\) is conditionally stable while designing an amplifier. Considering unilateral model calculate maximum gain.
column4:
70 Ma [10] asks only the justification; 80 Ba [5+5] “investigate the stability” at 6 GHz; 79 Bh [5+5] “determine the stability and compare maximum power gains for bilateral and unilateral modes”.
Step 1 to 3: stability
  • \(|S_{11}|^2 = 0.7992\), \(|S_{22}|^2 = 0.6100\), \(|S_{21}|^2 = 9.747\), \(|S_{12}S_{21}| = 0.06244\).
  • \(S_{11}S_{22} = 0.6982\angle{-88.2^\circ}\), \(S_{12}S_{21} = 0.0624\angle{-174.0^\circ}\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(\Delta = \boxed{0.6964\angle{-83.1^\circ}}\), \(|\Delta|^2 = 0.4850\).
  • \(K = \dfrac{1 - 0.7992 - 0.6100 + 0.4850}{0.1249} = \dfrac{0.0758}{0.1249} = \boxed{0.607} < 1\);  \(\mu = 0.863 < 1\).
  • \(|\Delta| < 1\) but \(K < 1\) \(\Rightarrow\) potentially unstable: some passive terminations make it oscillate.
Step 4: stability circles, and the proof that it is conditionally stable
CircleCentre and radiusNearest point to originStable side
Output (\(\Gamma_L\))\(C_L = \frac{(S_{22} - \Delta S_{11}^*)^*}{|S_{22}|^2 - |\Delta|^2} = 1.363\angle46.7^\circ\), \(R_L = 0.500\)\(1.363 - 0.500 = 0.863 < 1\): cuts the chartorigin outside, \(|S_{11}| < 1\) \(\Rightarrow\) outside
Input (\(\Gamma_S\))\(C_S = 1.132\angle68.5^\circ\), \(R_S = 0.199\)\(0.933 < 1\): cuts the chartoutside
  • Both circles cut the unit circle, so part of the chart is unstable and the rest is stable: the device is conditionally stable. Pick \(\Gamma_S\), \(\Gamma_L\) outside the circles (deck figure, \(\S\)6.4).
The two circles drawn from the table: each cuts the chart, so a sliver of the chart (hatched) is unstable; the unilateral design points \(S_{11}^*\), \(S_{22}^*\) used in Step 5 sit on the stable side. Generated from the S-parameters by ampfig.py, which stops if these centres and radii differ from the table.
Step 5: unilateral maximum gain, and whether its design points are safe
  • \(G_{TU,max} = \dfrac{1}{1 - 0.7992}\times9.747\times\dfrac{1}{1 - 0.6100} = 4.981\times9.747\times2.564 = \boxed{124.5 = 20.95\text{ dB}}\).
  • Design points \(\Gamma_S = S_{11}^* = 0.894\angle60.6^\circ\), \(\Gamma_L = S_{22}^* = 0.781\angle27.6^\circ\): both lie outside their circles, and together give \(|\Gamma_{in}| = 0.912\), \(|\Gamma_{out}| = 0.848\), both \(< 1\). The design is stable. verified/added
  • But \(M = 0.557\): the error bound is \(-3.84\) to \(+7.07\) dB, so 20.95 dB is only a rough estimate for this strongly bilateral device.
Step 6 (79 Bh): the bilateral comparison
  • With \(K < 1\) there is no simultaneous conjugate match and no \(G_{T,max}\).
  • The limit is the maximum stable gain \(MSG = |S_{21}|/|S_{12}| = 3.122/0.020 = 156.1 = \boxed{21.9\text{ dB}}\), approached only with stabilising loss.
  • Compare: unilateral estimate 20.95 dB against an MSG ceiling of 21.9 dB.

A GaAs power FET has the S-parameters at 5 GHz with 50-ohm line measured as S\(_{11}\) = 0.45\(\angle\)163\(^\circ\), S\(_{12}\) = 0.04\(\angle\)40\(^\circ\), S\(_{21}\) = 2.55\(\angle\)-106\(^\circ\) and S\(_{22}\) = 0.46\(\angle\)-65\(^\circ\). column4:
Step 1 to 4: as Problem 1 (values in Problem 2's tables, 72 Ma row)
  • \(K = 3.332\), \(|\Delta| = 0.306\): unconditionally stable.
  • \(\Gamma_S = 0.4011\angle{-160.6^\circ}\), \(\Gamma_L = 0.4131\angle67.2^\circ\), \(G_{T,max} = 1.1917\times6.5025\times1.2636 = \boxed{9.79 = 9.91\text{ dB}}\) (total power gain).
Step 5: input matching network (open shunt stub, then a line)
  1. Start at the \(50\,\Omega\) source: \(y = 1\), the chart centre.
  2. A shunt stub moves along the \(g = 1\) circle to \(y = 1 + jb\); this must land on the circle \(|\Gamma| = |\Gamma_S| = 0.4011\): \(b = \dfrac{2|\Gamma_S|}{\sqrt{1 - |\Gamma_S|^2}} = 0.8757\).
  3. Open stub with \(b = +0.8757\): \(l_{stub} = \dfrac{\tan^{-1}0.8757}{2\pi} = \boxed{0.1145\lambda}\).
  4. At the stub \(\Gamma = \dfrac{1 - y}{1 + y} = 0.4011\angle{-113.6^\circ}\); a line of length \(l\) rotates it clockwise by \(720l\) degrees to \(\angle{-160.6^\circ}\): \(l = \dfrac{160.6 - 113.6}{720} = \boxed{0.0652\lambda}\).
Step 6: output network, the same way
  • \(b = 0.9072\), open stub \(\boxed{0.1173\lambda}\), line \(\boxed{0.2477\lambda}\) to present \(\Gamma_L = 0.4131\angle67.2^\circ\).
  • Circuit: source \(\rightarrow\) stub \(\rightarrow\) line \(\rightarrow\) FET \(\rightarrow\) line \(\rightarrow\) stub \(\rightarrow\) load, as in the deck's final diagram (\(\S\)6.4).
  • amp.py walks both networks forward and recovers \(\Gamma_S\), \(\Gamma_L\) exactly.
Steps 5 and 6 on the chart. From the \(50\,\Omega\) centre the open stub moves the point along the admittance \(g = 1\) circle (green) onto the \(|\Gamma_S|\) or \(|\Gamma_L|\) circle (dotted); the line then rotates it clockwise to the required \(\Gamma\). column1: Chapter 7 — Microwave Antennas and Propagation: how is it examined?
column4:
3 hrs  \(\cdot\) asked in 23 of 24 papers  \(\cdot\) 3 syllabus sub-topics  \(\cdot\) 162 marks, 8.4% of 24 papers \(\rightarrow\) almost every mark is on sub-topic (c), radiation hazards; antenna types and propagation have never been examined.
READ THIS FIRST
Chapter 7 is the one guaranteed question of the paper: only 72 Ash skips it in 24 sets. It comes as a 4 to 10 mark theory answer, usually two parts glued together.
  1. Radiation fields / zones (11 papers) \(\rightarrow\) \(\S\)7.1. Three zones, two boundary formulas, one figure. The BTS and microwave-oven versions put numbers in them: worked in the numerical companion.
  2. How microwaves are hazardous; HERP, HERO, HERF (17 papers) \(\rightarrow\) \(\S\)7.2. Always the same chain: non-ionizing \(\rightarrow\) dielectric heating \(\rightarrow\) no internal heat sensors \(\rightarrow\) poorly cooled organs.
  3. SAR (3 papers, one of them for 10 marks) \(\rightarrow\) \(\S\)7.3.
  4. Safety standards (4 papers) and safety practices (7 papers) \(\rightarrow\) \(\S\)7.4 and \(\S\)7.5. Name the body, the frequency range and one number each.
Two things worth knowing before the paper starts:
  • Nearly every question is “part A + part B” from the list above. Answer each part under its own heading and draw the zone figure whenever “fields” appears.
  • Every limit is built on one number: a whole-body SAR of 4 W/kg warms the body by about 1\(^\circ\)C. Divide by 10 for workers (0.4 W/kg), by 50 for the public (0.08 W/kg). Quote this and the standards section writes itself.

column1: Name and explain the microwave radiation fields: reactive, radiating near and far field
column4:
• Radiation = energy carried away by EM waves. Round any antenna (or leaking oven, or waveguide opening) the field is split into three zones by distance \(R\), antenna largest dimension \(D\) and wavelength \(\lambda\).
  • Near field = the first two zones. Far field = the third.
ZoneBoundary
Reactive near field\(R < 0.62\sqrt{D^3/\lambda}\)
Radiating near field (Fresnel)\(0.62\sqrt{D^3/\lambda} < R < 2D^2/\lambda\)
Far field (Fraunhofer)\(R > 2D^2/\lambda\)
Reactive and radiating near field, then far field. Karkee, Ch-7 PDF p5 (white on black in the source, inverted for print).

  • Hazardous vs safe (deck): reactive and radiating near field are treated as hazardous, the far field as the safe side, where exposure falls as \(1/R^2\) and can be checked against a limit (\(\S\)7.4).
  • Validity verified/added: the two formulas assume an antenna larger than a wavelength. For a small antenna (\(D < \lambda\), e.g. a quarter-wave whip) they give a “far field” that starts inside the reactive region. Use instead: reactive field out to \(\lambda/2\pi\), far field beyond about \(2\lambda\). The 82 Ba quarter-wave question and the deck's 150 MHz example fall here (ant.py).

column1: Radiation zones of a microwave oven; radiation fields round a GSM BTS
column4:
Microwave oven, \(f = 2.45\) GHz, \(D = 0.5\) m
  • \(\lambda = 0.1224\) m, \(D > \lambda\) so the formulas hold.
  • Reactive: \(R < 0.63\) m. Fresnel: \(0.63\) to \(4.08\) m. Far field: \(R > 4.08\) m.
  • In practice the cavity is a closed metal box (Faraday cage) and the door mesh holes are far smaller than \(\lambda = 12\) cm, so almost nothing leaks. Leakage limit (US FDA): 1 mW/cm\(^2\) at 5 cm when sold, 5 mW/cm\(^2\) over its life. verified/added
  • Zones matter only for leakage at a damaged door seal or hinge: stay out of the reactive zone (arm's length) while it runs.
GSM / LTE base station (BTS)
  • Panel antenna on a mast, main beam tilted a few degrees down, hitting the ground tens to hundreds of metres away (figure).
  • Reactive and Fresnel zones: within a few metres in front of the panel, reached only by riggers on the tower or a rooftop \(\rightarrow\) occupational exclusion zone.
  • Far field: everywhere the public is. Power density there is far below the limit (81 Bh: zones \(0.65\) m and \(4.33\) m).
  • Radiation parameters (81 Ba): frequency, transmit power, antenna gain, EIRP, beam tilt and beamwidth, polarization, power density (W/m\(^2\)), field strength (V/m), SAR.

column1: How are microwaves hazardous to humans (living body)? Microwave radiation hazards (short note)
column4:
1. Microwaves are non-ionizing
  • Photon energy \(E = hf\): at 2.45 GHz only \(1.0\times10^{-5}\) eV.
  • Ionizing a molecule needs about 10 eV \(\rightarrow\) a microwave photon is a million times too weak. It cannot break bonds or DNA directly (unlike X-rays, gamma rays).
  • So the established hazard is heat, not ionization.
2. Thermal effect: dielectric heating
  • The field rotates polar water molecules and drives ionic currents in tissue \(\rightarrow\) friction and \(I^2R\) loss \(\rightarrow\) heat.
  • Absorbed power per kg \(= \sigma E^2/\rho\) = SAR (\(\S\)7.3).
  • Microwaves heat inside out. Sunlight heats outside in, where skin sensors warn and sweat cools (figure).
Sun heating (outside in, felt) vs microwave heating (inside out, trapped). Gangaju, Ch-7 deck, slide 4.
Microwaves sit far below visible light and the ionizing bands. KEC Ch-7 deck, slide 5.
3. Why the heating is dangerous
  • No internal heat sensation: the body senses heat only in the skin, so deep tissue can be damaged before the person notices.
  • Poorly cooled organs (little blood flow to carry heat away):
    • Eye lens \(\rightarrow\) cataract.
    • Testes \(\rightarrow\) temporary sterility.
    • Stomach, intestines, bladder, gall bladder \(\rightarrow\) thermal damage at high power.
  • Body resonance: absorption peaks when body size is comparable to \(\lambda\) (whole adult body about 70 to 100 MHz). The deck adds: significant absorption even when body size is \(\lambda/10\). That is why every limit chart dips lowest at 30 to 300 MHz (\(\S\)7.4).
  • Penetration falls with frequency: deep at UHF (several cm), about 1 to 2 cm at 2.45 GHz, only the skin above about 10 GHz \(\rightarrow\) lower microwave bands heat deep tissue unfelt, higher bands burn the surface. verified/added
  • Long low-frequency magnetic exposure can also induce damaging currents (deck).
4. Other effects
  • RF burns and shocks: touching a metal object (fence, mast, vehicle) in a strong field drives contact current through the hand.
  • Implants: pacemakers and other active implants can malfunction; metal implants concentrate the field and heat.
  • Microwave hearing: pulsed radar is heard as clicks (thermoelastic expansion in the head).
  • Behavioural complaints reported by RF workers: headache, irritability, fatigue, sleeplessness (deck). Not reproduced in blind studies.
  • Cancer: IARC (WHO) 2011 classes RF fields Group 2B, “possibly carcinogenic”, meaning limited evidence. Correction: one student deck calls microwaves “known” to cause cancer and another slide calls non-thermal effects “several times more harmful” than thermal; neither is established. verified/added
Link to the zones (69 Bh, 72 Ma, 81 Bh): “how is non-radiating radiation hazardous?” 458
  • The reactive near field does not radiate, but its stored \(E\) and \(H\) fields are strongest there. A body inside it loads the antenna and draws energy out of the stored field \(\rightarrow\) absorbed as heat, although nothing is “radiated”.
  • Radiating near field: full beam power confined to a column about the antenna's size \(\rightarrow\) highest power density a person in front of the antenna meets.
  • Far field: \(S = P_tG/4\pi R^2\) falls with distance \(\rightarrow\) distance is the simplest protection (\(\S\)7.5).

column1: Types of electromagnetic radiation hazard (RADHAZ); HERP short note
column4:
HERP: to personnel
  • Harmful biological effects in humans.
  • Cause: thermal effect of absorbed energy (points 2 and 3 above).
  • Eg: eye lens exposed \(\rightarrow\) too little blood flow to cool it \(\rightarrow\) cataract.
  • Controlled by exposure limits (SAR, power density).
  • “Hazards of Electromagnetic Radiation to Personnel”.
HERO: to ordnance
  • RF induces current in the leads of electro-explosive devices (EEDs: detonators, squibs, airbag igniters, missile motors) \(\rightarrow\) premature firing.
  • Ordnance is more sensitive than people: no blood flow to shed heat.
  • But easier to protect: metal enclosures reflect the field.
  • A chain explosion is possible \(\rightarrow\) HERO limits are lower than personnel limits.
HERF: to fuel
  • RF-induced arcs ignite fuel vapour during refuelling near radar or radio transmitters.
  • Ignition likely for arcs above about 50 VA.
  • Rules (deck):
    • no transmitting from a vehicle or aircraft being fuelled, or the one beside it
    • no connecting or breaking cables or ground wires while fuelling
    • radar lighting the area at 5 W/cm\(^2\) peak: shut off
    • antennas of 250 W or less at least 50 ft from fuelling (500 W at sea)

column1: Define SAR. Discuss microwave radiation hazards based on SAR exposures; what is non-ionizing SAR
column4:
Definition
  • SAR = rate at which RF energy is absorbed per unit mass of body tissue, in W/kg. \[ \boxed{\mathrm{SAR} = \frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{dW}{dm}\right) = \frac{\sigma E^2}{\rho} = c\,\frac{dT}{dt}} \]
  • \(\sigma\) = tissue conductivity (S/m), \(E\) = rms field inside the tissue (V/m), \(\rho\) = mass density (kg/m\(^3\)), \(c\) = specific heat (J/kg K), \(dT/dt\) = initial temperature rise rate.
  • Correction: the deck prints the density unit as kg/m\(^2\); a mass density is kg/m\(^3\), which is what makes \(\sigma E^2/\rho\) come out in W/kg. verified/added
  • Non-ionizing SAR (81 Ba): SAR measures heating from non-ionizing RF. It is the dose quantity for RF the way absorbed dose (Gy) is for ionizing radiation.
Averaging and measurement
  • Whole-body SAR: total absorbed power / body mass.
  • Localized (peak spatial) SAR: averaged over any 1 g (FCC) or 10 g (ICNIRP, IEEE 2019) cube of tissue: the phone-against-head case.
  • Averaged over time (6 min in ICNIRP 1998).
  • Measured with a phantom head or body filled with tissue-simulating liquid: a robot moves an \(E\)-field probe through it (SAR \(= \sigma E^2/\rho\)), or a temperature probe logs \(dT/dt\) (SAR \(= c\,dT/dt\)).
  • Eg (ant.py): muscle at 900 MHz, \(\sigma \approx 0.94\) S/m, \(\rho \approx 1040\) kg/m\(^3\); \(E = 10\) V/m inside gives \(0.09\) W/kg.
Hazards based on SAR exposure (the 10-mark body)
Whole-body SAREffect and what the standards do with it
below 0.08 W/kgpublic limit. No established health effect.
0.4 W/kgoccupational limit for trained workers.
about 1 to 4 W/kgbody temperature rises up to about \(1^\circ\)C, thermoregulation (blood flow, sweat) copes in healthy adults.
4 W/kgthreshold: about \(1^\circ\)C core rise, animals show disrupted behaviour. With no heat loss, 4 W/kg warms tissue 1\(^\circ\)C in about 15 min (\(c \approx 3500\) J/kg K).
well above 4 W/kgheat stress, heat stroke; local hot spots burn tissue, cataract in poorly cooled lens.
  • Safety factors: threshold \(4 \xrightarrow{\div 10} 0.4\) (occupational) \(\xrightarrow{\div 5} 0.08\) W/kg (public). The student deck's “one-tenth of the observed threshold SAR (0.4 W/kg)” means the limit is 0.4; the threshold is 4. verified/added
  • Localized SAR limits: public 2 W/kg over 10 g head and trunk (ICNIRP, IEEE 2019), 1.6 W/kg over 1 g (FCC, US and India phones); workers 10 W/kg.
  • Mobile phones: SAR is declared by the maker (typically 0.2 to 1.6 W/kg). Using a hands-free kit or speaker cuts it sharply because the head leaves the reactive near field of the handset antenna.

column1: RF/MW radiation hazards and safety practices; list and describe five major RF safety practices
column4:
Five major practices (79 Ch)
  1. Time, distance, shielding:
    • cut exposure time
    • keep out of the main beam and out of the near field (power density \(\propto 1/R^2\))
    • metal panels or mesh, RF absorbers, Faraday enclosures
  2. Engineering controls:
    • safety interlocks that cut RF when a door or panel opens
    • RF gaskets, choke joints, oven door mesh
    • test into a dummy load, never an open waveguide
    • grounding straps not bent at sharp angles (they radiate)
  3. Administrative controls:
    • RF survey of the site, marked exclusion zones, warning signs (figure)
    • lockout / tagout before work on a tower or transmitter
    • never look into a live waveguide, horn or dish
    • training and exposure records
  4. Personal protective equipment: RF protective suit (stainless steel woven into fire-retardant fibre) for high-field areas; personal RF monitor that alarms.
  5. Regular inspection:
    • visual: housekeeping, interlocks present, high-voltage grounding rods, condition of cables and coax, RF shielding intact
    • operational: RF level survey in occupied spaces, interlock tests, lockout used properly
RF warning sign at an exclusion-zone boundary. KEC Ch-7 deck, slide 24.
More practices (deck)
  • Operate stray-RF sources (induction and dielectric heaters) remotely.
  • Keep workers below the recommended limits (\(\S\)7.4).
  • HERO: keep EEDs away from transmitters.
  • HERF: no RF devices in flammable atmospheres; fuelling rules of \(\S\)7.2.
  • RF-sensitive equipment and people with implants away from sources.
  • Switch equipment off when not in use.
  • Public: antennas high and beams tilted clear of rooftops; hands-free phones; awareness and school teaching.

column1: Choose a proper microwave measurement tool to test an antenna as a DUT; explain its working principle
column4:
Tool 1: vector network analyzer (VNA), port 1 to the antenna
  • Measures \(S_{11}\) vs frequency \(\rightarrow\) return loss, VSWR \(= (1 + |S_{11}|)/(1 - |S_{11}|)\), input impedance on a Smith chart, and the bandwidth where VSWR \(< 2\).
  • Working: internal source sweeps; directional couplers split incident and reflected waves; receivers compare amplitude and phase; calibration (short, open, load) removes cable and coupler errors. Detail in Ch 8.
Tool 2: anechoic chamber (pattern and gain)
  • Walls lined with RF absorber cones (no reflections). Known source horn at one end, antenna under test on a rotating positioner at the other.
  • Separation \(R > 2D^2/\lambda\) so the test is in the far field (\(\S\)7.1).
  • Rotate and record received power (VNA \(S_{21}\) or spectrum analyzer) \(\rightarrow\) radiation pattern, beamwidth, side lobes.
  • Gain: compare with a standard gain horn, or three-antenna method with Friis.

column1: Propagation characteristics: line of sight, atmosphere, ground and plasma effects
column4:
Line-of-sight (space wave)
  • Ground wave dies within a short range and the ionosphere does not reflect microwaves (they pass through) \(\rightarrow\) terrestrial links are LOS, satellites use the fact that they pass.
  • Radio horizon with \(k = 4/3\) earth (refraction bends the ray down): \(d \approx 4.12\sqrt{h}\) km, \(h\) in m. Two masts: \(d = 4.12(\sqrt{h_1} + \sqrt{h_2})\); 30 m and 50 m give 51.7 km.
  • Fresnel clearance: keep \(60\%\) of the first Fresnel zone \(r_1 = \sqrt{\lambda d_1 d_2/(d_1 + d_2)}\) clear of obstacles; 50 km hop at 6 GHz needs \(r_1 = 25\) m at mid-path.
  • Free-space path loss: \(L = 32.44 + 20\log d_{km} + 20\log f_{MHz}\) dB; Friis \(P_r = P_tG_tG_r(\lambda/4\pi d)^2\).
The refracted path bends down toward the earth, beyond the straight line-of-sight path: why the \(4/3\)-earth horizon is longer than the geometric one. Pozar Fig 14.28.
Atmosphere, ground and plasma effects
  • Gas absorption: water vapour peak at 22 GHz, oxygen at 60 GHz; little below 10 GHz. The 60 GHz peak suits short private links and satellite crosslinks.
  • Rain and fog: drops comparable to \(\lambda\) scatter and absorb \(\rightarrow\) rain fade, serious above about 10 GHz (Ku, Ka bands).
  • Refraction: ducting and super-refraction extend or bend paths \(\rightarrow\) fading and interference.
  • Ground effect: reflection off ground or water adds a second ray \(\rightarrow\) multipath fading; earth bulge blocks long hops.
  • Plasma effect: ionosphere rotates polarization (Faraday rotation) and causes scintillation at low GHz; the plasma sheath round a re-entering spacecraft blocks signals (blackout).
  • Diffraction round obstacles is weak at short \(\lambda\) \(\rightarrow\) shadowing behind buildings and hills.
Gaseous attenuation (dB/km) against frequency, at sea level and at 9150 m: the \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\) peak at 22 GHz, the \(\text{O}_2\) peak at 60 GHz, windows between them. Pozar Fig 14.29.

  • Both antennas are electrically small, so the near-field region is tiny: anyone more than a metre away is in the far field of either, and exposure there is set by power and distance (\(S = P_tG/4\pi R^2\)), not by zone.

column1: Chapter 8 — RF/Microwave Measurements: how is it examined?
column4:
6 hrs  \(\cdot\) asked in 22 of 24 papers  \(\cdot\) 9 syllabus sub-topics  \(\cdot\) 181 marks, 9.5% of the archive \(\rightarrow\) 149 of those 181 marks are power measurement, and the tool is picked by one number: how many milliwatts.
READ THIS FIRST
Chapter 8 is descriptive and it repeats harder than any other chapter: five short-note titles (bolometry, double-channel bolometer, circulating calorimetry, spectrum analyzer, VNA) and three long-answer shapes cover everything asked in 24 papers.
  1. “Choose a proper power measuring tool and explain its working principle” (72 Ma 7.5 mW, 74 Ma airport radar, 73 Bh, 82 Bh BTS) \(\rightarrow\) one table, \(\S\)8.2. Say which band the number falls in, name the sensor, then give that sensor's working principle from \(\S\)8.3 or \(\S\)8.5. The table is the mark.
  2. Calorimetry (9 papers) \(\rightarrow\) \(\S\)8.5. Static vs circulating, one formula each, and they are the same formula with \(m/t\) replaced by \(v\,d\).
  3. Bolometer bridge (9 papers) \(\rightarrow\) \(\S\)8.3. Barretter vs thermistor, single bridge, its two faults, double bridge that cures them.
Three things worth knowing before the paper starts:
  • Every microwave power meter is a substitution instrument. It never measures RF. It measures how much dc or low-frequency power had to be taken away to keep a bridge balanced, or how much a temperature rose. Open any power answer with that sentence.
  • The three bands are the whole decision: low \(<\) 10 mW, medium 10 mW to 10 W, high \(>\) 10 W. A radar is quoted in peak power, so convert with the duty cycle before choosing (\(\S\)8.2).
  • Measurement questions are worded as “describe how X and Y are measured”. X and Y are almost always VSWR meter and some power sensor, which is two separate answers glued together (72 Ash, 70 Bh).

column1: How are microwave measurements different from low-frequency measurements? List the major RF/MW measurement parameters
column4:
Why voltage and current stop being useful
  • At low frequency the circuit is lumped: \(V\) and \(I\) are the same everywhere in a wire, so measure them and compute \(Z\), power factor and phase angle.
  • At microwaves the line is distributed: \(V\) and \(I\) are functions of distance along the line, so a “the voltage” does not exist. In a waveguide there is no unique voltage at all.
  • Power is the invariant: on a lossless line the transmitted power is the same at every plane. So measure power, and get everything else from ratios of powers and from the standing-wave pattern.
  • Probes and leads are a significant fraction of a wavelength, so any contact instrument loads and detunes what it measures. Measurement is made by directional coupling and by sampling the field, not by touching nodes.
  • Circuit behaviour is described by S-parameters, which are themselves defined from travelling waves rather than terminal \(V\) and \(I\) (\(\S\)3.1).
  • Cost dodge used in every teaching laboratory: rather than process microwave signals directly, the source is 1 kHz square-wave modulated, the microwave signal is detected by a square-law crystal, and all the amplitude information is then read with an ordinary 1 kHz low-frequency amplifier, the VSWR meter.

column1: Choose a proper power measurement tool for the stated source and explain its working principle
column4:
• Power = energy dissipated or stored per unit time. At microwaves it is the average power that a sensor responds to: \[ P_{av} = \frac{1}{T}\int_0^T v(t)\,i(t)\,dt, \qquad P_{av} = P_{peak}\times \text{duty cycle}, \quad \text{duty} = \tau f_r = \tau/T \]
  • Unit: \(P(\mathrm{dBm}) = 10\log_{10}[P(\mathrm{mW})/1\,\mathrm{mW}]\), so 0 dBm = 1 mW, 30 dBm = 1 W, \(-30\) dBm = 1 \(\mu\)W.
The decision table: this is the answer to every “choose a tool” question
BandRangeSensor, and whySection
Low\(<\) 10 mWresistance changes with power: thermistor or barretter bolometer bridge (floor about \(-20\) dBm), Schottky diode detector (down to \(-70\) dBm = 100 pW), thermocouple sensor\(\S\)8.3, \(\S\)8.4
Medium10 mW to 10 Wthermistor bolometer behind a calibrated attenuator or 20 dB directional coupler; static or circulating calorimeter\(\S\)8.3, \(\S\)8.5
High\(>\) 10 Wtemperature changes with power: calorimeter (static for moderate, circulating / flow for kW), calorimetric wattmeter\(\S\)8.5
Measurement procedure, common to every power meter (the “zeroing” marks)
  1. Attach a calibrated sensor to the line port where the unknown power appears; connect it to the power meter.
  2. Turn the RF off and zero the meter (“zero setting”): this removes sensor self-heating and ambient drift from the reading.
  3. Turn the RF on. The sensor reacts, the meter reads, and the reading is by substitution: the dc or low-frequency power displaced, or the temperature rise.
  4. Correct for the coupler or attenuator in front of the sensor, and for the calibration factor (mismatch plus sensor efficiency).
The three PYQ cases worked (numbers checked in meas.py)
  • 72 Ma, “about 7.5 mW” 10: 7.5 mW \(=\) 8.75 dBm, below 10 mW, so low power. Answer: thermistor bolometer bridge, sensitivity floor about \(-20\) dBm \(=\) 0.01 mW, so 7.5 mW sits comfortably inside its range. Then give the bridge working principle (\(\S\)8.3). A Schottky diode sensor is the alternative.
  • 74 Ma, airport surveillance radar 8: a radar is quoted in peak power and is pulsed. Take a representative set, 1 MW peak, \(\tau = 1\ \mu\)s, PRF 1 kHz: duty \(= 10^{-3}\), so \(P_{av} = 1\) kW, which is high power. Answer: a circulating (flow) calorimeter on a dummy load, or a thermistor behind a high-directivity coupler plus a calibrated attenuator; report \(P_{peak} = P_{av}/\text{duty}\). Never put a bolometer directly in the line: it would burn out.
  • 73 Bh, “low microwave power measurement device” 8: name the parameters first (\(\S\)8.1), then the bolometer bridge in full.

column1: Explain the working principle of bolometry used in microwave measurements
column4:
• A bolometer is a power sensor whose resistance changes with temperature as it absorbs microwave power. RF energy is turned to heat inside the element, the element warms, its resistance moves, and that resistance change is read.
  • Bolometer impedances are 100 to 200 \(\Omega\). The mount provides a good impedance match, low loss, thermal and mechanical isolation and shielding against leakage.
  • Two types:
    • Barretter: a short thin metal wire (platinum or tungsten, like a fuse), positive temperature coefficient. More delicate, so used only for very low power, a few mW at most.
    • Thermistor: a semiconductor bead, negative temperature coefficient. Small, rugged, easily mounted in a waveguide or coaxial mount; the usual choice. Sensitivity floor about \(-20\) dBm.
Resistance vs temperature: thermistor falls (negative coefficient), barretter rises (positive). Karkee, Ch-8 deck slide 8.
  • Principle: the element sits in one arm of a Wheatstone bridge. With no RF, \(R_5\) is adjusted to balance the bridge. Incident microwave power heats the element, its resistance changes, the bridge unbalances, and the galvanometer or voltmeter current is calibrated directly in power.
  • Substitution: because the element responds only to total heating, the RF power is exactly the dc power that has to be withdrawn to restore balance. This is what makes it an absolute measurement rather than a comparison.
Bolometer mount in one arm of a Wheatstone bridge; the galvanometer current measures the incident power. Deck slide 9.
column5: HOT 6 70 Bh, 72 Ash, 72 Ma, 73 Bh, 79 Ch, 80 Ch  \(\cdot\) 79 Ch for 10 marks, 80 Ch as a 5 mark short note

column1: Single bridge, its two faults, and the double-channel (double bridge) cure
column4:
Single bridge
  • Balanced under zero incident power by adjusting \(R_5\); the bolometer arm is \(R_4\).
  • Microwave power into \(R_4\) changes its resistance, unbalances the bridge, and the non-zero output is read on a voltmeter calibrated in power.
  • With dc bias voltage \(E_1\) at balance and \(E_2\) after RF is applied, the change \((E_1 - E_2)\) is directly proportional to the microwave power.
  • Two faults (this is the whole of 80 Ba's 2 marks):
    1. A mismatch at the microwave input reflects power, so the element absorbs less than is incident: the reading is wrong and there is no way to tell.
    2. The thermistor is sensitive to ambient temperature: room drift is read as RF power. A false reading with no warning.
Self-balancing single bolometer bridge. Deck slide 10.
Double-channel bolometer bridge
  • Two identical bridges. The upper one carries the RF sensing thermistor and measures the power. The lower one carries a matched thermistor with no RF, exposed to the same ambient, and compensates temperature drift by forcing \(V_1 = V_2\).
  • The extra heating caused by mismatch is taken out automatically by negative dc feedback: the self-balancing loop lowers the dc power in the sensing thermistor until balance is restored, that is until the net resistance change is zero.
  • Zero setting: with no input, adjust \(E_1 = E_2 = E_0\). Without RF the dc voltage across the sensor at balance is \(E_1/2\); with RF it is \(E_2/2\).
  • Average input power is the dc power the RF displaced: \[ P_{av} = \frac{E_1^2}{4R} - \frac{E_2^2}{4R} = \frac{(E_1-E_2)(E_1+E_2)}{4R} \]
  • If ambient drift moves both rails by \(\Delta E\), \[ P_{av} + \Delta P = \frac{(E_1-E_2)(E_1-E_2+2\Delta E)}{4R} \] and since \(E_1 + E_2 \gg \Delta E\) in practice, \(\Delta P \approx 0\): the meter reads the line above. That inequality is why the second bridge works.
Double-channel bolometer bridge: upper bridge measures, lower bridge compensates ambient temperature. Deck slide 12.
  • Worked, to fix the formula (meas.py): \(R = 200\ \Omega\), \(E_1 = 6\) V, \(E_2 = 4\) V. Sensor dc power falls from 45 mW to 20 mW, so \(P_{av} = (36-16)/800 = \) 25 mW. A \(+50\) mV ambient drift on both rails would move a single bridge to 25.25 mW, an error of 1%, which the second bridge removes.

column1: Other low-power sensors: the square-law diode detector and the thermocouple
column4:
Schottky barrier diode detector
  • A zero-biased metal-semiconductor (point contact) diode used as a square-law detector: output is proportional to the square of the input voltage, therefore to input power.
  • RF input is applied to \(R_1\) and passes through \(R_2\); the diode rectifies, and the resulting low-frequency or dc current is read.
  • Sensitivity down to \(-70\) dBm (100 pW), up to about 18 GHz. It is the fastest and most sensitive of the low-power sensors.
  • The circuit is arranged so the input match does not depend on the diode resistance, which is a strong function of temperature.
  • Caution: it is square-law only over a limited range. Above roughly \(-20\) dBm it enters a transition region and eventually becomes linear, which is exactly why the VSWR meter misreads a high SWR (\(\S\)8.6).
Schottky barrier diode detector. Deck slide 6.
Thermocouple sensor
  • A thermocouple is a junction of two dissimilar metals or semiconductors (here n-type Si). A thin film of tantalum-nitride resistive load is deposited on a Si substrate and forms one electrode.
  • Microwaves are absorbed in the resistive load, heat one end of the junction more than the other, and the junction generates an emf proportional to incident power.
  • \(C_2\) is the RF bypass capacitor, \(C_1\) the input coupling capacitor (dc block). Emfs of the parallel thermocouples add across \(C_2\); the output leads are at RF ground, so the dc voltmeter reads pure dc.
  • For a square-wave modulated signal the peak power follows from the average: \(P_{peak} = P_{av}\,T/\tau\), \(T\) the period and \(\tau\) the pulse width. Same relation as the radar case in \(\S\)8.2.
  • Wider dynamic range and better match stability than a bolometer, and no dc bias, but no substitution: it must be calibrated.
Thermocouple power sensor. Deck slide 14.

column1: What is calorimetry in microwave? Explain how microwave power is measured with a static calorimeter
column4:
Calorimetry: the 2 mark definition
  • Calorimetry measures microwave power by converting it entirely into heat, absorbing that heat in a known medium, and measuring the medium's temperature rise. It is the standard method for medium and high power, and it is an absolute measurement: nothing is compared against a reference source, only against the specific heat of a fluid.
  • Two heating arrangements (both used with either calorimeter below):
    • Direct heating: the rate of heat production is found from the temperature rise of the dissipating medium itself.
    • Indirect heating: heat is transferred to another medium before it is measured.
Static (dry) calorimeter
  • A 50 \(\Omega\) coaxial line terminated in a lossy dielectric load with a high hysteresis loss, thermally isolated from its surroundings. No fluid circulates, hence “dry”.
  • The load dissipates all the microwave power; a thermometer or thermocouple reads the rise \(T\) of the thermometric medium over a time \(t\): \[ \boxed{P = \frac{4.187\, m\, C_p\, T}{t}\ \ \mathrm{watts}} \] \(m\) mass in grams, \(C_p\) specific heat in cal/g, \(T\) rise in \(^\circ\)C, \(t\) in seconds, and 4.187 is joules per calorie.
  • Where the formula comes from: \(m C_p T\) is the heat in calories, dividing by \(t\) makes it calories per second, and 4.187 converts to watts. Quote this and the formula cannot be mis-remembered.
  • Worked (meas.py): 100 g of water raised 5\(^\circ\)C in 60 s is \(4.187\times100\times1\times5/60 = \) 34.89 W.
  • Limits: slow (thermal inertia), and the load must stay isolated, so it suits steady medium power rather than a kilowatt transmitter.
Static calorimeter: RF into an isolated calorimetric body, compared against low-frequency power. Deck slide 18.

column1: Circulating (flow) calorimeter; circulating Vs flow calorimetry
column4:
• The calorimeter fluid (usually water) is pumped continuously through a water load in the waveguide. Microwave power heats it in transit, so the outlet temperature \(T_2\) exceeds the inlet \(T_1\): \[ \boxed{P = 4.187\, v\, d\, C_p\,(T_2 - T_1)\ \ \mathrm{watts}} \] \(v\) flow rate in cc/s, \(d\) specific gravity in g/cc, \(C_p\) specific heat in cal/g.
  • Same law as the static one: \(v\,d\) is grams per second, which is the static formula's \(m/t\). Confirmed in meas.py.
  • Worked: 10 cc/s of water with a 2\(^\circ\)C rise is 83.7 W. To take 1 kW with a 10\(^\circ\)C rise needs 23.9 cc/s.
  • Instrumentation: pump, flow meter, glass tube through the guide, inlet and outlet thermocouples, heat exchanger to return the water cool.
Circulating (flow) calorimeter: water load, pump, flow meter, inlet and outlet thermometers. Deck slide 19.

Answer the question that is meant, which is static vs circulating, and say so in one line: if a distinction is forced, circulating returns the same fluid round a closed loop through a heat exchanger, while a plain flow calorimeter passes fluid once and discards it.

column1: Power measurement using a calorimeter wattmeter
column4:
• A calorimeter run as a self-balancing comparison bridge, so the answer comes out as a meter reading instead of a temperature calculation.
  • The unknown RF power is checked against a 1200 cps (Hz) comparison power in a bridge circuit. Two temperature-sensitive resistors serve as gauges.
  • Operation:
    1. The unknown RF heats an input load resistor.
    2. That resistor and one gauge sit in close thermal contact, so the gauge warms and unbalances the bridge.
    3. The unbalance signal is amplified and applied to the comparison load resistor, which is next to the second gauge, and rebalances the bridge.
    4. The meter reads the power supplied to the comparison load, which at balance equals the unknown RF power.
  • Both loads and gauges are immersed in an oil stream for efficient, equal heat transfer.
  • Why it is better than a bare calorimeter: it is a null method, so gauge calibration and ambient drift cancel, and it reads continuously.
Calorimetric wattmeter: input load and comparison load, two temperature gauges, 1200 cps comparison power, oil stream. Deck slide 20.
column5: PIN 1 80 Ba  \(\cdot\) paired with the single-bridge limitations of \(\S\)8.3
column7: 8.5 Calorimetric Methods

column1: Describe how standing waves and microwave power are measured with a VSWR meter
column4:
Slotted line carriage: where the standing wave is seen
  • A coaxial E-field probe penetrates a rectangular waveguide (or coaxial line) through a longitudinal slot cut in the centre of the broad wall, over 2 to 3 wavelengths.
  • The slot lies where the wall current has no transverse component, so cutting it does not disturb the field. Both ends are tapered to zero width to reduce discontinuity, and the probe is thin and shallow for the same reason.
Slotted-line carriage: longitudinal slot on the broad wall, probe, crystal detector, vernier scale. Deck slide 22.
  • The carriage moves the probe along the slot at constant depth, so coupling is uniform, and a vernier scale reads its position. It carries a tunable stub and a crystal detector, whose 1 kHz output goes to the VSWR meter.
  • It measures: standing-wave pattern and VSWR, wavelength (\(\lambda_g = 2\times\) distance between successive minima), and by the minima-shift method impedance, reflection coefficient and return loss (\(\S\)8.7).
The pattern the probe traces: maxima and minima \(\lambda_g/2\) apart, each minimum \(\lambda_g/4\) from its neighbouring maximum. Deck slide 27.
VSWR meter
  • A high-gain, high-\(Q\), low-noise voltage amplifier tuned to a fixed 1 kHz, the frequency at which the microwave source is square-wave modulated. Overall gain about 125 dB, switchable in 10 dB steps.
  • Input is the detected output of the crystal detector; output goes to a square-law calibrated voltmeter, which therefore reads \(V_{max}/V_{min}\) directly once it has been set to 1.0 at a maximum.
  • Procedure (low VSWR):
    1. Set the attenuator to about 10 dB, tune the probe stub for maximum reading.
    2. Slide the carriage to a maximum and adjust the gain until the meter reads 1.0 (0 dB).
    3. Move to the adjacent minimum. The meter now reads \(S\) directly.
  • Three scales: SWR NORMAL top (1 to 4), SWR NORMAL bottom (3.2 to 10), EXPANDED (1 to 1.3) for a nearly matched load, plus a dB scale. For \(S\) between 10 and 40 increase sensitivity by 20 dB, read on the 1 to 4 scale and multiply by 10.
1 kHz modulation, mixer, amplifier, detector: the meter reads \(V_{max}/V_{min}\). Deck slide 31.
Low-VSWR bench: source, attenuator, slotted line, crystal detector, power meter. Deck slide 28.
