column1: How is the VSWR of a microwave transmitter measured when VSWR \(>\) 10?
column4:
• Why the direct reading fails. With \(S > 10\) the gap between \(V_{max}\) and \(V_{min}\) is large. To read \(V_{max}\) the detector is driven out of its square-law region (diode current past about 20 mA, response turning linear), while at \(V_{min}\) it is in the noise. A meter calibrated on \(I = kV^2\) is then simply wrong, and the error grows with \(S\).
  • The cure: never look at the maximum. Take two readings either side of a single minimum, where the level is low and the detector is safely square-law. This is the double-minimum method.
  • Procedure:
    1. Terminate the line with the load and find a voltage minimum on the slotted line; note its position and meter reading.
    2. Move the probe either side until the detected power is twice the minimum (voltage \(\sqrt2\,V_{min}\)). Record the two positions \(d_1\) and \(d_2\); \(\Delta x = d_2 - d_1\).
    3. Short the line and measure \(\lambda_g\) as twice the distance between two successive minima.
    4. Compute \(S\).
The two “twice minimum power” points either side of a minimum, \(\Delta x = d_2 - d_1\). Deck slide 29.
  • The formula, and where it comes from. Near a minimum the detected quantity is \(|V|^2 = V_{min}^2 + (V_{max}^2 - V_{min}^2)\sin^2\beta\delta\) with \(\delta\) measured from the minimum. Setting \(|V|^2 = 2V_{min}^2\) gives \((S^2-1)\sin^2\beta\delta = 1\), so with \(\Delta x = 2\delta\) and \(\beta = 2\pi/\lambda_g\): \[ \boxed{S = \sqrt{1 + \frac{1}{\sin^2(\pi\Delta x/\lambda_g)}}} \qquad\longrightarrow\qquad S \approx \frac{\lambda_g}{\pi\,\Delta x} \ \ \text{for large } S \]
  • Both forms verified in meas.py against a simulated standing wave: at \(S = 25\) the exact form returns 25.00 and the short form 24.97 (0.12% error); at \(S = 60\), 0.04%. The short form is only for large \(S\): at \(S = 2\) it returns 1.63, 19% out, which is precisely why the direct method is used there instead.
  • Threshold: the deck sets the changeover at \(S > 10\) (which is the wording of 79 Bh), Das at \(S > 20\). Say “above about 10, where the detector leaves its square-law region” and the distinction never matters.

column1: Measurement of an unknown load, of reflection coefficient, and of frequency
column4:
Unknown impedance from the slotted line (minima-shift method)
  • Impedance is complex, so two numbers are needed: the slotted line supplies \(S\) (giving \(|\Gamma|\)) and \(d_{min}\) (giving the phase).
  • Set-up 1: load connected, measure \(S\) and the position of the first minimum. Set-up 2: replace the load with a short, which puts a minimum at the load plane, and measure the shift.
  • Shift towards the generator means the load is capacitive; shift towards the load means inductive.
  • The relations: \[ \rho = \frac{S-1}{S+1},\quad \phi_L = 2\beta d_{min} - \pi,\quad \beta = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda_g},\quad Z_L = Z_0\frac{1+\Gamma}{1-\Gamma} \] with \(\lambda_g = 2\times\)(distance between successive minima), \(\Gamma=\rho e^{j\phi_L}\).
  • Equivalent closed form, useful when no chart is at hand, \(t = \tan\beta d_{min}\): \[ Z_L = Z_0\,\frac{1 - jSt}{S - jt} \]
  • Both routes checked in meas.py: a simulated pattern from \(Z_L = 60 - j80\) on a 50 \(\Omega\) line is inverted back to \(60 - j80\) by each.
  • On the Smith chart: draw the \(S\) circle, start at the short-circuit point and move towards the load by \(d_{min}/\lambda_g\); the intersection is \(z_L\).
The two set-ups: unknown load, then shorted termination. Deck slide 24.
Reflectometer: two 20 dB directional couplers sample forward and reverse waves. Deck slide 26.
Reflectometer: \(|\Gamma|\) without a slotted line
  • Two directional couplers face opposite ways: the first samples the forward wave at port 4, the second the reverse wave at port 3.
  • With coupling \(C \ll 1\) the ratio of the two detected outputs is the reflection coefficient itself: \[ \left|\frac{b_3}{b_4}\right| = \sqrt{1-C^2}\,|\Gamma_L| \approx |\Gamma_L| \]
  • Calibrate by shorting port 2 (\(|\Gamma| = 1\)) and setting the meter to unity, then connect the load. Everything else follows: \[ \mathrm{VSWR} = \frac{1+|\Gamma_L|}{1-|\Gamma_L|}, \qquad \mathrm{RL(dB)} = -20\log_{10}|\Gamma_L| \]
  • Broadband and fast, but accuracy is set by coupler directivity, so it suits low VSWR; a high SWR still wants the slotted line.
  • Related loss family, all measured the same way: insertion loss \(=\) reflection loss \(+\) attenuation loss, with reflection loss \(=-10\log(1-|\Gamma|^2) = -10\log[4S/(1+S)^2]\). Return loss compares \(P_r\) with \(P_i\); insertion loss compares \(P_0\) with \(P_i\) (\(\S\)3.4).
Frequency measurement
  • Cavity (absorption) wavemeter: a cylindrical cavity with a variable short, coupled to the guide through a hole in the narrow wall. Tuning the plunger changes the resonant frequency; at resonance the cavity absorbs, and the power meter downstream shows a dip. The plunger scale is calibrated in frequency.
    • \(TE_{011}\) has the highest \(Q\) and no axial current, but it is a higher-order mode, so practical wavemeters use the dominant \(TM_{010}\), excited by magnetic coupling. Polytron absorber behind the plunger stops oscillation above it.
    • Accuracy follows \(Q\): 1% at \(Q = 1000\), 0.005% at \(Q = 50\,000\).
  • Slotted line: short the guide, measure \(\lambda_g\) as twice the minima spacing, then \[ \frac{1}{\lambda^2} = \frac{1}{\lambda_g^2} + \frac{1}{\lambda_c^2}, \qquad f = \frac{c}{\lambda},\qquad \lambda_c = 2a\ (TE_{10}) \] Worked (meas.py): WR-90 (\(a = 2.286\) cm) with \(\lambda_g = 4.00\) cm gives 9.96 GHz.
  • Frequency counter with a down-conversion front end: the unknown is mixed with a selected harmonic \(nf_1\) of a known oscillator, and the counter reads \(f_x = \) counter \(+ nf_1\). Direct and most accurate.

column1: Spectrum analyzer (short note): working principle and block diagram
column4:
• A swept-tuned superheterodyne receiver that plots amplitude against frequency: frequency on the horizontal axis, amplitude on the vertical. It shows what an oscilloscope cannot, namely the signal spectrum.
  • Working:
    1. The input microwave signal is mixed with a local oscillator swept electronically between two limits at a linear rate by a sawtooth sweep voltage.
    2. The difference product is amplified by a narrow-bandwidth IF amplifier, then detected and video amplified.
    3. The same sawtooth drives the horizontal deflection, with zero flyback time, so horizontal position tracks the LO frequency while the detected amplitude gives vertical deflection.
Block diagram: mixer, swept local oscillator, narrow-band IF amplifier, detector, video amplifier, display. Deck slide 33.
  • Measures: carrier power, harmonics, spurious products, sidebands, phase noise, occupied bandwidth; on a modern analyzer, demodulated WLAN, GSM or LTE signals.
  • Four design parameters: sweep rate, sweep range, IF bandwidth, IF centre frequency.
  • Resolution is the IF bandwidth (RBW). Narrow RBW resolves closer tones but needs a slower sweep, because the IF filter must have time to settle: sweep time rises as \(1/\mathrm{RBW}^2\). Keep the span as small as the measurement allows.
  • Image response: any signal \(f_i = f_0 \pm f_{IF} = f_s \pm 2f_{IF}\) also beats to the IF. Choose \(f_{IF}\) high to push the image out of band. Worked: \(f_{IF} = 450\) kHz puts the image 900 kHz from the signal; \(f_{IF} = 2\) MHz moves it to 4 MHz away, easily filtered (meas.py).
  • Types: swept-tuned (superheterodyne), FFT, real-time, audio.

column1: Describe the working principle of a network analyzer; VNA (short note)
column4:
Why it exists, and how it works
  • The slotted line measures amplitude and phase one frequency at a time, so broadband testing with it is slow and expensive. A network analyzer measures both over a wide band in a reasonable time.
  • Principle: everything is measured against a reference.
    1. A sweep oscillator feeds a power divider, splitting the signal into a test channel and a reference channel.
    2. The test signal passes through the DUT; the reference passes through a phase-equalising length of line.
    3. Microwave frequencies cannot be processed directly, so a harmonic frequency converter brings both to a fixed IF. A phase-locked loop makes the local oscillator track the reference channel, which is what allows a swept measurement.
    4. Conversion is in two steps, RF to an MHz IF, then to a kHz IF, where the magnitude and phase comparators compare test against reference.
  • Reflection and transmission are separated by a test unit built from dual directional couplers: \(S_{11}\) and \(S_{21}\) from one direction, then source and load are interchanged for \(S_{22}\) and \(S_{12}\). Each \(S_{ij}\) is a ratio of a coupler output to the reference, with the phase as the difference \(\phi_j - \phi_i\).
  • Two types: SNA (scalar) measures amplitude only; VNA (vector) measures amplitude and phase, so it can apply vector error correction and is far more accurate.
VNA: DUT alters the reference in magnitude (resistive) and phase (reactive); two comparators output the magnitude and phase vectors. Deck slide 36.

column4:
• The model: a black box with two ports, port 1 \((V_1, I_1)\) and port 2 \((V_2, I_2)\), both currents taken as flowing into the box. Any two of the four are independent, which is what gives the six standard parameter sets.

\(S\) (scattering)\(b_1 = S_{11}a_1 + S_{12}a_2\), \(b_2 = S_{21}a_1 + S_{22}a_2\)\(S_{11} = b_1/a_1|_{a_2=0}\)matched \(Z_0\) termination
  • Why \(S\) at microwaves (the same argument as \(\S\)3.1, and the reason this question sits in the measurements chapter): \(Z\), \(Y\), \(h\) and \(ABCD\) all need a short or open circuit at a port. At microwaves a short is not a short (lead inductance), an open radiates, and both are frequency dependent and may destabilise an active device. A matched load is realisable at every frequency, and \(a\), \(b\) are travelling-wave quantities that a directional coupler can sample: that is exactly what the network analyzer above does, which is why \(S\)-parameters are the set that can actually be measured.
  • Reciprocity \(S_{12} = S_{21}\), losslessness \([S]^\dagger[S] = [I]\), matched \(S_{ii} = 0\); conversions to and from \(Z\) exist, \([S] = ([Z]-[I])([Z]+[I])^{-1}\) for \(Z\) normalised to \(Z_0\) (\(\S\)3.2).
Noise figure measurement syllabus 8.9, never asked
  • Y-factor method: drive the DUT with a calibrated noise source that switches between hot and cold. \(Y\) is the ratio of the two output powers, and with the source's excess noise ratio: \[ F = \frac{\mathrm{ENR}}{Y-1}, \qquad T_e = \frac{T_h - YT_c}{Y-1}, \qquad F = 1 + \frac{T_e}{T_0} \]
  • Worked (meas.py): ENR 15 dB with \(Y = 10\) dB gives \(F = 3.51\), i.e. 5.46 dB, equivalently \(T_e = 729\) K. The floor any such measurement sits on is \(kT_0 = -174\) dBm/Hz.

column1: Working principle of a microwave measuring device to map the radiation zones around a GSM BTS
column4:
• The instrument: a broadband EMF survey meter (field-strength meter), which is a calibrated probe plus a display, usually backed by a spectrum analyzer when the individual operators' carriers must be separated.
  • Probe: an isotropic (three-axis) probe, three mutually perpendicular dipoles (E field) or loops (H field) whose outputs are squared and summed, so the reading does not depend on how the probe is held. Diode or thermocouple detection, high-resistance leads so the cable does not perturb the field.
  • Why both E and H must be measured in the near field: only in the far field is \(E/H = 377\ \Omega\) and \(S = E^2/377\). Closer in, the ratio is not fixed, so the two are measured separately and compared against separate limits (\(\S\)7.1).
  • Working principle: the probe dipoles develop a voltage proportional to the field; a square-law diode detector gives a dc output proportional to power density; high-resistance lines carry it to a meter calibrated in V/m, A/m or W/m\(^2\).
  • Procedure: zero the meter with the transmitter off, then walk a radial grid out from the tower at a fixed height, log position with GPS, and plot contours. Compare each contour with the ICNIRP or FCC limit for that frequency, and mark the compliance boundary.
  • Worked (meas.py, same formulas as \(\S\)7.1): a 1.3 m panel at 1800 MHz has \(\lambda = 16.7\) cm, so the reactive near field ends at \(0.62\sqrt{D^3/\lambda} = \) 2.25 m and the far field starts at \(2D^2/\lambda = \) 20.3 m. With 20 W into a 17 dBi sector, \(S\) at 50 m is 0.032 W/m\(^2\), against the ICNIRP public limit of \(f/200 = \) 9 W/m\(^2\): a margin of about 280 times.
  • Related ask: 74 Bh's “antenna as a DUT, choose a measurement tool” 8 wants a VNA instead (\(\S\)8.9): return loss and \(S_{11}\) give the match and bandwidth, and an anechoic range gives the pattern. It is filed in \(\S\)7.8.
